item.title: COP31 climate talks break down as EU and others reject deal
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: substance, learning value, freshness

U.N. climate talks fell into disarray on Sunday as the European Union and others rejected a final draft deal put forward by COP31 presidents Turkey and Australia, saying it was too weak to advance the fight against global warming.

After more than two weeks of negotiations, which had been due to end on Friday but stretched into the weekend, Turkey's COP31 President Murat Kurum said at the closing plenary that a deal was not approved.

"It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognize that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted," he said.

The last time UN climate talks failed to end with a deal adopted by all was in Copenhagen in 2009.

This time, the collapse comes against the backdrop of competing crises, including wars and public outcry over the cost of living, that have overshadowed the problems caused by a warming climate.

Ireland's environment minister Darragh O'Brien said the European Union could not support the proposed deal, in part because it made no mention of the fossil fuels that scientists say are driving global warming.

"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel, no reference to transitioning away from fossil fuels," he said.

Panama also said it could not support the current text because it fails to meet the scale of the climate crisis.

This year's COP is the first since the UN's environmental body in October that confirmed the rise in global temperature was set to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), a threshold countries agreed at Paris climate talks over a decade ago to try not to exceed, and beyond which extreme weather impacts intensify.

Pressure from Saudi Arabia and other oil producers

The proposed deal had acknowledged the overshoot, but called for faster development of carbon-removal technologies to eventually reverse it.

Observers at the venue said Saudi Arabia and other major oil-producing nations had pushed hard in negotiations to keep explicit mention of fossil fuels out of the text and carbon removal technologies in.

While scientists say removing carbon from the atmosphere—when paired with steep emissions cuts—is vital to avoiding the worst impacts of climate change, critics of the deal said they worry the carbon removal language would be used as a license to keep pumping oil.

A representative for the Saudi delegation told the summit he was surprised at the resistance to technology.

"If indeed the climate challenge, as some have mentioned today, is so important, it makes no sense that solutions, concrete solutions... will be taken off the table," he said.

The COP process is the main vehicle through which countries coordinate their efforts to curb global warming. Its annual summit gives nations an opportunity to signal they are willing to work together to find solutions and help finance the problems rising temperatures cause.

While a blow to efforts to ratchet up international action, the failure to agree on a political declaration in Antalya does not erase the obligations agreed by previous summits or remove the technical and legal frameworks governing multilateral action against climate change.

Source: CNBC Top | Published: 2026-11-22 14:13 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/22/cop31-climate-talks-break-down-as-eu-and-others-reject-deal.html

item.title: Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: substance, learning value

Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory

At least three people have been killed after a fire at a confectionery factory in western Java on Saturday, with the death toll expected to rise.

Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for around 36 missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.

Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.

Rescuers recovered 24 body bags from the fire as of Sunday evening, as search operations continue to locate missing people.

Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire on Saturday evening.

The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km (31km) west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.

Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.

Local media reported that the search had been called off for the night late on Sunday, and would resume on Monday.

"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.

Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP.

Firefighters had been called to the building at 16:30 local time (09:30 GMT) on Saturday - but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz.

"When we arrived (on location)... a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company's protection system was functioning properly or not," he said.

The factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, according to search and rescue authorities.

On LinkedIn the company describes itself as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.

item.title: Experts say ‘trusted messengers’ critical as Amish grapple with measles outbreak
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: substance, learning value

Tristan Sharratt, a family nurse practitioner and public health researcher, began serving an Amish community in central New York almost inadvertently. A friend told an Amish neighbor that Sharratt was accepting new patients and was a good, solid guy. Word spread quickly, and now Sharratt sees many members of the community, which numbers in the hundreds.

He is what is called a “trusted messenger” – someone who understands a community and has earned their respect. Other trusted messengers can be neighbors, co-workers, customers, midwives, or people who work as long-distance drivers for the Amish. Connecting with such people will be crucial for ending the measles outbreak and preventing future crises.

“We can’t build trust with these communities just dropping in and being like, ‘Hey, there’s a measles outbreak. You should get vaccinated.’ Trust-building with these communities takes months to years,” Sharratt said. “This is a hard lesson and a tremendous opportunity to start building connections with these communities, because that is what it’s going to take to prevent the next situation like this.”

The unfolding measles outbreak, which has killed at least eight people in Pennsylvania, two in Wisconsin, one in New York, and one in Virginia, also demonstrates the importance of funding public health long-term – for everything from water fluoridation to road safety, said Sharratt, who is also a clinical lecturer of nursing and public health at Binghamton University.

“There’s just this enormous amount of work to be done,” he said.

Measles has raged through communities of Plain Anabaptists – including Amish and Mennonites – in this and previous outbreaks, and they are “emblematic” of many rural communities that have not been reached well by public health, Sharratt said.

“We haven’t invested in rural communities in a long time from a public health perspective,” Sharratt said, “and we’re really seeing the consequences with this outbreak.”

A central belief for the Amish is Gelassenheit, which essentially means “God’s will” – the idea that one’s life belongs to God; both joy and suffering are God’s will. “Part of my conversations with them is trying to determine why scientific advancements don’t fit into the perspective of God’s will,” Sharratt said. “Why is it not God’s will that scientists have developed the technology to [prevent measles]?”

Being unvaccinated in Plain Anabaptist communities is usually “an outcome of this whole idea of plain living”, Sharratt said. But the work of anti-vaccine activists accelerated alongside the Covid pandemic, and “unfortunately it has started to creep in” to Amish communities as well, Sharratt said. Non-Amish anti-vaccine groups such as Children’s Health Defense – then led by Robert F Kennedy Jr, now the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services – held events and wrote articles for Plain Anabaptist publications, overtly targeting the communities with vaccine misinformation.

Amish life centers around community, and so should efforts to reach them.

“Human connection really should be at the center,” Sharratt said. “You really just have to approach these people as people, build relationships as peers first, and then be there when they’re ready to talk to you or ask your opinion about these health issues.”

Inroads to Amish communities are frequently informal. “Maybe the associate public health director just happens to drive by the Amish farm every day and buy something from the vegetable stand – it can be as simple as that,” Sharratt said. Business owners and contractors can be a good way to connect.

“The Amish will work as subcontractors, and then all of a sudden you’re working next to Amos on the build site, and you’re there for eight hours together doing rough carpentry, and you have the chance to talk,” he said. “Maybe you go to an Amish family’s bake stand every Saturday to get the pie, and you just happen to run into them and build a relationship.”

There are local health departments that have done a great job of building connections – Sharratt pointed to the Otsego county health department, which developed a strong relationship with two Amish communities two decades ago during a pertussis outbreak; they continue to run vaccine clinics three to four times a year with those communities.

Often, however, health departments might know where a Plain Anabaptist community is, but they might not know how many people live there, how many children there are, or what the vaccination rate is.

“We have a huge data problem with these communities,” Sharratt said. “That requires going back to old methods of epidemiology, of community public health.” And public health at the national and state level hasn’t been as focused on community-building, he said.

Many Amish people want access to modern medicine when they need it – but access is frequently a challenge. Most Amish communities participate in some version of community insurance, where everyone chips in to cover healthcare costs. But typically providers accept conventional insurance; even those who negotiate lower prices with uninsured patients may be cost-prohibitive – especially as medicine is more corporatized and profit-driven, Sharratt said. That means communities often end up with providers who may not be as locked into conventional medicine.

It’s important to note that one Amish community is one Amish community; each makes unique decisions about healthcare, he said. “It’s not as simple as saying, ‘OK, here’s the strategy for all Amish communities in New York state.’ You need to approach every single one as a unique entity.” And there may be variability even within the communities, with some families seeking out vaccines despite anti-vax perspectives from community leaders.…

Source: The Guardian World | Published: 2026-11-22 14:00 UTC | Difficulty: 40/100

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/22/measles-amish-outbreak

item.title: What next for Iraq’s push against militias following Jurf al-Sakhar deal?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: substance, learning value

What next for Iraq’s push against militias following Jurf al-Sakhar deal?

Thursday’s Iran-brokered compromise may bode poorly for Baghdad’s attempt to curb militia influence.

The entry of Iraqi government forces into Jurf al-Sakhar, a town 60km (37 miles) southwest of Baghdad long held by the Iran-backed armed group Kataib Hezbollah, has raised questions about the future of Iraqi militias in the country.

A deal reached between Iraqi authorities and Kataib Hezbollah about control of Jurf al-Sakhar, where oil smuggling was allegedly taking place, staved off a potential confrontation between the two sides.

It is the latest episode in Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s push to assert federal government control over the country and crack down on corruption, which is allegedly funding pro-Iran militias.

So how does Thursday’s compromise bode for the Iraqi state’s mission to rein in militias and weapons outside its control?

What happened at Jurf al-Sakhar?

Kataib Hezbollah seized Jurf al-Sakhar from ISIL (ISIS) in 2014, renaming it Jurf al-Nasr (“victory”). For the 12 years since then, it has prevented state authorities from re-establishing control and allegedly siphoned oil from local pipelines.

After an intelligence report was released this week about oil smuggling in Jurf al-Sakhar, the government formed a high-level committee to investigate the issue.

After an anti-corruption crackdown was announced, al-Zaidi then gave Kataib Hezbollah until Friday to withdraw from the town. A compromise deal was reached a day before the due date, with government forces entering Jurf al-Sakhar and establishing a joint operations centre in the town. This should see the gradual withdrawal of Kataib Hezbollah units and the phased deployment of an army brigade, a federal police brigade, an energy police regiment and two brigades from the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) to the town.

The compromise reportedly came after direct Iranian intervention brokered by Esmail Qaani, head of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) elite Quds Force, which once joined the PMF on the front lines against ISIL and maintains deep ties with several of Iraq’s militias.

Why is Baghdad moving against militias?

PM al-Zaidi, a businessman with a Shia background, took power in May, vowing to end corruption and the fragmentation of the country’s security landscape.

Initially, he set a deadline of September 30 for militias to place their weapons under state control, coinciding with the withdrawal of US and allied forces from Iraq. While US forces withdrew, the militias refused to comply, and the deadline was pushed to June 2027.

Of major concern to Baghdad is the use of Iraq by armed groups to launch unauthorised attacks at Iran’s behest. Since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, several Iraqi militias have pledged to support Iran’s war effort. Baghdad has acknowledged that attacks targeting neighbours have been launched from its territory and has vowed to put an end to them.

Akeel Abbas, an expert in Iraqi affairs, said Baghdad was the reason for the government’s intervention in Jurf al-Sakhar, not the issue of oil smuggling.

“This area, which the state could not enter since 2014, did actually participate in Iran’s war effort, bombing Gulf countries, bombing US interests in Iraq,” he told Al Jazeera.

“There are other areas, but this one is the strongest, most fortified, and the best weaponry is stored there.”

In July, after Iran-aligned militias attacked Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, the United States and Saudi Arabia launched retaliatory strikes against PMF targets across Iraq, killing at least 20 personnel and drawing condemnation from Baghdad.

By establishing a presence in Jurf al-Sakhr, once the site of former President Saddam Hussein’s military-industrial complex, Baghdad signalled to the US that it was removing it as a potential target.

What next?

Zeidon Alkinani, founding director of the Doha-based Arab Perspectives Institute, said the deal over Jurf al-Sakhar was a positive step, especially as it was secured through negotiation and not armed confrontation.

“The remaining questions are how long this will take and what the armed groups will want in return,” he told Al Jazeera. Kataib Hezbollah may also retain its influence in the area through PMF units, with the process of deployment likely to take weeks to complete.

“How the next phases go will determine whether this becomes a real return of state authority or just a rearrangement of who controls the area,” Alkinani said.

Tallha Abdulrazaq, an Iraq expert and strategy and security consultant, said that the deal was compromised by the presence of militia and pro-militia personnel in the security contingent sent by Baghdad.

“Effectively, we’re changing Shia militias for Shia militias, but in uniform,” he said. “There has been no announcement about them being disarmed and their missile and drone manufacturing facilities set up with Iranian expertise being dismantled.”

Where did Iraq’s militias come from?

Iran-backed armed groups have become some of the most powerful actors in Iraq since the US-led invasion of Iraq overthrew President Saddam Hussein’s government in 2003.

Some of Iraq’s most influential militias – like Kataib Hezbollah and Asa’ib Ahl al-Haq – found their genesis in the resistance to US occupation, many with the alleged support of Iran.

Others were formed in response to the threat posed by ISIL after a fatwa was issued by leading Iraqi Shia cleric Ali al-Sistani, fighting under the banner of the PMF.

The PMF are a recognised component of Iraq’s security forces, granting the militias semiofficial status. However, some Iraqi militias, such as Kataib Hezbollah, still operate outside the framework of the state and have been accused of undermining the government’s legitimacy.…

Source: Al Jazeera | Published: 2026-11-22 14:00 UTC | Difficulty: 40/100

Original link: https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/22/what-next-for-iraqs-push-against-militias-following-jurf-al-sakhar-deal?traffic_source=rss

item.title: Australia urged to wean off imported fossil fuels amid global supply shocks
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: substance, learning value

Capping lucrative diesel tax handouts to big business, building new “clean” refineries and targeting electric vehicle subsidies to less wealthy people could save Australians thousands of dollars in fuel per year, according to a major new report calling on the government to reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels.

The Grattan Institute, one of the nation’s most respected thinktanks, has warned Australia imports too much of its fuel, and that the country must brace for more global supply shocks – like that from the war in Iran. Under a plan already attracting criticism from business groups, Grattan urged diesel handouts to mining and primary industries be curbed in favour of incentives for electric trucks and a huge expansion of the EV charging network.

“Relying on fuel imports during an era of benign international relations and dependable strategic partners was a passable strategy. But in a more dangerous and unpredictable world, it is no longer tenable,” the report, released on Sunday, warned.

“Australia should expect the coming decades to be less stable than the past one. This means bracing, and preparing, for more oil shocks.”

Australia imports 97% of its liquid fuel. Grattan’s fuel plan report, Fuelling the Future, warns this “leaves us dangerously exposed to supply disruptions and price hikes”.

It argues that the US-Israel war in Iran has driven up inflation and cost Australians nearly $18bn, and the federal government directly at least $3bn, creating an opportunity the government “should seize” to boost fuel security.

Very little liquid fuel is produced or refined in Australia, with only two domestic oil refineries. But rather than boosting that number, Grattan says Australia should lower its reliance on imported fuels and fossil fuels generally by shifting towards EVs, including an ambitious target of 650,000 electric trucks nationwide by 2050.

That alone would cut Australia’s diesel use by 5bn litres a year, Grattan forecast. The report also calls for the fuel tax credit program – which costs Australia billions each year – to be capped at $35m per corporate group annually.

The biggest user of that program – which refunds taxes on fuel for machinery and heavy vehicles travelling on private, rather than public, roads – is the mining sector. The fuel tax credit scheme has become a political hot-button issue, with big business campaigning for it to be preserved amid calls for it to be reined in.

Tania Constable, CEO of the Minerals Council of Australia, rejected the Grattan proposal.

“Australia does need stronger fuel security, but making diesel more expensive for regional industries won’t create a single extra litre of fuel, build a refinery or improve supply-chain resilience. Instead, it would increase costs for miners, farmers, freight operators and regional businesses, with those costs ultimately flowing through to Australian households,” she said.

“If the goal is greater energy security, then Australia should be focused on increasing domestic production, expanding refining capacity and building more resilient supply chains – not making essential fuel more expensive.”

But the Grattan report says capping the scheme would save the government $3bn annually, and hasten the electrification of the mining sector – which it said would help the mining sector in the long run.

The report also recommends the government invest $1.1bn in a national network of chargers for EVs, as well as provide $2.4bn in vouchers for trucking firms to buy electric trucks. It calls for federal vehicle standards to be boosted to incentivise cleaner cars, as well as a restructuring of EV subsidies “to target people least able to afford them”.

Labor is widely expected to restrict current EV subsidies in next month’s mid-year economic update, as the government searches for budget savings.

In other areas of fuel use, Grattan notes Australia produces no “clean” jet fuel, and recommends the government direct $6bn to the first generation of so-called “clean refineries” to make that fuel.

Grattan says these refineries could provide nearly 10bn litres of clean jet fuel per year by 2050, but notes that it could cost $100bn to build them all, and that importing clean jet fuel would be cheaper.

But it argues that $6bn – the savings generated from just two years of capping the fuel tax credits to mining companies – would cover a quarter of the cost of the first five refineries, kickstarting the sector and providing fuel security in future supply shocks.

“Historically, making fuel meant making fossil fuels. But in an age of electrification and clean fuels, Australia now has more options,” the report said.

Source: The Guardian World | Published: 2026-11-22 14:00 UTC | Difficulty: 40/100

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/23/australia-urged-to-wean-off-imported-fossil-fuels-amid-global-supply-shocks

item.title: Saudi Arabia, Bahrain report new attacks as Iran says it remains open to a deal with U.S.
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: substance, learning value

Saudi Arabia and Bahrain reported attacks by Iran-linked forces over the weekend, as Iran's foreign minister said his government remains open to a deal to end the war with the U.S.

"Intercepted and destroyed a drone launched by the Houthi terrorist militia toward the Riyadh area," the Saudi-led Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen, which has been leading the fight against the Iran-backed group, said Sunday in a post on X.

The coalition said late Saturday that its air defenses "intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile" launched by the Yemen-based Houthis toward Saudi Arabia's western region, which includes some of the country's sensitive energy refining and export infrastructure.

Neighboring Bahrain also said it came under Iranian fire.

"As a result of the heinous Iranian aggression, a civilian industrial facility was targeted, causing a fire at the site," Bahrain's Ministry of Interior said on X. The ministry later said two people, a Bahraini citizen and a Pakistani resident, were injured in the attack.

Bahrain is home to the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet.

Iranian state media reported late Saturday that the country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fired missiles and drones at U.S. military facilities in Bahrain.

A separate Iranian media report claimed the IRGC's air defenses intercepted and destroyed a U.S. MQ-9 drone.

U.S. Central Command did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on either Iranian report.

Reaching a final agreement

Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said his government remains open to a negotiated settlement to the war. An agreement aimed at developing a permanent peace deal signed in June between President Donald Trump and his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian — the so-called Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding — later broke down.

"The Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding is no longer on the table and has no implementation relevance," Araghchi told the Iran newspaper.

"However, the commitments that the U.S. had accepted in that Memorandum of Understanding and the principle that the implementation of those commitments can pave the way for reaching a final agreement are still accepted by both sides," he said.

The war, which began with U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iranian targets on Feb. 28, has resulted in major disruptions to energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reported that two tankers near Oman were struck by unidentified projectiles on Saturday.

Iran has imposed curbs on vessels moving through the strait, a major sticking point in negotiations with the U.S.

Oil prices have fallen for three straight weeks, however, as traders weighed strong Middle East flows and rising U.S. inventories.

International benchmark Brent crude fell 3.4% for the week, while U.S. crude tumbled 5.2%.

Source: CNBC Top | Published: 2026-11-22 13:25 UTC | Difficulty: 40/100

Original link: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/22/saudi-houthi-bahrain-iran-attacks-araghchi-talks.html

item.title: COP31 climate talks end without consensus on how to fund vulnerable countries or move the world away from coal, oil and gas use
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: substance, learning value

Climate talks break down over fossil fuel exit and funding

November 22, 2026

After two weeks of tough talks, the COP31 climate summit has closed without a consensus on how to quit fossil fuels or fund countries struggling to adapt to a hotter world.

Almost two days into overtime, climate talks in the Turkish city of Antalya have collapsed as countries led by the European Union rejected a deal that critics say undermines the shift away from planet-heating fossil fuels.

After two weeks of tough negotiations, the EU said it could not support the proposed agreement, known as the Antalya Pact, put forward by the COP presidency, saying it does not respond to the science.

"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time," said Irish climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU on Sunday.

He said adopting a decision that omitted fossil fuels would be "unconscionable" and risked "deepening the chasm between global commitment and the action required."

Panama also rejected the deal, describing it as a step backwards in addressing the climate crisis, and adding that any decision must acknowledge "the truth about the collective failure on 1.5 degrees Celsius [2.7 degrees Fahrenheit]." That is the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avert runaway climate change.

"Those who contributed to this crisis ... must shoulder the responsibility to deal with it," the Panamanian delegation said.

The Marshall Islands, which faces an existential threat from sea level rise, formally objected to the cover decision, saying "we will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests."

Chris Bowen, Australia's COP31 negotiating president said the breakdown in talks was very disappointing.

Russia, however, supported the decision to leave out wording on accelerating a phaseout of fossil fuels, arguing that they are still a necessary power source and that each country should be able to determine its own pathway on how to cut emissions.

Pakistan and Ghana, defended the agreement as a necessary compromise in the spirit of multilateralism. "We need to build bridges not barriers," said the Pakistan negotiator.

Deep divisions over climate finance

The marathon talks, held at a time when the window is rapidly closing to avoid the escalating impacts of climate change, including drought, deadly heat and flooding, also saw major disputes over financing.

Developing states blamed the collapse in talks on the EU and other wealthier nations for failing to scale up financing to help them adapt to climate-linked weather extremes and the damage they cause. The EU is the largest provider of climate finance and has resisted new adaptation finance targets.

Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign accused wealthy countries of demanding greater climate ambition while refusing to stump up the cash to pay for it.

"You can't ask developing countries to transform their economies while they're drowning in disasters and debt," he added.

The final cover decision had proposed further discussions on "an implementation pathway for tripling adaptation finance by 2035" but without mentioning a figure. It noted that developing countries need some $300 billion annually for adaptation until 2035, and expressed concern about "the gap between climate finance flows and needs."

Fossil fuel exit on the sidelines

Outside formal negotiations, a separate initiative to Transition Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF) has been gaining momentum.

Maina Talia, Tuvalu's minister for climate change and the environment, said TAFF was "moving beyond debating whether fossil fuels are simply mentioned in a text, to creating detailed plans for a global transformation."

At the same time, a growing number of states, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany and Finland, have either completed or are working on so-called national roadmaps to wean themselves off fossil fuels.

But Brandon Wu, director of Policy and Campaigns ActionAid USA, dismissed such plans as "meaningless" and "nothing more than restatements of inadequate existing policy" on the part of rich countries not stepping up on climate finance.

"COP31 was one of the worst COPs ever, and it's because the EU and other developed countries came with zero spirit of solidarity, cooperation or compromise. They may as well have come to the COP shouting at vulnerable communities: 'we don't care if you die.'"

The push for global electrification

The rejected cover decision had recognized that electrification can deliver emissions reductions, improve energy security and expand access to energy.

It included a call to increase the share of electricity in final energy demand from around 20% now to 35% by 2035 — a proposal heavily touted by co-host Turkey.

Still, about 75 countries, including solar powerhouse China, adopted the pledge outside of the formal negotiations. It is non-binding and does not specify whether that additional electricity must come from clean sources. Critics say this leaves open the possibility that expanded electricity demand could be met by fossil fuels.

Hottest ever climate conference

The talks in Turkey marked the first time a COP was taking place under the explicit knowledge that global temperatures will exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Countries were split on how to deal with that so-called "overshoot."

The cover decision had called on states to commit to limiting overshoot , acknowledging that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems.”

It also recognized the need for "deep, rapid and sustained" emissions cuts and for action on ramping down potent greenhouse gas methane.…

Source: DW Top Stories | Published: 2026-11-22 13:18 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Uncovering a Criminal Network on the Early Internet | True Crime Reports
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: learning value

True Crime Reports

Uncovering a Criminal Network on the Early Internet | True Crime Reports

A global manhunt for one of the internet’s earliest paedophile rings. How did police finally bring it down?

In the early days of the internet, police uncover one of the largest and most sophisticated paedophile networks of its time, sparking a global manhunt. As investigators sift through thousands of messages, one crucial piece of evidence sets off one of the biggest international arrest operations ever seen. How did police bring down the internet’s first global criminal network?

item.title: Milky Way simulation reaches record resolution with the help of three supercomputers
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: highly technical and detailed, with clear reporting

Milky Way simulation reaches record resolution with the help of three supercomputers

Scientific Editor

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

A team of researchers, including those from the University of Tokyo, have developed a new way to model the Milky Way at a level of detail never achieved before. They simulated the entire galaxy down to the level of individual stars by combining the power of some of the world's most powerful supercomputers using an AI-accelerated model that works on a variety of hardware platforms. Their methods can improve our understanding of galactic evolution.

Their paper was presented at the International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis (SC 2026), held Nov. 15–20 in Chicago.

It's nice to know where we came from and where we're going. This is true in ways we can see on different timescales: day to day, year to year, century to century, or even longer periods too. On the galactic level, scales of time and space can be so vast they become difficult to model. Galaxies contain hundreds of billions of stars, as well as gas and other materials, all interacting under gravity and other forces.

The computational cost of finer detail

That means simulations are always based on models that are simplified in some way, often in temporal resolution or spatial complexity, because the more closely you try to represent everything we see in the galaxy, especially at small timescales, the more computing power is required. This is particularly challenging in a galaxy as large as the Milky Way, where small regions can change rapidly and demand many more calculation steps than the rest of the galaxy.

"We expect better simulations as computational power increases, but this still requires work on improving resolutions, and for a Milky Way–sized galaxy, it's not straightforward," said Professor Michiko Fujii from the Department of Astronomy at the University of Tokyo.

"When we look at smaller regions in detail, we encounter areas where the gas is denser and changes rapidly. This means the simulation needs to take much shorter steps in time, which greatly increases the amount of calculation required. We overcame this problem by using an AI model to predict how gas around supernova explosions evolves. This allowed us to carry out the simulation more efficiently and achieve a level of detail where individual stars can be represented."

AI shortcuts for supernova calculations

They call the simulation PHEASANT, and the key to the approach is an AI model developed by postdoctoral researcher Keiya Hirashima from RIKEN. When a star goes supernova, it heats and pushes surrounding gas outward. Simulating this process in detail normally requires very small time steps. Hirashima's AI model predicts how the gas will change over time, allowing the main galaxy simulation to skip many of these smaller calculations.

According to the researchers, this makes the simulation around 20 times faster than directly calculating the same process in the usual exhaustive way. The team's most recent key development was to adapt their software to work efficiently on three different supercomputer systems, using different kinds of hardware including a mixture of CPUs and GPUs from different makers.

"One of my parts was to develop an AI model that predicts how the gas surrounding a supernova explosion changes over time. If we calculate this process directly, we need time steps of around 100 years," said Hirashima. "My model predicts gas distribution after 100,000 years. This means that, rather than having to calculate every small step, we can use a much longer time step for the entire galaxy simulation.

"Making this work efficiently on different supercomputers was a challenge because each system uses different AMD, Intel or NVIDIA CPUs and GPUs. Achieving good performance across all three systems required some specific optimizations."

Individual stars shape the wider galaxy

Astronomers think it's important to represent individual stars in simulations because their effects can extend far beyond their immediate surroundings. Massive stars form in groups, often within the spiral arms of galaxies, where cold gas provides their raw material. These stars heat the gas around them, and some eventually explode as supernovae. When several explosions occur close together, they can create enormous bubbles of hot gas, triggering further star formation while driving material away from the galaxy's disk.

A simulation with insufficient detail can miss important connections between individual stellar events, producing a very different picture of how gas is distributed, changing how the simulated galaxy evolves.

"Something we want to understand is how events on the scale of individual stars connect to the larger structure of the Milky Way," said Fujii. "With this simulation, we can investigate how individual supernovae affect the number of stars that form, the size of these giant gas bubbles and the material that flows out of the galaxy. We can also study how groups of stars form and how they may eventually develop into star clusters."

Tracing the Milky Way's elemental circulation

The researchers hope their simulation will allow investigations into how material circulates through the Milky Way. Elements, including those that make us up, are produced inside stars and released into the surrounding gas through processes including supernova explosions. Following these processes could help researchers understand how the galaxy becomes enriched with different elements over time, and how smaller-scale stellar activity influences its larger structure. The team has already confirmed that the model produces a star formation rate similar to the one estimated from observations of the real Milky Way, demonstrating its reliability.…

item.title: Parasite makes mice more attractive to blood-feeding bugs, which may aid its spread
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original research with clear implications

November 22, 2026 feature

Parasite makes mice more attractive to blood-feeding bugs, which may aid its spread

Ingrid Fadelli

Author

Gaby Clark

Scientific Editor

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

Some parasites, such as Trypanosoma rangeli and Trypanosoma cruzi, can be passed between mammals and blood-feeding insects called triatomine bugs. Bugs can acquire these parasites when feeding on infected mammals, while mammals can also become infected through encounters with infected bugs.

Researchers at Fiocruz in Brazil and INBIOTEC-CONICET in Argentina recently set out to explore how infection with the parasites T. rangeli and T. cruzi influences interactions between mice and blood-feeding bugs. Their paper, published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences, suggests that contracting the parasite makes mice more attractive to blood-feeding insects and could contribute to the infection spreading.

"We have a research line on T. rangeli and T. cruzi in which we study how the parasites interact with their hosts, and we had already shown that infection with both parasites alters the behavior of the vector," Alessandra A. Guarneri, senior author of the paper, told Phys.org. "Since there are reports of vector-borne parasites that alter the behavior of the vertebrate host, we decided to evaluate whether this could also happen in our system."

How infections change mice-insect encounters

Guarneri and her colleagues carried out a two-part experiment. In the first part, they released a healthy mouse and a mouse infected with T. cruzi or T. rangeli into an arena, each within a separate container, along with a group of nymphs (i.e., juveniles) of the blood-feeding bug Rhodnius prolixus.

The researchers allowed the nymphs to move freely, observing which mouse they approached. They found that the insects were significantly more attracted to mice infected with T. rangeli than to uninfected mice.

In the second part of the experiment, the team looked at how often T. rangeli-infected and healthy mice ate bugs that approached them. In addition, they tested the bugs that fed on infected mice to determine whether the parasite was transferred to them.

"We measured the ability of these mice to prey on nymphs that attempted to feed, because if predation rates increased along with attractiveness, there would be no fitness gain for the parasite," explained Guarneri.

"This assay showed a lower predation rate for infected mice and transmission rates of nearly 50% among the insects that survived feeding. Based on these transmission rates, it is possible to suggest that an increase in the number of insects approaching the host would also increase the number of individuals acquiring the infection, since the defensive behavior of the mice is reduced by infection."

The researchers observed that being infected with T. rangeli, but not T. cruzi, made mice more attractive to blood-feeding bugs. They also found that bugs approaching T. rangeli-infected mice were less likely to be eaten than those approaching uninfected mice. Among bugs that fed on infected mice, 46.5% acquired the parasite.

Under their experimental conditions, Guarneri and her colleagues did not detect a significant effect of T. cruzi infection on how attractive mice were to bugs. Instead, infected mice appeared less attractive to bugs. As this was a modest difference, further research is needed to determine whether it reflects a genuine effect.

New clues to how parasites spread

The results of this study indicate that infection with some parasites, particularly T. rangeli, can alter mice-bug interactions in ways that help the parasite to reach more hosts. The experimental methods used by Guarneri and her colleagues could potentially be adapted and used to study the transmission of other parasites between different animal species.

Notably, T. rangeli is generally considered nonpathogenic for mammals. However, it can cause diseases in some invertebrates (i.e., animals with no backbone), particularly its insect hosts.

"Most triatomine bugs with systemic T. rangeli infections die before reaching the adult stage, and the reproductive success of infected adults is substantially affected," said Guarneri.

"Perhaps for this reason, only a small proportion of insects with intestinal infections also develop systemic infections, which are necessary for the production of infective forms for the vertebrate host. It is possible that behavioral alterations, which also occur in infected insects, are important both for increasing the chances of encounter between the two hosts and for increasing the number of insects that acquire the infection."

The researchers are now assessing possible factors that could contribute to the increased attractiveness to bugs that they observed in mice infected with T. rangeli.

"We collected volatile odors from mice infected or not infected with the parasite and submitted the samples to gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) analysis," added Guarneri. "We are still analyzing the data obtained, but preliminary results showed that the odor profiles released are modified during infection, suggesting that these changes may be responsible for the behavioral change in the insects."

Written for you by our author Ingrid Fadelli, edited by Gaby Clark, and fact-checked and reviewed by Robert Egan—this article is the result of careful human work. We rely on readers like you to keep independent science journalism alive. If this reporting matters to you, please consider a donation (especially monthly). You'll get an ad-free account as a thank-you.

item.title: Erectile dysfunction drug could hold promise for Alzheimer’s disease
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original research with potential implications for medicine

A drug developed to treat erectile dysfunction might seem an unlikely treatment for Alzheimer’s disease. But researchers are increasingly interested in whether medicines such as Viagra could also help protect the brain.

These drugs affect blood flow and other processes that may play a role in brain health. An experimental drug called AR1001 has produced encouraging results in a large international clinical trial.

In one group of people with early Alzheimer’s, the drug was reported to slow the worsening of symptoms by 31% over a year, compared with a placebo.

On supporting science journalism

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

AriBio, a South Korean biotechnology company, announced the results at the 19th Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference in Boston, US. A full scientific paper, reviewed by other researchers, has not yet been published.

The phase three trial—the final phase of testing in humans—involved 1,535 people with early Alzheimer’s in 13 countries. Participants took either 30mg of AR1001 or a placebo every day for a year.

Researchers measured changes in memory, thinking and everyday activities. They looked at two groups: everyone who took part in the trial and a smaller group of 604 people who were not taking other Alzheimer’s medicines to ease their symptoms, such as donepezil or memantine.

Only this smaller group saw a 31 percent reduction in worsening symptoms. Across the whole trial, AR1001 did not produce reliable benefits.

How could erectile dysfunction drugs affect the brain?

Erectile dysfunction drugs work by blocking an enzyme that normally breaks down a chemical messenger – called cGMP – in the body. This allows cGMP to build up, helping the muscles around blood vessels relax. The vessels widen, allowing more blood to flow through them. This is how the drugs help treat erectile dysfunction.

The same chemical messenger also helps brain cells communicate with each other. Researchers think that increasing its levels could help brain cells survive and maintain the connections they need to share information.

These connections are essential for learning and memory. Alzheimer’s gradually damages them, making it harder to remember things and think clearly. Researchers hope that AR1001 might help protect some of these connections and slow the damage caused by the disease.

However, this is still a theory. The clinical trial does not show that these biological changes explain the reported benefits in people.

Some laboratory and animal studies support the idea. In a 2022 study, mice with features of Alzheimer’s disease performed better in memory tests after receiving AR1001. The treatment also reduced levels of amyloid-beta and abnormal tau, two proteins linked to Alzheimer’s.

Other experimental researchin mice has found that AR1001 can increase levels of cGMP and a protein that helps brain cells survive. However, results in animals do not always translate into benefits for humans.

Interest in this family of drugs has also grown following research in people. A 2024 studyfollowed more than 269,000 men with erectile dysfunction. It found that men prescribed these drugs were 18% less likely to be diagnosed with Alzheimer’s than men who were not prescribed them.

But this was an observational study, which means it cannot show that the drugs themselves reduced the risk of Alzheimer’s. The two groups may have differed in other ways that influenced the results.

A complicated relationship

The relationship between erectile dysfunction and Alzheimer’s is complicated. Erectile dysfunction can be associated with conditions such as diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease, which can damage blood vessels. These same conditions are also linked to poorer brain health and a higher risk of dementia.

This means that some of the apparent link between erectile dysfunction, its treatments and dementia could be down to shared risk factors affecting blood vessels, rather than a direct effect of the drugs.

Erectile dysfunction drugs are not an established treatment for Alzheimer’s, and nothing in these results suggests people should take them to protect their memory.

The latest trial does, however, keep alive an interesting possibility: that drugs that improve blood flow and help brain cells communicate might also slow the damage caused by Alzheimer’s.

Whether this is the case will depend on the full trial results and further research in people, including studies looking at why the apparent benefit was seen only among those not taking other Alzheimer’s medicines.

item.title: Black holes can split apart 'like pants' if they spin too fast, study hints
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: interesting concept with clear explanation

Black holes can split apart 'like pants' if they spin too fast, astrophysics study hints

New research shows how fast-spinning black holes may split apart.

Black holes are known to collide and combine in monstrously violent merger events, but new research suggests these celestial stalwarts can also fragment into smaller bodies, like a cosmic pair of pants splitting down the middle.

In a paper published Oct. 22 in the journal Physical Review D, researchers used several mathematical modeling methods to propose a "pair-of-pants" topology for black holes. The hypothesis suggests that under extremely specific conditions, these dark behemoths could fragment into numerous less-massive black holes.

"Understanding precisely what is forbidden, what is merely unlikely, and what becomes possible once the assumptions are relaxed is the central goal of this work," the researchers wrote in the paper.

Black hole fragmentation could play into other cosmic mysteries. For example, it could help to explain black holes with masses that are too small to be formed through conventional astrophysical processes. These hypothesized black hole "morsels" would be so small that astronomers could see them evaporating before their eyes on observational timescales.

Do black holes wear pants?

In the new paper, the researchers explored whether black holes' event horizons — the boundaries beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape — could split under various cosmological conditions. These situations included classical four-dimensional general relativity (Einstein's description of our large-scale universe as we currently understand it) as well as cosmologically esoteric frameworks such as higher-dimensional space-time and modified gravity scenarios.

But modeling black hole dynamics, especially the split of an event horizon, is messy work. So the researchers simplified it by comparing discrete slices of space-time, effectively condensing the fragmentation process into static snapshots from before and after the split.

In our classical cosmos, it seems mostly impossible for black holes to split, the researchers found, but they did identify a loophole that might allow it to happen.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The first impediment is entropy, the possible arrangements of an isolated system's energy, which cannot spontaneously decrease but only stay the same or increase. This has been theorized by Stephen Hawking and recently demonstrated through detections of ripples in space-time called gravitational waves, suggesting that a black hole's surface area cannot decrease.

For these reasons, splitting a static Schwarzschild black hole — the simplest type of black hole in our four-dimensional general relativity — would be strictly forbidden because it would violate the second law of thermodynamics.

The second impediment is kinematics, the motion of orbital dynamics, which precludes the possibility of a permanent split because the black hole fragments would recombine into a single body incredibly quickly.

But there is a loophole: A rapidly rotating black hole could literally spin itself apart.

"This is why, in four-dimensional general relativity, an isolated black hole in empty space could only split if it spins very close to the maximum rate the theory allows, what we call a near-extremal black hole," study co-author Manuel Del Piano, a theoretical physicist at the University of Southern Denmark, told Live Science via email. "Loosely speaking, the equator of the horizon is then dragged around at nearly the speed of light."

Through this theoretical process, the two resultant black hole fragments could be gravitationally slingshotted away from each other before they could recombine. So under conventional space-time conditions, it seems "black holes do not wear pants."

Then, the researchers mathematically modeled black hole fragmentation in versions of space-time with more than four dimensions.

In models of higher-dimension space-times, a black hole's rotational velocity is no longer limited because gravity weakens with increasing dimensionality. Therefore, any such ultrafast spinning black holes could theoretically fragment, the researchers explained in the paper.

In the "black string" model, a normally spherical black hole would become cylindrical or string-like, stretching across any extra dimensions. It could then pinch off to fragment into multiple smaller bodies, akin to "beads on a string."

Additionally, the researchers calculated that black hole fragmentation may be entropically favored in space-time models with modified gravity, which alter the gravitational interactions in extremely warped environments near the black hole.

"The fragments are tiny, though: in one of our benchmarks, a black hole of ten solar masses would favour fragments … a few times the mass of the Great Pyramid of Giza squeezed into a region smaller than a proton, and the heavier the parent, the smaller the fragments," Del Piano explained.

Fragmentation also may be more likely if there is a "bumpy horizon" around black holes, akin to a dense blanket or shroud of exotic matter that acts as a singular-but-gigantic quantum entity. The superfluid qualities of this matter could create strange vortices that eventually cause a black hole to fragment into multiple smaller bodies.

Scientists might see a black hole decrease in size, an actual fragmentation, or simply an indirect gravitational signature, depending on the dimensions and whether it intersects the viewer's "brane," or slice of dimensionality.

Smaller relativistic waistlines may be more conducive to wearing pants…

item.title: Quantum physics can now prove where you really are
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: explains complex concept with clear language

Your “bank” is texting again: You’ve been hacked, and you need to send your information over immediately. You’re 99 percent sure it’s a scam. It’s the other 1 percent that keeps your thumb hovering over the reply button. Nothing on your screen can tell you whether the sender is who—or where—they claim to be.

Physicists now have a way to determine the “where,” at least in the lab. In a new experiment led by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and described in Nature on Wednesday, researchers confirmed someone’s location by having them catch a photon fired right at them through a fiber-optic cable.

See, a vault can keep a physical object in its place, and cryptography is pretty good at showing digital information is what it claims to be. Bridging the gap between the digital and physical is much harder. A password can be cracked, an identity can be faked, and even security camera footage shipped over the internet can be spoofed. Location falls into the same gap, which is how a scammer on another continent can pass for bank,

The NIST team found its answer in quantum physics. Quantum information, like the polarization of the fired photon’s electric field, obeys different rules than the bits and code that make up standard computer communications. For instance, “They can’t be copied, so they have to be measured at one location,” says Krister Shalm, a NIST physicist who led the experiment.

A photon that can’t be copied can still be intercepted, though, and measured somewhere else. So the researchers built two stations on NIST’s Boulder campus nearly 200 meters apart and put the person in question somewhere in between. One station sent the photon down the fiber, and both fired off random bits dictating how to measure it. Then they timed how long it took the person to catch the photon, measure it and send back a response to both stations. “By measuring that round trip time from when they sent the bits to when they got the answer, they can actually localize where that signal had to have come from,” says Shalm.

Shalm and his collaborators created a sort of quantum echolocation, pinging signals from different locations to triangulate a position. Only the photon sender and the pinpointee need any sort of quantum technology. So the other “ear”—as in, the average person’s computer—could check locations without any quantum capability. The hope is that a network of optical fiber could let anyone prove where they are to anyone else in the same city.

That idea has excited quantum researchers for years. “I’ve been telling everyone for the last two years that this is my new obsession,” says Henry Yuen, an associate professor of computer science at Columbia University. He says he used to be very skeptical of the need for this kind of work. The rise of AI agents and AI-enabled scamming changed his mind, and making sure someone actually is where they say they are strikes him as urgent.

The experiment isn’t scalable yet, though. NIST cautions that real-world use may be more than a decade away. Yuen believes the holdup is mainly a matter of engineering and building out quantum-friendly networks. “We went from zero to one this year with this NIST experiment,” he says. “It’ll take a few years, but it seems like this is going to happen.”

Others are less bullish on such a quick timeline. George Siopsis, a physics professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, notes that the scheme only works if whoever sends the photon is much more technically advanced than any would-be spoofer. He also warns that the speedy photons may be harder to measure precisely outside a lab. After all, he says, “Light travels at the speed of light.”

Quantum technology usually makes headlines for its promises of faster computers. Shalm’s photon suggests it could also make lying about your location a lot harder. And it would be a relief to know that the next text from your bank actually came from, well, the bank.

Source: Scientific American | Published: 2026-11-22 12:00 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

item.title: The best way to pack a suitcase, according to science
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: practical advice with some science

While recently packing for an overseas excursion, I stuffed every spare space I could find in my carry-on. I used what I call the “Mary Poppins” packing method: willing myself to believe that whatever I wanted to put in my luggage would fit, regardless of the size of the object or the size of my bag. Somehow my system worked, but when I arrived at my destination and unzipped my bag, everything within it exploded onto the floor. “There’s gotta be a better way,” I thought.

To find out how best to pack according to science, Popular Science turned to Anne McAlpin, a travel expert and author of the book, Pack it Up: the Essential Guide to Smart Travel. Over the course of her lifetime, McAlpin has estimated she’s packed—and unpacked—more than 25,000 times! She’s a whiz at minimizing dead space, maximizing volume, and keeping clothes looking more like they came off a closet hanger than straight out of a laundry bin.

Start with a flat foundation

Many carry-on bags have “ruts” or internal grooves to accommodate a recessed trolley handle. This handle uses two narrow metal poles that retract straight into the middle or sides of the interior lining, causing the interior surface of the suitcase to be uneven.

“If you don’t have a flat foundation, make one,” says McAlpin. Having a flat foundation maximizes space, prevents wrinkles, and adds stability to your bag. To do this, consider evening out the space between ruts with packing or compression cubes. “You can put all of your underwear into a compression cube,” a small bag made of breathable nylon or polyester mesh used in part to organize items, and then place it between the ruts. This will even out the bottom of a hard-shell suitcase. Flexible items such as toiletry kits and rolled-up socks can help to form this base layer as well. “I then pack my clothing on top of that flat foundation.”

McAlpin puts her shoes (she usually packs two pairs and wears a third) towards the bottom of the suitcase so that the weight is on the wheels. “You don’t want to put your heavy items on the top of the inside of your suitcase,” she says. “This will cause it to constantly topple.”

The interlayering method

When it comes to clothing, McAlpin rolls some items and flat packs others. “I call it interlayering,” she says.

For example, with pants, rather than folding them to stack in a pile, McAlpin lays each pair out along its natural creases as if she were going to put them on a hanger. Then, she places them in her suitcase: waistband at the top of one side of the bag, legs dangling out the other side of the bag. They’re not folded, but laid out straight. This way, McAlpin can then wrap them around the rolled items that she’ll later place on top of them.

She does the same with cotton shirts, sundresses—anything that might wrinkle. With each item, McAlpin alternates the direction, so that there are no two waistbands or shirt collars bulking up one side of the suitcase.

“I then roll my knit items and synthetic things that don’t wrinkle as much. I roll them up like Tootsie Rolls and I place them side by side,” in the middle of the laid-out items. While folding clothes and stacking them leaves pockets of air both inside the folds and within the layers, rolling wraps fabrics into a smooth, tight cylinder, which reduces the overall amount of space each item uses. It’s the best of both worlds! Your laid-out items aren’t as wrinkled and your wrinkle-resistant items are more tightly packed. This allows for more room in your suitcase overall.

When McAlpin has all her rolled items tightly packed together, she takes the pant legs and skirts that are still hanging off the sides of the suitcase, and “bends them up and over the ‘roll bar’ I’ve made of sweaters, pajamas, and sweats.” This helps avoid the knee creases that come when you’re simply folding pants. It also keeps items compact, and is a game-changer when it comes to unpacking. You can just lift all of the interlayered items out of your suitcase in one fell swoop.

Other useful tools and tips

Fill up empty space. For example, McAlpin says that if you’re a couple packing together, you may be able to slide a woman’s sandal right into a man’s shoe, or at least use the shoe’s interior cavity to store phone chargers, socks, or small items like earrings and even an eyeglasses case. Not only is it a space-saver, but filling up unused space prevents transit damage by keeping items inside from shifting.

Stuff the corners of a suitcase with socks, rolled-up t-shirts, etc, “because all those awkward corners offer prime packing space,” says McAlpin. Filling up those pockets also distributes structural stress throughout the bag, helping to keep features like zippers and fabric intact during excessive handling.

Related 'Ask Us Anything' Stories

Why are airplanes so cold? It’s for your health.

The best way to sleep on a plane, according to science

Why are airline seats so small? It all started in 1978.

Why airplane toilets are tiny engineering marvels

Is turbulence really like Jell-O? Pilots weigh in.

How pilots avoid thunderstorms—and what happens when they can’t

What do TSA bag scanners actually see?

Why do our ears pop on a plane? An audiologist explains.

Why do we put seatbacks up for landing? An aviation expert explains.

Another trick: laying belts around the luggage perimeter so that they’re easier to find.

To keep things condensed and organized, McAlpin suggests compression cubes. These small bags feature two zippers: a main zipper that closes the cube like a standard bag, and a second perimeter zipper that pulls the cube’s top and bottom panels closer together, squeezing out excess air and reducing volume. Compression cubes help eliminate air pockets that come with traditional folding and can reduce the volume of soft clothes like T-shirts and pants up to 30 percent.…

item.title: 2,200-year-old Celtic silver coin hoard unearthed at construction site in Hungary
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: historical find with clear context

2,200-year-old Celtic silver coin hoard unearthed at construction site in Hungary

Archaeologists discovered a stash of Celtic coins ahead of a construction project for an electrical substation in Hungary.

Archaeologists in Hungary have discovered a stash of more than 200 Celtic silver coins that are over 2,000 years old. It's one of the largest hoards found there in decades.

Researchers unearthed the coins during excavations ahead of construction for an electrical substation in western Hungary between 2023 and 2025, according to a translated statement from the power company E.ON. The hoard dates to sometime between the late second century B.C. and the early first century B.C.

The coin cache weighs roughly 4.4 pounds (2 kilograms). In today's market, it's worth more than $2,000 as raw silver alone, but its rarity and historical value effectively make it priceless, the statement said.

The site was once part of a farm, and plowing there had unearthed several individual coins in recent decades, the statement said.

During the latest excavations, archaeologists initially found a few coins and then searched the area with metal detectors, which led them to the coin hoard. The treasure had been packed inside a small ceramic vessel and sat about 16 inches (40 centimeters) below ground.

"This is a rarity in Europe," Eszter Kreiter, an archaeologist at Hungary's National Archaeological Institute, said at a news conference, according to local news outlets. She added that the last similar find was made in Hungary in the late 1960s.

Copycat coins

The hoard's silver coins are modeled on Greek tetradrachms — a very early type of large silver coin that was introduced in the late sixth century B.C.

The newfound Celtic tetradrachm copies are a type known as "Velem," which are named after Velem-Szent Vid, a fortified Celtic hilltop settlement, or oppidum. Similar coins have been found at that site, which is located about 10 miles (15 kilometers) to the west.

Each coin has a stylized head on one side that probably depicts the Greek god Apollo, and portrays a helmeted rider and horse on the other side.

The excavations have revealed evidence of more than 7,000 years of occupation at the site, officials wrote in the statement. The artifacts include a nearly 7,000-year-old polished stone chisel used for woodworking and a glass bead with a peacock's eye pattern that seems to have been part of jewelry from the sixth or seventh century B.C.

A Roman-era villa was built at the same site in later centuries, without disturbing the hoard of buried silver, Kreiter said at the news conference.

The villa has long since been demolished, but the excavations enabled the archaeological team to reconstruct its floor plan, including its underfloor heating system, she said. They also found a Roman-era brick with a dog's paw print.

The artifacts from the site will become part of a museum exhibition.

Celtic fringe

According to Museum Wales, the Celts were loosely related Iron Age peoples descended from Proto-Indo-European speakers. Emerging in Central Europe, Celtic groups occupied much of Central and Western Europe from about the 10th to the first century B.C. The Celtic Gauls were finally defeated by the Romans, led by Julius Caesar at Alesia, now in eastern France, in 52 B.C. The Britons were also Celtic, though most people of Celtic descent would not have recognized that name.

Several modern ethnic groups, including the native Irish and the Bretons of coastal France, trace their descent to the Celts. Regions with strong Celtic origins are sometimes called the "Celtic fringe" of Western Europe.

Writing in the Journal of Roman Studies, the British coin expert Christopher Howgego, an honorary curator and professor emeritus of Greek and Roman numismatics at the University of Oxford, stated that Celtic tribes in the Carpathian Basin, now in Hungary and Romania, started minting their own silver coins after Celtic mercenaries had seen them when serving with Hellenistic armies in Greece and Macedonia.

Howgego has written that the Greek-inspired Celtic coins included adaptations of classical Greek portraits, as well as distinctive Celtic designs. These copycat tetradrachms held very high value for their makers, so they were rarely used for everyday purchases. Instead, they were often hoarded as wealth or buried as ritual offerings.

Source: Live Science | Published: 2026-11-22 13:00 UTC | Difficulty: 41/100

item.title: Beaver Moon 2026: When to see a full 'supermoon' rise this week, and another on Christmas Eve
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: interesting celestial event with clear information

Beaver Moon 2026: When to see a full 'supermoon' rise this week, and another on Christmas Eve

November's full Beaver Moon rises on Tuesday, Nov. 24, giving us a preview of the spectacular Christmas Eve supermoon coming next month.

November’s full moon, known as the "Beaver Moon," will rise in the east at dusk on Tuesday (Nov. 24), marking the first of three consecutive supermoons.

It will be the third and final full moon of fall in the Northern Hemisphere and the first in a series of unusually close full moons that includes December's spectacular Christmas supermoon — the closest full moon since 2018.

The Beaver Moon gets its name from the time of year when nocturnal beavers in North America traditionally build dams and prepare for winter under the full moon, according to TimeandDate. Other nicknames include the Frost Moon and Snow Moon, and the Anishinaabeg people in North America call it Baashkaakodin Giizis — the Freezing Moon — according to the Center for Native American Studies.

The moon will reach its full phase at 9:53 a.m. ET on Tuesday, when it will be below the horizon in North America. The best time to see the Beaver Moon is at moonrise that evening, as it rises in the east around the same time the sun sets in the west. That's when the moon will appear against a relatively bright twilight sky, making it easier to appreciate its size and color.

The moon will appear full on Monday and Wednesday as well, but Tuesday offers the best opportunity to see it rise during twilight.

The Beaver Moon will be the first of three consecutive supermoons, according to EarthSky. A supermoon occurs when a full moon coincides with the moon being relatively close to Earth in its elliptical orbit. The moon's distance from Earth changes throughout the month. On average, the moon is 238,900 miles (384,472 kilometers) from Earth. When a full moon occurs near perigee, or its closest point during its orbit, it appears slightly larger and brighter than usual. Here's what's coming up:

- Full Beaver Supermoon on Nov. 24, 2026 (224,170 miles / 360,768 km)

- Full Cold Supermoon on Dec. 24, 2026 (221,667 miles / 356,740 km)

- Full Wolf Supermoon on Jan. 22, 2027 (222,229 miles / 357,644 km)

November's Beaver Supermoon is just the beginning: It's the smallest of the three upcoming supermoons. December's full Cold Moon will be the closest, biggest and brightest full moon of 2026, bringing the moon closer to Earth than at any time since Jan. 2, 2018, according to late astrophysicist Fred Espenak.

His work appears regularly in Space.com, Forbes, New Scientist, BBC Sky at Night, Sky & Telescope, and other major science and astronomy publications. He is also the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com.
