item.title: New imaging technology reveals previously unseen immune cell patterns in tissue
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth scientific reporting with clear language and valuable vocabulary for learning.

New imaging technology reveals previously unseen immune cell patterns in tissue

Scientists can now see a previously hidden dimension of the immune system thanks to BCR-MERFISH, a new imaging technology developed by researchers at Boston Children's Hospital. By mapping where different groups of antibody-producing cells are located in tissue, the technology could help researchers better understand how immune responses contribute to disease and eventually inform new approaches to diagnosis and treatment. The breakthrough, published in Nature Methods, opens new possibilities for investigating inflammatory bowel disease, autoimmune disorders, infections and cancer.

"This work allows us to see the aspects of spatial organization of the adaptive immune system in tissues that we could never see before," said Jeffrey R. Moffitt, senior author and investigator in the Program in Cellular and Molecular Medicine at Boston Children's Hospital.

Building on existing technologies

Plasma cells are immune cells that produce antibodies, the proteins that help the body recognize and fight threats. Two plasma cells may look nearly identical under a microscope yet produce antibodies that recognize very different targets. Previously, imaging technologies could identify cell types and states but could not readily distinguish these important differences among plasma cells.

BCR-MERFISH builds on MERFISH, short for multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization, which uses microscopy to measure RNA and reveal which genes are active in cells. Evan Yang, a former graduate student in Moffitt's lab and lead author, adapted MERFISH to distinguish groups of plasma cells based on selected antibody receptor gene features while also measuring gene activity in surrounding cells.

"People have started to put this information in space, but BCR-MERFISH increases the resolution we have dramatically," Moffitt said.

Applying BCR-MERFISH in the gut

To demonstrate the technology's capabilities, researchers studied the small intestines of mice. In two extended sections of intestinal tissue, they imaged more than 300,000 cells and identified 434 distinct plasma-cell groups based on antibody receptor gene usage.

The maps revealed that some groups of antibody-producing cells formed unexpected clusters along the intestine rather than being evenly distributed throughout the tissue. "We did not expect to see these clusters at all," Moffitt said. Researchers do not yet know what causes the clusters or what they mean for immune function, he added.

The team also compared mice with typical gut microbes with germ-free mice raised without microorganisms. As expected, germ-free mice had fewer plasma cells and less diversity among the identifiable groups.

The ability to connect immune-cell identity with its precise location could help researchers understand how antibody-producing cells behave at sites of inflammation and disease. For example, in inflammatory bowel diseases such as Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, tissue architecture changes and plasma cells gather at affected sites. Until now, scientists have had limited ability to distinguish groups of antibody-producing cells within these tissues and examine how they relate to surrounding cells.

Beyond inflammatory bowel disease, BCR-MERFISH could help researchers investigate immune activity in tumors, B-cell lymphomas and other conditions involving the adaptive immune system.

Moffitt's laboratory is especially interested in the immune system's role in the intestine. His team is already studying human biopsy samples through clinical collaborations, including samples from patients with inflammatory bowel disease. Although BCR-MERFISH is not a diagnostic test or treatment, translating its findings into advances in patient care will require further research.

"Our goal is to build a better understanding of these diseases so that researchers and clinicians can use that knowledge to make a difference in patients' lives," Moffitt said.

item.title: Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Important topic with insightful analysis on the rise in disability benefits among young Scots.

Why are so many more young Scots claiming disability benefits?

Every month, more than 12,000 applications are made to Social Security Scotland for disability support.

The number of Scots receiving these benefits has risen sharply since the Covid pandemic, and is projected to hit one million by the end of the decade.

This has been driven in part by younger people and claims for mental health conditions.

The cost of the system has been growing, posing additional challenges for Scottish ministers facing a tight budget settlement.

But with the UK government considering a radical redesign of support in England and Wales, they insist that Scotland's welfare state does not need to be trimmed.

Why has there been such an increase in claims in Scotland, and can the government afford to continue its more generous approach?

Scotland has long had a higher rate of ill health among adults than other parts of the UK, often attributed to its history of heavy industry and relatively high levels of poverty in certain areas.

But the change seen in recent years has different roots.

There has been a notable uptick in disability across the UK since the Covid pandemic - and it is most pronounced north of the border.

The percentage of Scotland's working-age population, aged 16 to 64, reporting having a disability increased from 19% in 2020-21 to 28% in 2023-24, external.

In children aged under 16, it doubled from 6% to 12%.

That has translated into a rising number of people receiving disability benefits - in total there are about 800,000 people in receipt of them today.

The Scottish Fiscal Commission says there has been a "shift in the age profile of applicants" since 2020.

Some 35% of the new applicants for Adult Disability Payment, external, since it was rolled out as Scotland's main disability benefit in 2022, have been people under 35. Over half are under 45.

Mental health is a key element in this, with 41% of the ADP caseload concerning "mental and behavioural disorders".

Almost half of those are "neurotic and stress related" conditions, such as anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder.

If you look back before social security was devolved to Holyrood, mental and behavioural disorders accounted for only 26%, external of the claims for Personal Independence Payments, the main disability payment in the UK system.

Among children, these conditions now account for 64% of applications in Scotland - with the number of people under 16 receiving the Child Disability Payment for them more than doubling from 30,000 in 2020 to 75,000 this year.

Meanwhile, mental health conditions play a much smaller role in benefit claims from older people, accounting for 13% of the Pension Age Disability Payment caseload - behind both back and joint issues and diseases of the circulatory system.

Why is this happening?

There are inevitably some who characterise it as the product of an overly sensitive "snowflake generation".

But others note that the current cohort of young people spent their formative years in lockdown before emerging into a cost-of-living crisis and the destabilising rise of AI - with polling suggesting that the majority believe they will be worse off than their parents, external.

Mental health charity Scottish Action for Mental Health (SAMH) says young people today are "growing up significantly more mentally distressed".

Chief executive Billy Watson said they face a "relentless" pace of life, with social media constantly exposing them to unsettling news and world events and unrealistic social comparison.

Data published this week from the Scottish Health Survey, external suggested that mental wellbeing - measured using an internationally-recognised scoring system - had recovered to pre-pandemic levels.

However, the 16 to 24 age group had the lowest score of any included, and around a quarter of young adults reported poor enough mental health to suggest a possible psychiatric disorder.

An independent review for the UK government by Prof Peter Fonagy last month said the problems faced by young people were real, with dramatically increasing cases of mental distress including depression and anxiety.

But Fonagy also warned of an "increasing risk of overdiagnosis or misdiagnosis".

He said this was because "diagnosis has become the primary gateway to support that could and should be available earlier".

This was echoed by Alan Milburn, author of the UK government's review of support for young people in England and Wales.

He said that "in too many places, diagnosis has inappropriately become the key that unlocks help", which has "created pressure on people to seek a diagnosis".

As an aside, it should be noted that while Milburn's review centred on employment prospects, benefit uptake does not always read across directly to this; Adult Disability Payment is not an "out of work" benefit like Jobseeker's Allowance.

The employment rate among disabled people in Scotland is more than 50%, and on the flip side studies have suggested, external that almost half of those not in education, employment or training are not claiming benefits either.

Milburn's review, external proposed sweeping changes to the youth support network in England and Wales, including faster access to mental health services and a complete replacement of Personal Independence Payments.

But in Scotland, "Pip" has already been replaced by Adult Disability Payment.

There was a very deliberate wave of publicity around the launch of the new benefit in 2022 - alongside the versions for children and pensioners - in a bid to increase uptake among people who might have been entitled to the likes of Pip, but never claimed.

With more money being spent on the Scottish system - it costs about Â£1bn a year over and above the block grant from Westminster - there is an easy narrative that it is inherently more generous.

A report last year concluded that it was more "significantly more compassionate" and "kinder in tone and approach".…

item.title: I lost my dad, mum and sister to the same aggressive brain cancer
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Personal story with clear language on the impact of a rare and aggressive form of brain cancer.

I lost my dad, mum and sister to the same aggressive brain cancer

After firstly losing her dad to an aggressive brain tumour, Iola Williams then had to watch as her mother and sister both died of similar diseases.

It was in 2004 that Billy died from glioblastoma, external - the most common and fastest growing type of brain cancer - with mum Eleanor dying a decade later, followed by Helen in 2024.

Charity Brain Tumour Research said about 3,200 people are diagnosed with glioblastoma in the UK each year, with only a third surviving past a year.

Iola said she has seen little change in treatment options since her dad was diagnosed 20 years ago and wants changes.

The Welsh government said it was developing a National Cancer Strategy for Wales, external to try and improve things.

"My dad was diagnosed in 2004, my mum in 2014 and Helen in 2024," said Iola, 68, from Llanfrothen, Gwynedd.

"Nothing has really changed.

"They get the diagnosis, they get radiotherapy or chemotherapy, but they still can't tell us where these tumours come from.

"If nothing happens then other people are going to have to go through what we have as a family."

Brain Tumour Research described her family's story as "highly unusual".

Opening up on her family's experience, Iola said the effects of the disease has remained with the family long after their deaths and was calling for increased funding and improved access to clinical trials.

In 2004, Billy died within weeks of being diagnosed with glioblastoma.

Iola, a retired psychiatric nurse, described her father's initial diagnosis after he collapsed while gardening for a friend in the village.

Family members initially feared he had suffered a stroke, but hospital scans revealed multiple tumours on his brain.

Despite undergoing radiotherapy, his condition deteriorated quickly.

"He loved his job," said Iola.

"He worked as a groundsman at Morfa Bychan Golf Club [near Porthmadog] and adored his grandchildren.

"We managed to look after him at home, but he passed away very rapidly."

Exactly a decade later, the family faced another cancer battle when Iola's mother, Eleanor, developed a brain tumour.

She had already been treated for breast cancer and lung cancer and, according to Iola, was "a fighter", dying from complications related to her cancer treatment.

Then in January 2024, Iola's younger sister, Helen, was told she had the same aggressive form of brain cancer as her father.

The diagnosis was confirmed on Helen's 56th birthday.

Deciding against chemotherapy and radiotherapy treatment, she chose instead to focus on quality of life in the time she had left.

"All she wanted to do was go home," said Iola.

She died 12 weeks after her diagnosis.

Having watched three close relatives deteriorate quickly, Iola says it was only afterwards that the full emotional impact began to sink in.

"At the time you just cope and get through it for everyone else," said Iola, 68.

"You never forget it. It's still there all the time.

"With the support of my husband and family we've come through it, but it's always there."

Hugh Adams from Brain Tumour Research said it remains one of the most underfunded areas of cancer research.

There are around 150 different types of brain tumour ranging from slow-growing to aggressive cancers, each of which can respond differently to treatment.

The charity said only a third with glioblastoma survive beyond a year, and just 4% for five years or more.

"Brain tumours, sadly, are the biggest cancer killer of children and adults under the age of 40, and we need to invest in research to get closer to cures," he said.

"Now, historically, that research from central government, from the devolved nations and governments, has been poor. It's been less than 1%.

"It is starting to increase, but it needs to be greater."

He described Iola's family story as "highly unusual".

"I've worked in this area for a long time and I've not heard of three members of one family, so tragically, being affected by the same tumour type," he added.

"We're not aware of any links based on hereditary makeup.

"So, this is something that's very, very unusual, and perhaps we just say it's just terrible, terrible luck for Iola and her family."

Iola urged the Welsh government to put more money into support and research on this "horrible, horrible illness".

A Welsh government spokesperson said: "We are sorry to hear of Iola's loss, and we recognise how much this matters to everyone whose life has been affected by cancer.

"We are developing a National Cancer Strategy for Wales to transform the way the health service prevents, diagnoses and treats this set of diseases - including brain cancer.

"The 10-year strategy will set out an ambitious future for cancer care in Wales and give the NHS the clarity it needs to focus on this set of conditions and to deliver better services for the people of Wales."

They said that since 2015, more than 200 patients in Wales have been recruited in nearly 20 brain tumour research studies.

item.title: Virginia child dies in state’s first measles-associated death of 2026
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: News article with clear reporting on a public health issue, measles, with useful context.

Virginia reported its first measles-associated death of 2026 on Friday, involving a child who tested positive for the infectious disease, the state’s health department said.

The department said the child was age four or younger. It did not disclose additional details, including the child’s vaccination status, citing the family’s privacy.

The death adds to a worsening national measles outbreak that recently cost the US its measles elimination status after 26 years.

Pennsylvania, the hardest-hit US state, reported an eighth measles-related death and confirmed 1,631 measles cases as of Friday.

Wisconsin has also reported two deaths, while New York state recorded its first measles-associated death, involving a child.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has confirmed six measles-associated deaths so far in 2026, though it does not specify the states where the deaths were recorded.

A discrepancy between state and federal death tallies arose after the CDC, under the Trump administration’s health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, began using National Center for Health Statistics mortality data instead of state figures.

Virginia has reported 220 measles cases so far in 2026, including 40 among children four years old or younger and 75 among those age five to 12, state health department data showed as of Thursday.

Of those cases, 179 involved unvaccinated individuals, 39 were associated with people whose vaccination status was unknown and two occurred with vaccinated individuals.

“Virginia has not had a measles-related death since 1978,” said Frederic Bertley, immunologist and chief executive officer of the Center of Science and Industry. Bertley added that the measles virus infection is both alarming and evidence that measles is gaining a foothold and becoming a growing problem for the US.

Virginia health officials have reported increased measles activity driven largely by outbreaks in the state’s central region. Buckingham county has reported 127 cases, the most in the state, while neighboring Charlotte county has recorded 34 cases.

item.title: Princess of Wales speaks about impact of cancer diagnosis in BBC film Heal
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Personal account of a public figure's experience with cancer, with some useful vocabulary.

The Princess of Wales has spoken candidly about the impact of her cancer diagnosis in a BBC documentary to be aired later this month.

“Cancer does change you,” Catherine, 44, says in the trailer for the 30-minute programme. “It changes your body. It changes you physically, but there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.”

The film records Catherine taking on the Three Peaks challenge – climbing the three highest mountains in England, Scotland and Wales in 24 hours – and meeting with other people undergoing cancer treatment. Described by the BBC as a “highly personal film”, the documentary, titled Heal, will be shown on BBC One on 29 November.

The trailer emerged as it was reported that King Charles will voluntarily pay “mansion tax” on relevant royal household properties, despite crown exemption. The high-value council tax surcharge, often referred to as a mansion tax, will take effect in 2028 and apply to properties valued at more than £2m.

Catherine was diagnosed with an undisclosed form of cancer in early 2024, for which she received chemotherapy, and by January 2025 announced she was in remission.

She was treated at the Royal Marsden hospital in London, a world-leading oncology centre, with funds from the distribution of the documentary, which will also be broadcast in other countries, going to the Royal Marsden cancer charity.

When people successfully finish cancer treatment at the hospital they often ring a bell in celebration. “I didn’t ring the bell,” Catherine says in the trailer, speaking to her brother, James Middleton, as they are walking together.

“Maybe this is your ringing the bell,” he says, in reference to her undertaking the Three Peaks challenge and making the programme.

When she completed the challenge in June, 18 months after announcing that the cancer was in remission, she became the first royal to have achieved the feat – climbing Ben Nevis, Scafell Pike and Yr Wyddfa in less than 24 hours, having started on a Saturday evening.

In the programme, which will be introduced by the presenter Kirsty Young, Catherine talks about how she has learned through her recovery to find “a sense of hope and joy alongside uncertainty”.

Kate Phillips, the BBC’s chief content officer, said she hoped the documentary “will resonate with BBC viewers and provide comfort and support to those navigating their own health challenges”.

item.title: What Is an AI Inference Engine? DeepSeek DeepInfer Explained and Compared
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth explanation with useful vocabulary and context

Short answer

It decides how requests are batched, how memory is used and how work is spread across GPUs. In October 2026 DeepSeek open-sourced DeepInfer, the engine behind its own API. It is impressive but narrow: one model, the newest NVIDIA and Huawei hardware, and offline inference only. Most teams should still choose vLLM, SGLang or a managed API, and treat DeepInfer as a sign of where inference is heading.

- 1 - model DeepInfer supports at launch: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash

- 2 - hardware families: NVIDIA SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs

- 3 - parts of a full service DeepSeek left out: KV cache system, disaggregation, load balancing

- Apache - licence: Apache 2.0, free for commercial use

Most conversations about AI focus on models: which one is smartest, which tops a benchmark, which is cheapest per token. Far less attention goes to the software that actually runs those models in production. Yet that layer, the inference engine, often decides whether an AI feature responds in half a second or five, and whether it costs a few hundred dollars a month or tens of thousands.

This guide explains what an inference engine is in plain English, how it works, what DeepSeek released with DeepInfer, how it compares with the engines most teams use today, and what all of it means for different kinds of organisations, from start-ups and agencies to enterprises with strict data rules.

What is an AI inference engine?

Building an AI model has two phases. Training is when the model learns from data, a huge one-off job. Inference is when the trained model is used: you send it a prompt and it produces an answer. Every chatbot reply, code suggestion and document summary is an inference request.

A model on its own is just a very large file of numbers, its weights. To answer a question, something has to load those weights onto hardware, feed in the prompt, run billions of calculations, pick the next word, and repeat until the answer is complete, all while serving many users at once. That something is the inference engine.

A useful comparison is a database. The data is valuable, but it is the database engine, such as PostgreSQL or MySQL, that decides how queries run, how memory is used and how many users it can serve. Two companies with the same data can see very different performance depending on the engine and how it is tuned. Models and inference engines work the same way.

Inference engine, inference server, inference API

The engine runs the model. An inference server wraps it with an HTTP API, queues and monitoring. An inference API, such as OpenAI's or DeepSeek's, is a hosted service where the provider runs engine and servers for you. When you pay per token, you are paying for someone else's inference engine.

How an inference engine works

Large language models generate text one token (roughly a word fragment) at a time. Each request goes through two stages, and most engine design is about making both efficient.

- Prefill. The engine reads the whole prompt at once and builds an internal memory of it, called the KV cache. This is heavy on computation and decides how long the user waits for the first word.

- Decode. The engine produces the answer token by token, each step reading the KV cache. This is limited by memory speed and decides how fast the answer streams out.

On top of that, a production engine juggles hundreds or thousands of requests of different lengths at the same time. The main techniques it uses are:

- ⚡ Continuous batching

- 🧠 KV cache reuse

- 🗜️ Quantisation

- 🔮 Speculative decoding

- 🧩 Parallelism across chips

- 🛠️ Optimised kernels

TechniqueWhat it doesWhy it mattersContinuous batchingAdds and removes requests from the running batch at every step instead of waiting for a batch to finishKeeps expensive GPUs busy, often the biggest single throughput gainKV cache managementStores and reuses the memory of each conversation efficiently, sometimes shared between requests with the same prefixLets more users fit on the same hardware and speeds up repeated promptsQuantisationRuns the model with smaller numbers, such as 8-bit or 4-bit, instead of 16-bitCuts memory and cost, sometimes at a small quality costSpeculative decodingA quick draft predicts several tokens ahead and the full model checks them in one stepFaster answers with the same output qualityParallelismSplits a model too big for one chip across many, by layer, tensor or expertMakes very large models servable at allOptimised kernelsHand-tuned low-level code for attention and matrix maths on specific chipsSqueezes out performance that general code leaves on the tablePrefill/decode disaggregationRuns the two stages on separate machine pools sized for eachBetter latency and cost at large scale

None of these change what the model knows. They change how fast, how cheaply and how reliably it answers, which is exactly what users and finance teams notice.

Why inference engines matter now

Three shifts have pushed inference from a technical detail to a board-level cost line.

- Inference is where the money goes. Training happens once per model version; inference runs every time anyone uses the product. For a successful AI feature, inference spending keeps growing with usage.

- Open-weight models are good enough for many jobs. Models from DeepSeek, Meta, Mistral, Alibaba and others can be downloaded and run on your own infrastructure. Once you run a model yourself, the engine choice is yours too.

- Agents multiply the number of calls. An AI agent may call a model dozens of times to complete one task. Small gains in latency and cost per call compound quickly, as we discuss in our guide to scaling agentic AI without agent sprawl.

DeepSeek DeepInfer: what was released…

item.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released with Online Table Repacking and Query Planning Controls
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Technical detail and original reporting

The PostgreSQL Global Development Group released PostgreSQL 19, introducing changes to database maintenance, query planning, replication, and application development. The release focuses on reducing administrative overhead and improving performance, with new tools for reorganizing tables without downtime and controlling query plans.

One of the main additions is REPACK, which reclaims unused table space and can reorder data to match an index. Its CONCURRENTLY option allows the operation to run without blocking reads or writes, making it a potential replacement for common uses of VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER. PostgreSQL 19 also introduces pg_plan_advice and pg_stash_advice, extensions that let administrators influence query plan selection and apply stored advice to queries by identifier, without changing application code.

Other maintenance improvements include parallel index vacuuming, changes to autovacuum prioritization, and additional monitoring views. EXPLAIN ANALYZE and related logging now report asynchronous I/O activity and WAL generated for full-page images. PostgreSQL also reports that changes to foreign key checks made bulk inserts nearly twice as fast in testing. Query planner improvements include more efficient anti-joins for eligible NOT IN clauses and eager aggregation before joins.

The release adds several features for replication and application development. Logical replication now supports sequence values, and PostgreSQL automatically raises the effective WAL level to logical when the first logical replication slot is created. The new WAIT FOR LSN command lets applications wait until a standby has replayed a specified WAL position before querying data, providing read-your-writes consistency. Developers also get INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT for get-or-create operations, JSON output from COPY, additional SQL/JSON string methods, and IGNORE NULLS support for window functions.

Security and compatibility changes include server-side TLS Server Name Indication (SNI), which allows a server to present different certificates based on the hostname used by the client. PostgreSQL 19 also warns after successful MD5 password authentication. MD5 was deprecated in PostgreSQL 18 and is planned for removal in a future release, with SCRAM recommended instead. JIT compilation is now disabled by default because its cost estimates proved unreliable, while LZ4 becomes the default TOAST compression method when supported by the build.

The release has also prompted discussion on Hacker News about whether production users should wait for PostgreSQL 19.1.

Another user recommended waiting for the first minor release on critical production systems:

Personally, I would say, for critical production systems, it's still good to wait for the .1 release.

PostgreSQL 19 is available now. The complete list of changes is available in the official release notes.

In Pudding Escape, one button controls when a jelly jumps and dives. The timing changes where it lands and how much speed it carries. oddbout-bench uses the browser game’s physics to test those decisions. The simulator pauses while an agent replies, so inference latency does not change the score.

Run and verify the same attempts

From a checkout with Node.js 22.18 or newer, run the included rule-based agent on three public practice seeds.

node tools/bench/bench.mjs run --seeds 1-3 --out bench-out/heuristic -- node tools/bench/examples/heuristic-agent.mjs

node tools/bench/bench.mjs verify bench-out/heuristic/summary.json

The agent covered 2,219 m, 1,598 m, and 1,433 m. The verifier replayed all three stored traces and reproduced the scores, with zero invalid actions recorded. Three practice runs show how verification works. A model comparison needs matched seeds and enough cases to show variation.

Agents exchange JSON lines with the runner on standard input and output. For a narrower test, the same-state scenarios give agents an identical starting state and measure the result of a single decision. You can compare landing recovery without relying on both agents to reach the same spot in a full run.

The runnable examples and protocol are in the MIT-licensed oddbout-bench repository.

item.title: Common reasons why some USB ports are red
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Technical detail and original reporting

Common reasons why some USB ports are red

While there's no color-coding standard, red USB ports typically indicate these features.

Pick a USB port at random and you'll probably see either black, white or blue. While those colors are fairly standard, red, yellow or purple USB ports have also popped up on some devices. It's often unclear what exactly the color signifies. The unsatisfying yet true answer is "it depends," but it's worth looking into what a red USB port on your device could mean.

An organization known as the USB Implementers Forum sets the specifications of various USB types, but it doesn't determine what ports themselves can look like, so manufacturers are free to apply colors like red however they see fit. Different companies typically stick to one use for each color, though, and they tend to use red to signify a few similar things, including fast speeds and always-on ports.

There's no set standard for red USB ports

In general, red is used on ports of the USB 3.2 or 3.1 Gen 2 standards. Ports of this type can transfer data at up to 20 Gbps, making them some of the fastest ports in common usage. These standards were succeeded by USB4, which can reach speeds of 40 to 80 Gbps, but is only available in USB-C formats, and these are not color-coded. For most purposes, that means a red USB port is likely to indicate the fastest port available on your device.

Red ports can carry other meanings, though. Some manufacturers use red to mark always-on charging ports, which can continue supplying power to connected devices even when your computer is turned off. Red USB ports are usually best suited to SSDs or other storage devices due to their transfer speeds, but they can also be helpful to keep other devices charged overnight.

How to be sure what a USB port's color means

Since colors aren't standardized, red USB ports might not all have the same functionality even on devices from the same manufacturer. The only way to really be sure of what different colors mean without testing every port yourself is to check the manual for the specific device model you're using. While USB 3.2 and always-on ports are both fairly common, they're more likely to show up on higher-end devices like gaming laptops and motherboards than on everyday electronics.

If you can't find a model number or just want some idea of what a port does at a glance, you can also check the port itself for more information. Manufacturers often mark faster ports with the symbol SS to indicate SuperSpeed or use a number to indicate the exact speed. A lightning bolt is commonly used to mark always-on ports, though it's possible that a port with this symbol also offers a higher speed.

The good news is that the only risk you run by using the wrong colored USB port is not getting the most power out of it. USB ports are made to be backward compatible, so you can plug a cable into a port of an earlier or later USB generation and it will still work, even if it can't take advantage of its highest transfer speeds.

item.title: Solve Systems of Equations on Your TI-84: Matrices in 10 Minutes
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Technical explanation with clear steps

Solving a system of equations by hand is slow, and one small arithmetic slip can ruin the whole problem. On a TI-84 Plus, matrices turn that work into a ten-minute routine for homework, quizzes, and tests.

Why use matrices?

A system of equations is really several equations written at once. A matrix stores all the coefficients and constants in a neat grid, and the calculator does the elimination for you.

Try this 2x2 system first:

2x + 3y = 7

x - y = 1

Step 1: Enter the system as a matrix

Press 2nd then x^-1 to open the MATRX menu. Use the right arrow to choose EDIT, then select [A]. Set the size to 2 rows by 3 columns: two rows for the equations, and three columns for x, y, and the number on the right-hand side.

Type the numbers row by row, pressing ENTER after each one:

2 3 7

1 -1 1

Use the (-) key for a negative number, not the subtraction key. When the matrix is complete, press 2nd MODE to return to the home screen.

Step 2: Use rref to solve it

Press 2nd x^-1 again, then use the right arrow to choose MATH. Select rref(, then press 2nd x^-1, choose [A], close the parenthesis, and press ENTER. The calculator shows:

[1 0 2]

[0 1 1]

Read the last column as the solution: x = 2 and y = 1. Check it quickly: 2(2) + 3(1) = 7, and 2 - 1 = 1.

Solving a 3x3 system

The same method works for three equations and three unknowns:

x + y + z = 6

2x - y + z = 3

x + 2y - z = 2

Create a 3 by 4 matrix in [B], with one row for each equation and one extra column for the constants. Keep the same order every time: x, then y, then z, then the constant. Use rref([B]) exactly as before. The result should read x = 1, y = 2, and z = 3. If an answer comes out as a fraction, press MATH and choose Frac to see it clearly.

Step 3: Check your answer by graphing

For a 2x2 system, graphing is a fast sanity check. Solve each equation for y, enter both expressions in the Y= menu, and press GRAPH. The lines should cross at your solution — in the example above, at (2, 1). If they do not, check the numbers you typed into the matrix first; a single wrong coefficient is the most common mistake. You can also use 2nd TRACE and choose intersect to find the crossing point precisely. For a 3x3 system, substitute your answers back into the original equations.

Keep the equations in the same variable order, and clear an old matrix before reusing it. Once you have done this twice, it takes less than a minute to use. For more practice and worked examples with a TI-84 calculator for solving systems of equations, try a new system, enter it as a matrix, solve it with rref, and then check it by graphing.

item.title: ‘The show is starting soon. Please turn on your headphones.’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Technical explanation with clear steps

Up a few concrete steps and through the front door of a 200-year-old row house in New York City, I follow a crowd of people into the 178-seat SoHo Playhouse. As we filter to our seats, ushers hand each person a black drawstring bag with a pair of wired headphones connected to a small Auracast receiver. Then, soon after the play begins, we’re instructed to put them on.

‘The show is starting soon. Please turn on your headphones.’

Auracast broadcasts are an integral part of the storytelling in this off-Broadway show about love, connections, and hearing loss.

The headphones are an integral storytelling tool of Love Me — a one-man show from the minds of stand-up comedian and former Saturday Night Live writer Drew Michael and director Prashanth Venkataramanujam. It’s a show about love and the bid for connection, told in five chapters about different relationships in Michael’s life, bound by the threads of his hearing loss and self-discovery.

Love Me’s experimental sound design is possible thanks to Auracast, a technology based on Bluetooth that can broadcast a high-quality audio stream to any number of nearby devices. As the show follows Michael from childhood through adulthood, sound designer Daniel Kluger uses the headphones in combination with the theater speakers to create experiences that wouldn’t be possible with a traditional setup. Tinnitus ringing and hearing test tones play in the music between sections as subtle clues as the show builds to Michael’s epiphany about his hearing loss. Kluger also explores the world through varying levels of sonic clarity. Sound playing through the theater’s speakers is sometimes intentionally muffled, which is then further dulled by the headphones, giving the audience a sense of what Michael is hearing in those moments.

But one sound that stays clear and pristine is Michael’s inner monologue, heard in the headphones throughout the show. The inner monologue consists of both prerecorded tracks and the live feed from Michael’s microphone on stage as he talks back and forth with himself. “Any time you’re in my head — anything in the headphones is coming through clearly,” Michael tells me after the show. “[We’re] trying to also highlight that the appeal of the inner world is such that it’s the highest fidelity space for this person. It’s more comfortable.”

The different sound sources and treatments of the sound can lead to intentionally confusing scenes for the audience. During one, where Michael is doing a stand-up set at a comedy club, three sounds compete for attention: The theater speakers play the crowd’s reactions (including a heckler whose voice is sometimes muffled and sometimes clear); his prerecorded inner monologue reacting to the crowd plays in the headphones; and on stage, Michael is performing the set, with his mic muffled so our focus is on his inner monologue. It’s one of the definitive moments where the audience feels the constant concentration necessary to parse what’s happening when sounds aren’t clear and become overwhelming.

But the biggest impact comes during a climactic scene the sound design has been building toward, a realization that also incorporates the visuals of a series of Michael’s audiograms over the years. “I had this massive breakthrough about the whole history of what I’ve been doing — the cognitive labor, the invisible to myself labor that was affecting every single minute of my life,” Michael says. “That was a huge moment.”

That’s when the audience is instructed to remove the headphones we’ve been wearing for nearly the entire show. As Michael comes to the recognition of his relationship with his hearing loss and the clarity of mind that gives him, what we’ve become used to for the entire show’s experience — the headphones — are now gone, as is that literal weight from our heads. It’s an emotional moment, one that I’ve thought about multiple times since seeing the show.

It also leads into the final act, where Michael begins to understand his own Deaf identity. “The deafness is not the culprit, it’s the denial of it.” he tells me. “My hearing currently has never been worse, but I’ve never been more self-affirmed or self-actualized or felt happier in myself. It’s a misconception, I think, about deafness as a tragedy, deafness as a deficit, deafness as a burden, deafness as something that plagues a person.”

The ability of Auracast to broadcast an audio stream that any number of headphones can connect to is what made Love Me a possibility. Any Auracast headphones can connect to the audience broadcast — I brought along the Nothing Pro 1 to test the ability and connected to the audience broadcast channel in seconds — but I used the provided Auri receiver and Austrian Audio headset for the performance. The show’s sound was designed with those in mind, and I didn’t want the differing isolation of the Nothing headphones to affect the intent of the experience.

Love Me is presented in partnership with Deaf West Theatre, which supports Deaf-centered storytelling in theatrical productions. In addition to the audience Auracast feed, there’s one for users of hearing aids and cochlear implants that’s designed for compliance with those devices, and iPads with captions are also available. During the performance, Michael connects to his own broadcast channel with Auracast-enabled Phonak Eon Sphere hearing aids. “We talked about using in-ear monitors, but if I use an in-ear monitor, then I don’t have amplification from my environment, so then I lose contact with the audience,” Michael says. “These function as two things: They’re hearing aids and also in-ear monitors.”…

item.title: DaisyRose 27B Draws a Python Reading a Book
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Technical explanation with clear steps

We asked DaisyRose 27B to draw a python reading a book using the turtle module. It’s one of five tasks in Real Python’s informal model comparison, which explores how models handle everyday Python work. Here’s the drawing from this run:

We use the same prompts and no system prompt for each model. The results come from the returned code and replies. These informal tests explore a few habits that can affect your everyday Python work:

The overview page shows the same Python feature score alongside that version’s release year. Code can use newer features and still receive a lower score.

New Model Drops?

The run: radixark/daisyrose-27b via OpenRouter, at its default reasoning settings, with no system prompt and the returned code left unchanged.

The Five Tasks

The Snake

The script ran without errors. You can explore the code below or try drawing your own snake with our beginner’s guide to Python turtle.

turtle.py

import math

import turtle

# -------------------------------

# Setup

# -------------------------------

screen = turtle.Screen()

screen.title("Python reading a book")

screen.setup(900, 650)

screen.bgcolor("#f8f7ee")

t = turtle.Turtle()

t.speed(0)

t.hideturtle()

t.penup()

# -------------------------------

# Helper drawing functions

# -------------------------------

def line(x1, y1, x2, y2, color="black", width=3):

"""Draw a line from (x1, y1) to (x2, y2)."""

t.pencolor(color)

t.pensize(width)

t.penup()

t.goto(x1, y1)

t.pendown()

t.goto(x2, y2)

def polygon(points, fill=None, outline="black", width=3):

"""Draw a polygon from a list of (x, y) points."""

t.pencolor(outline)

t.pensize(width)

t.penup()

t.goto(points[0])

t.pendown()

if fill:

t.fillcolor(fill)

t.begin_fill()

for point in points[1:]:

t.goto(point)

t.goto(points[0])

if fill:

t.end_fill()

def circle(x, y, radius, fill=None, outline="black", width=3):

"""Draw a circle centered at (x, y)."""

t.pencolor(outline)

t.pensize(width)

t.penup()

t.goto(x, y - radius)

t.setheading(0)

t.pendown()

if fill:

t.fillcolor(fill)

t.begin_fill()

t.circle(radius)

if fill:

t.end_fill()

def polyline(points, color="black", width=3):

"""Draw a connected line through a list of points."""

t.pencolor(color)

t.pensize(width)

t.penup()

t.goto(points[0])

t.pendown()

for point in points[1:]:

t.goto(point)

# -------------------------------

# Draw the book

# -------------------------------

def draw_book():

# Blue covers of an open book

left_cover = [

(-15, -210),

(-190, -235),

(-155, -95),

(-15, -70)

]

right_cover = [

(15, -210),

(190, -235),

(155, -95),

(15, -70)

]

polygon(left_cover, fill="#1976d2", outline="#0d47a1", width=4)

polygon(right_cover, fill="#1976d2", outline="#0d47a1", width=4)

# White pages

left_page = [

(-10, -195),

(-170, -215),

(-140, -105),

(-10, -85)

]

right_page = [

(10, -195),

(170, -215),

(140, -105),

(10, -85)

]

polygon(left_page, fill="#ffffff", outline="#757575", width=2)

polygon(right_page, fill="#ffffff", outline="#757575", width=2)

# Center fold / spine lines

line(-10, -85, 10, -85, "#424242", 6)

line(-10, -85, -10, -195, "#424242", 6)

line(10, -85, 10, -195, "#424242", 6)

# Fake text lines on the pages

for i in range(1, 6):

y = -105 - i * 15

line(

-125 + i * 3,

y + i * 2,

-20 - i * 3,

y - i * 3,

"#bdbdbd",

2

)

line(

20 + i * 3,

y - i * 3,

125 - i * 3,

y + i * 2,

"#bdbdbd",

2

)

# -------------------------------

# Draw the python/snake

# -------------------------------

def draw_snake():

# Spiral parameters for the snake body

cx, cy = 0, 40

r_start, r_end = 100, 35

turns = 2.5

# End the spiral at the bottom so the head faces downward

end_angle = -math.pi / 2

total_angle = turns * 2 * math.pi

start_angle = end_angle - total_angle

points = []

steps = 800

for i in range(steps + 1):

frac = i / steps

theta = start_angle + frac * total_angle

r = r_start + (r_end - r_start) * frac

x = cx + r * math.cos(theta)

y = cy + r * math.sin(theta)

points.append((x, y))

# Draw a dark outline, then a green body over it

polyline(points, color="#1b5e20", width=28)

polyline(points, color="#43a047", width=20)

# Head position: end of the spiral

hx, hy = points[-1]

# Draw the head

circle(hx, hy - 8, 27, fill="#66bb6a", outline="#1b5e20", width=4)

# Eyes looking down at the book

eye_y = hy - 18

circle(hx - 11, eye_y, 7, fill="#ffffff", outline="black", width=2)

circle(hx + 11, eye_y, 7, fill="#ffffff", outline="black", width=2)

circle(hx - 11, eye_y - 2, 3, fill="#000000", outline="black", width=1)

circle(hx + 11, eye_y - 2, 3, fill="#000000", outline="black", width=1)

# Reading glasses

circle(hx - 11, eye_y, 11, fill=None, outline="#212121", width=4)

circle(hx + 11, eye_y, 11, fill=None, outline="#212121", width=4)

line(hx - 2, eye_y, hx + 2, eye_y, "#212121", 4)

# Mouth

line(hx - 8, hy - 26, hx + 8, hy - 26, "#212121", 3)

# Tongue

line(hx, hy - 26, hx, hy - 44, "#d32f2f", 5)

line(hx, hy - 44, hx - 6, hy - 52, "#d32f2f", 4)…

item.title: Vertex’s executive chairman: Here’s how we got our drug-trial success rate over 70% when the industry’s is 10% to 20%
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: highly informative and well-structured

Corporate America is locked in an innovation arms race – a race that is turning out very few winners. Companies are spending billions on R&D, acquisitions and new technologies, operating on the seemingly intuitive premise that making more bets is the best way to approach the uncertainty of the future.

But more bets don’t necessarily produce more successes.

There’s no more extreme example of this problem than pharmaceuticals and biotech. It takes an average of 10 to 15 years for a drug to go from the lab to regulatory approval. And more than 90% of drugs that enter clinical development fail. Just look at the headlines: one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical companies recently suffered three drug trial failures in a single week despite an enormous R&D budget, many talented scientists and a deep pipeline.

But this problem is far from unique to healthcare. In consumer tech, many startups flame out after a single hit; in automotive, EV pioneers are routinely outpaced by fast followers; digital investments in retail often fail to translate into customer growth.

The instinctive response when innovation fails is to do more of it: fund more projects, pursue more ideas, make more acquisitions and place more bets. If innovation is inherently unpredictable, the thinking goes, the best way to improve your chances of success is to increase the number of shots you take.

This kind of thinking is completely backward. It’s not about the shots. It’s about the target.

Imagine entering a darts tournament and throwing five consecutive bull’s-eyes, only to discover that you have been throwing at the wrong board. Your accuracy doesn’t matter. You’ve lost.

More activity creates the appearance of innovation without improving its effectiveness. I learned this the hard way.

When I joined Vertex Pharmaceuticals in 2009, the company had spent two decades investing heavily in R&D across 20 different programs. Yet, it produced only a single breakthrough product, which was rendered obsolete just two and a half years later with the approval of a better and more tolerable treatment discovered by another company.

When we examined why drug development failed so frequently, the problem wasn’t that scientists had failed to create a drug that hit its intended biological target. The problem was that they had chosen the wrong target in the first place.

Building a Smaller Sandbox

The solution was to take away choices, constraining ourselves to a “sandbox” of diseases with genetically- or pharmacologically-validated targets where we believed we had a much higher probability of success.

Most importantly, both R&D and business development had to stay inside the same sandbox. A fascinating scientific discovery or enticing acquisition wasn’t enough. If it didn’t fit our strategy or if we didn’t have a validated target to address, we walked away.

That last part may be the most difficult lesson for any leader. Companies often celebrate the ability to say yes to innovation. Sustainable innovators also become very good at saying no. Focus and strategy don’t limit innovation, they accelerate it.

Stop Treating Innovation as an R&D Department

A thriving innovation program requires many parts of an organization working in harmony. Yet companies unintentionally divide innovation into functional silos, with each group incentivized differently and no one focused on the big picture.

Researchers discover something and hand it to developers. Developers hand it to manufacturing. Eventually, commercial teams are asked to sell it. Business development may operate on a separate track entirely, hunting for external opportunities.

But a brilliant invention that cannot be efficiently developed, manufactured or commercialized isn’t a successful innovation.

To break down internal silos, leaders from research, development, regulatory, manufacturing, commercial and other key business units should be included in decisions about new product development from the earliest stages of the innovation process. And internal and external innovation must be tightly integrated into the same strategy. Business development can’t be given permission to roam the universe looking for any interesting assets; partnerships and acquisitions must reinforce the same strategy, diseases, and targets where a company believes it has a high probability of success.

Innovation shouldn’t be measured by how many ideas an organization generates. It should be judged by how effectively the entire organization converts its best ideas into products that meet people’s needs and create meaningful value.

Success Should Lead to More Serial Innovation

Once innovation succeeds, companies tend to become complacent and stop innovating to create better and better medicines for the same disease. Our experience seeing one of our breakthrough drugs quickly made obsolete by an innovative competitor created a sense of urgency, and even some paranoia, which drove our organization to continuously try to “out-innovate ourselves.”

Being first doesn’t guarantee long term success. Competitors will learn from your breakthroughs and improve on the foundations you laid. We decided that if someone was going to build a better second-generation product, it should be us.

The results were dramatic. Vertex went on to develop multiple transformative medicines, including 5 medicines that alter the course of cystic fibrosis for 95% of patients and, with CRISPR Therapeutics, the first FDA-approved human gene-editing therapy for patients with severe Sickle Cell Disease and transfusion-dependent B-thalassemia. More recently we created a completely new class of non-opioid medicines for moderate to severe acute pain.…

item.title: Nvidia’s next CEO must lead a supervised international business—amid the ‘complete reorganization of the AI equilibrium,’ investor says
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: in-depth analysis of a significant business challenge

Following the ouster of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO, the company’s next chief executive will inherit a company facing a fundamentally different set of challenges than the ones that once propelled it to become the world’s most valuable company.

Beyond sustaining demand for its AI chips, the next leader needs to navigate intensifying U.S. export restrictions, investigations into the company’s China business and scrutiny of its financial arrangements.

That’s according to Nvidia investor Bill Birmingham, managing director at REX Financial—the parent company of REX Shares, which oversees $8.5 billion in assets under management.

“The bigger problem going forward isn’t actually who sits in the CEO chair. It is the Chinese chip access,” he told Fortune via email.

For years, U.S. restrictions sought to limit China’s ability to purchase Nvidia’s most powerful processors. But Huang’s affair with an executive at Singapore-based tech company Megaspeed raised concerns about Chinese companies accessing restricted hardware.

The Trump administration is now moving to plug those gaps. Last Sunday, the federal government announced a rule to close a loophole that allowed remote access to advanced AI chips and servers via overseas data centers. And on Friday, President Donald Trump said he wanted to prevent American companies from building data centers overseas.

“Whoever runs Nvidia next will inherit a narrower, more closely supervised international business and the complete reorganization of the AI equilibrium that comes with it,” Birmingham said.

The company’s latest earnings demonstrate how big its commercial momentum remained following its news spiral. Nvidia reported $115.8 billion in revenue for Q3 2026, a 103% increase from a year earlier. Its data center business generated $107.6 billion, accounting for approximately 93% of total revenue.

But Birmingham argued that the earnings are becoming less important than what management says about future demand, pricing power and the sustainability of the AI investment cycle.

A company under heavy investigation

The California attorney general’s office subpoenaed Nvidia as part of an investigation into whether the company or Huang enabled China to obtain advanced chips or confidential information—or misled investors about the associated risks.

The SEC is also investigating the company over whether the company misled investors in its public disclosures, according to the New York Post. The civil probe comes amid questions from officials on whether Nvidia knew about its potential diversion of chips to China and whether its disclosures adequately addressed the risks.

Trump has also said the FBI is investigating Huang’s relationship with Megaspeed’s Alice Huang and any ties to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations.

Congress will join in the scrutiny too. Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter have agreed to appear before three House committees about the company’s potential role in allowing Chinese entities to access advanced American chips.

Lawmakers will probe the Commerce Department’s role after the House Foreign Affairs Committee disclosed on Thursday that the Commerce Department had approved 879,868 advanced semiconductor shipments to Chinese companies across 21 license applications between December 2025 and May 2026.

There’s also an AI infrastructure problem

Export restrictions are also just one piece of the puzzle Nvidia needs to solve. The company has to contend with the financial structure supporting unprecedented expansion of AI infrastructure, according to Birmingham.

The concern is that demand for Nvidia’s processors are tied to the ability of hyperscalers and smaller cloud providers to finance enormous data center investments. But that creates a fragile relationship between Nvidia’s hardware sales and the financial health of its customers, Birmingham said.

“Given the AI ecosystem is being heavily supported by vendor financing and debt markets, the potential for a telecom style bust is significant,” he warned.

Birmingham said Nvidia’s August announcement that it intended to mobilize more than $500 billion in third-party capital through partnerships with major financial institutions—including BlackRock, Goldman Sachs, KKR and others—to finance AI infrastructure was concerning. He said the commitments were “clear” they were “made exclusively by Huang,” meaning investors would need clarity about whether the company intends to maintain them.

In its latest quarterly filing, Nvidia disclosed that the financing platforms were still preliminary arrangements that might not result in definitive agreements. The company outlined that it could provide limited residual-value support for specific projects at its discretion.

Unlike established hyperscalers, neocloud providers have less flexibility to absorb rising hardware and financing costs, Birmingham said.

“They need near-perfect utilization to stay profitable,” he added. “In general, they can only pass along higher costs to new contracts, and only when compute stays scarce.”

This means if demand weakens, neocloud providers could find themselves paying for expensive computing infrastructure without being able to generate the revenue to service their debt.

“Investors are assessing whether the AI supply cycle is running too hot, and if a break point in compute demand will force a pullback in datacenter build out that becomes self-reinforcing across the system,” he explained.

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-22 12:30 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

Why it is here: clear reporting on a current issue with useful context

Centrica boss 'hugely concerned' over impact of soaring energy bills

The boss of British Gas owner Centrica says he is "hugely concerned" about the impact the expected jump in energy bills in January will have on consumers.

Chris O'Shea told the BBC he thought the number of people unable or unwilling to pay their energy bills would rise when prices go up in the new year.

The new energy price cap to take effect from January will be announced on Wednesday and consultancy Cornwall Insight has forecast it will jump by Â£443 a year for a typical household.

The government has said some households will get Â£100 to help with energy bills, but Citizens Advice said it was a "drop in the ocean" while one pressure group called for action on "inflated energy firm profits".

Speaking to the Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme, O'Shea said the predictions were for a "substantial increase" in bills from January were "materially correct", adding that the first quarter of the year was the time when most energy was consumed.

"That's right at the point where people will be paying for Christmas and the like. So I am hugely concerned," he said.

O'Shea added there was a "massive problem" with people not paying their bills in the UK, with some not able to pay their bills and an "increasing number of people that are choosing not to pay their bills".

He said the collective impact of that was that "every single electricity consumer, is paying about Â£1.50, Â£1.60 a week to cover the cost of people that are not paying their bills, and it's just going to get worse when bills go up".

The amount owed to energy suppliers by households hit Â£5bn in the April to June period, according to energy regulator Ofgem.

Wholesale energy prices paid by suppliers have been rising this year as a result of the conflict in the Middle East, which has pushed up bills for households.

Cornwall Insight has predicted Ofgem's energy price cap will rise by 26% to Â£2,166 a year for a typical household from 1 January.

The price cap affects about 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales and sets a maximum price for each unit of gas and electricity, so the actual level of bills will vary according to energy usage.

The government has said some households will get a Â£100 payment to help with energy bills, a policy which was announced in the Budget.

The government has also temporarily cut 5% VAT from electricity bills until the end of June next year, which is expected to save the typical household about Â£45 a year.

But consumer groups have argued the Â£100 payment announced in the Budget will not be enough for some.

Citizens Advice said it was a "drop in the ocean" and that we would see "cold-related deaths" this winter.

"For someone in a lot of debt, who can't afford their bills, it's not going to touch the sides."

The Fuel Poverty Action Group said the government and Ofgem needed to take stronger action against energy companies.

"Our inflated energy prices are driven by inflated energy firm profits," the group said.

"Government and Ofgem must take stronger action against this blatant profiteering whilst we suffer in cold homes, or are forced into debt."

Energy firms operating in the UK are subject to a windfall tax that was introduced in 2022.

When the windfall tax is added to other taxes levied, it means the overall tax rate on profits earned by oil and gas companies operating in the UK is 78%.

item.title: How to finance nature
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting on a unique approach to conservation

From debt-for-nature swaps to wildlife bonds, new financial deals are bringing private investors into conservation

A version of this article originally appeared in Quartz’s members-only Weekend Brief newsletter. Quartz members get access to exclusive newsletters and more. Sign up here.

Most people don’t think of going to a climate summit to close a financial deal. But this year’s U.N. climate summit is shaping up differently.

A week before COP31 was due to open in Antalya, Turkey, Bank of America . It backs companies that protect ecosystems, from supply-chain tracking to DNA-based wildlife monitoring.

Daily Brief

Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz.

By subscribing, you agree to our Terms of Service and Privacy Policy.

and a sustainable investing group founded by King Charles III launched

More deals making time was set up for the summit. The COP organizers are putting on a Finance Day that will cover how to make nature projects something investors can actually buy and a Nordic development fund has planned a session where climate funds would pitch investors directly.

There are several financial instruments for financing nature. The oldest and best known is the debt-for-nature swap. A country with heavy debt gets some of it bought at a discount, then renegotiated on better terms in exchange for spending part of the savings on conservation. Bolivia struck the first in 1987, which was worth $650,000.

The deals have grown since. Ecuador’s 2023 swap for the Galapagos Islands bought roughly $1.6 billion of its bonds for $656 million and freed about $450 million for conservation. Many of the biggest swaps relied on a safeguard. Guarantees from the U.S. government promised to repay investors if political turmoil interrupted payments, which made the new debt safe enough to buy.

The market went quiet for a while, with only about $6 billion in swaps with private capital being done from 2021 to 2024. Renewed interest returned in February, when Britain’s biggest asset manager, Legal & General, committed up to $1 billion to anchor a new generation of deals.

Bonds are another route, and come in a variety of setups. The World Bank’s “rhino bond” was one. In 2022 it raised $150 million from investors who gave up their interest payments, about $9 million in all, so the money could go to protecting black rhinos in two South African parks. Investors were due their principal back in March 2027, plus a bonus of up to $13.8 million if the rhino population grew.

Others looked more like ordinary business. Funds like the one with King Charles III put money into companies and expected a commercial return. Payments for ecosystem services, usually run by governments, rewarded the conservation of a forest or wetland, and environmental credits, which works like carbon offsets, sold verified conservation as a tradable certificate.

It's still early to judge how well many of these instruments work. Some of the biggest deals are only a few years old, and their conservation commitments will take much longer to measure.

But there's pressure to scale them: the market is being built against an enormous funding gap. Private finance classified as nature-related has grown from $9.4 billion in 2020 to $102 billion in 2024, but even that jump left a vast amount of conservation unfunded, with BloombergNEF estimating the debt swap market could be as large as $1 trillion.

The deals themselves have drawn criticism. Debt Justice, a British campaign group, found that four swaps cut national debt by an average of 3%, while ordinary restructurings cut it about seven times more.

A French advocacy group calculated that Belize put $84 million of a $553 million deal toward nature. In Gabon the figure was $67.5 million, with the rest going to repay debt and pay fees.

Then there is Washington. Political risk guarantees from the U.S. government underpinned swaps in Ecuador, Belize, Gabon and El Salvador, and that went away after Donald Trump returned to office.

That leaves private investors to carry more of the load. But getting them to invest means finding conservation projects that can deliver a return, and there aren't enough of those yet. McKinsey cited fragmented data and ecosystem outcomes that are hard to price as two reasons why.

Even if private investment grows, the hardest conservation work may remain beyond its reach. Markets can channel money toward nature where they can extract a return. They are less equipped to pay for protection whose benefits are diffuse, long-term or impossible to monetize.

Source: Quartz | Published: 2026-11-22 10:10 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: I am SNL’s ‘sister.’ caregiving is an act of love, but love isn’t a care plan
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: engaging narrative with clear business implications

The Saturday Night Live’s “Sister” sketch struck a chord with families across the nation. Why? Because they saw themselves in the story. Let’s face it: when an aging parent needs care, it’s often the women, the “Sisters”, who step up and take on the responsibility.

I’m grateful to SNL for bringing this topic forward. Sometimes humor opens the door to a conversation we have been avoiding. But recognizing the problem is only the beginning. We have to change what we expect from the women in our families.

For me, watching the video was painful and hit very close to home. And the many texts I received afterward, as CEO of A Place for Mom, were even more heartbreaking. I am the sister. I know firsthand what that responsibility feels like because my mom and I cared for my incredible grandparents for nearly 20 years.

I came to the United States as a teenager and helped my grandparents navigate senior care while still learning the system myself. I know what it means to feel tremendous guilt, worry about people you love, and not know where to turn.

For 25 years, we have been helping families navigate one of life’s most difficult and emotional journeys: finding care for an aging loved one. More than 2.3 million families have turned to us for support, and approximately 40% of family caregivers we serve are daughters, daughter-in-laws, nieces and sisters-in-law. In fact, more than two-thirds of the people that reach out are women.

Once we connect with the family, our goal is to help them understand where to start, make sense of their options, navigate difficult decisions, and feel more confident about what comes next. When families are ready to explore care, we connect them with providers across our network of more than 15,000 senior living communities and home care agencies, helping them find options that align with their individual needs, preferences, and budgets.

The service we provide is at no cost to families as we are paid by our provider network.

Over the past seven years at the company, I’ve also witnessed firsthand the uncertainty, guilt, and fear that so many of the families we support experience. When Mom or Dad falls, who gets the call? Who manages medications, makes appointments, and researches care options? Nationally, women account for 61% of unpaid caregivers, according to AARP. And once she starts, everyone assumes she will keep doing it. And she does. In A Place for Mom’s 2026 Women and Caregiving report, we found that women caregivers report stress, guilt, and overwhelm more often than men, and 53% have trouble sleeping at least once a week. They also give up more of what they earn: 33% of household income, compared with 29% for men, from households already bringing in about $15,000 less.

We have somehow talked ourselves into the idea that the more a woman sacrifices, the more we should praise her. She steps back from work. Puts off her own appointments. We tell her how strong she is. We should be asking what support she needs and taking responsibility for providing it.

Two things need to change.

First, caregiving has to be a family responsibility. Brothers, sons, and other family members need to be involved. Many already are. We need more.

Make the appointment and handle the follow-up. Research the care options. Commit to regular support. “Tell me what you need” still leaves her responsible for figuring it out and assigning it.

Every person’s contribution will look different. Distance, finances, health, and work matter. Discuss those realities instead of assuming one person will cover everything.

Second, we have to stop treating sacrifice and suffering as proof of love. You are not a better daughter because you are losing income or neglecting your health. Getting support does not mean you love your parents less.

This holiday season, my wish is that families have an honest conversation about what help Mom or Dad needs and who will take responsibility.

An easy way to start is by discussing needs, expectations, and what each person can contribute. Importantly, the conversation needs to be candid, specific, and have clear follow-through. And please, don’t leave it to “Sister” to organize that, too. Siblings can start together, then bring Mom or Dad into the conversation, with their preferences at the center of the plan.

Having a sister is a gift, not a senior care strategy.

To our sisters: We see you. You deserve support and time to be a daughter or sister, not always the caregiver.

To everyone counting on her: Take responsibility for something she can stop carrying.

item.title: MP criticises Guernsey and Jersey company ownership register plans
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: important topic with clear reporting, though less in-depth

MP criticises company ownership register plans

Plans to improve transparency over company ownership in Guernsey and Jersey have come under criticism from a Westminster MP, who says they "do not go nearly far enough".

The comments come after Guernsey, external and Jersey, external set out plans to allow approved applicants access to information about who owns or controls companies when investigating suspected financial crime.

Sir Andrew Mitchell, who has campaigned for greater scrutiny of company ownership, said there were "immediate indications" the proposals would fall short.

He said limits on access to the information could mean "national security threats may remain entirely invisible to investigators".

The plans follow a joint commitment made by Guernsey, Jersey and the Isle of Man in December 2023 to increase transparency around company ownership and help tackle money laundering, terrorist financing and other financial crime.

Currently, information about who ultimately owns or controls companies is generally only available to law enforcement agencies, regulators and certain regulated businesses carrying out anti-money laundering checks.

The new proposals would allow journalists, academics and other applicants with a legitimate interest to apply for access.

'Defeats the object'

Sir Andrew said investigators could face a "catch-22" because they may need access to the register to prove wrongdoing in the first place.

He also said he understood applicants would have to show they had been unable to find the information elsewhere, arguing: "This entirely defeats the object of a register."

Jersey's consultation response says applicants would be expected to show that "all reasonable alternative sources have been exhausted" before access was granted.

Guernsey's published response does not explicitly set out the same requirement.

He said: "Access should be open to those from other jurisdictions, for example those in the global south from whom much of the world's dirty money was stolen in the first place."

Sir Andrew also questioned whether users would have to pay to access the information, saying: "This information should be free at the point of access."

He said the proposals should eventually lead to fully public registers.

'Effective transparency framework'

Both the governments of Guernsey and Jersey rejected Sir Andrew's criticism and said they continue to meet international standards in tackling financial crime.

A Government of Jersey spokesperson said the concerns raised by him "do not accurately reflect what is in Jersey's consultation response paper".

They said the policy was intended to help Jersey meet its international commitments while maintaining "a fair, proportionate, and effective transparency framework".

They added: "Jersey continues to meet international standards for transparency and countering money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation financing."

'Tried and tested'

Deputy Andrew Niles, from Guernsey's Policy & Resources Committee, rejected Sir Andrew's criticism and pointed to a positive 2025 assessment of the island's efforts to tackle financial crime, external.

He said: "Guernsey does not accept the suggestion that our proposals fall short of the commitments we've made on beneficial ownership transparency or that the island does not meet international standards on beneficial ownership transparency."

He said the framework would provide access for people with a legitimate interest in investigating crime while protecting privacy and vulnerable individuals.

"The proposal is based on a tried and tested model adopted in the EU," he added.

Source: BBC Business | Published: 2026-11-22 07:22 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100
