item.title: Employers are being asked to give interview feedback - here's what applicants want
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful information for job seekers, though not a deep dive

Employers are being asked to give interview feedback - here's what applicants want

Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer?

So-called "job ghosting" has become a big problem for jobseekers in the UK, leaving them "demoralised", denting their confidence and undermining their hopes of finding work.

It's an issue that was mentioned in former minister Alan Milburn's major review into young people who are not in employment, education or training - those dubbed as Neets - this week.

Among his recommendations - aimed at reducing the proportion of Neets from 13% to about 5% by 2036 - Milburn proposed that large employers should give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 "meaningful feedback".

The report's proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.

But is feedback for all applicants realistic, given the vast number of applications these firms receive? And what can people do to improve their chances in such a tough job market?

Yugraj Samrai, 23, from Coventry is currently unemployed and says he has submitted hundreds of job applications since he graduated from his marketing degree in July.

But 30 to 40% of the time he hears nothing back at all, which can make him "feel like a statistic, not a person".

He tells the BBC: "I understand there are very few graduate jobs available, but at least give me a response to say whether I'll progress onto the next stage or not."

'I'm just not hearing anything'

Ffion Johns, from Llanelli, has been unemployed since June and did not get an interview until September after submitting 70 applications.

The 24-year-old says her biggest problem throughout the job-hunting process has been the lack of feedback about why she didn't get the job, so she knows what to fix next time.

Sometimes she has even been ghosted after attending an interview.

"With most of these roles I'm not getting a rejection. I'm just not hearing anything, which can be quite frustrating," she says.

Research by head-hunting firm Robert Walters last year found 86% of UK job hunters said their applications had been ignored, with no response at all from the hiring organisation.

The Milburn report, external says this "wall of silence" is especially hard on young people as it gives them "nothing to learn from". It adds that "time and emotional investment" goes into their applications.

"It can really take hours and hours, so it just feels even worse to not even have that be recognised," says Jessica Anderson, 21, from Swindon.

Employers say they are being flooded with job applications in a very competitive jobs market and it can be hard to respond to all of them.

And AI is adding to the problem, enabling applicants to submit large numbers of applications in the hope of improving their chances.

But Meg Burton, a career coach based in Leeds, says firms should at the very least inform job applicants when they are unsuccessful and that AI could help achieve this.

Candidates should also be given proper feedback if they reach the interview stage, she says.

"It doesn't have to be hugely detailed, it's just some pointers on why they were unsuccessful and what they can learn from that experience going forward," she says.

The government could choose to adopt the Milburn proposals and crack down on job ghosting.

But it raises another question: if candidates began receiving significantly more rejections than before, could this itself have a demoralising effect?

Ellie McCrone, 20, from Northampton understands the concern but thinks hearing back and getting constructive feedback where possible is always best.

"If you are applying for hundreds of jobs and never getting anything, I think something is going wrong... You can't fix something unless you know what the problem is."

There are things applicants can do to improve their chances and avoid ghosting, such as tailoring their CV to each job and not submitting "hundreds and hundreds of applications" that all look the same, Burton adds.

Candidates should also never take being ghosted personally, she adds.

"Not hearing back doesn't mean you aren't a great candidate. Put it down to experience and move on."

item.title: Tech’s biggest names sank a tax on billionaires’ wealth with $425m and a familiar playbook
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: interesting case study with some relevance to business

In the hours after polls closed on election day, tech industry players began praising Sergey Brin, the co-founder of Google, on social media.

“Huge thanks to Sergey Brin here,” wrote Garry Tan, the CEO of Y Combinator. Venture capitalist Ilya Sukhar posted: “God bless Sergey Brin.” And David Marcus, a crypto entrepreneur, simply wrote: “Hero.”

They were all referring to Brin’s instrumental role in the defeat of California’s wealth tax ballot measure, known as Proposition 40. The proposed one-time 5% tax on billionaires in the state was defeated by just over five points. Simultaneously, an opposition initiative that would ban any taxation on billionaire wealth, Proposition 42, put on the ballot by Brin and a cohort of the state’s ultra-rich, is poised to pass.

Brin, whose net worth is about $230bn, contributed at least $132m to the fight – more than any other donor. The runner-up was former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, who gave more than $48m. Millions more were donated by executives from Palantir, DoorDash, Stripe and Reddit, along with prominent venture capitalists. All told, Silicon Valley’s elite raised nearly $425m to sink the tax, according to campaign finance filings, making it the most expensive opposition campaign in state history.

Over the last month, the campaign poured those dollars into highly produced ads and mailers that bombarded voters with warnings that the tax was dangerous and would hurt everyday people. Taglines from the campaign said Prop 40 was an “everyone tax”, “reckless experiment” and “you’re next”. While supporters of the tax said the money would go toward funding the state’s healthcare losses from Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, opponents repeatedly sent the message to voters that it would make healthcare funding worse.

Even without Prop 40’s outsized opponents, the pro-billionaire tax campaign had a difficult task. It had to convince Californians that this specific one-time tax, chiefly geared toward healthcare funding, was the right way to address losses from Trump’s bill. The idea of zeroing in on billionaires ruffled feathers across the state with major political figures opposing it, including Gavin Newsom, the governor, and Xavier Becerra, the governor elect.

Then there was the funding. In comparison with the billionaires’ war chest, the pro-Prop 40 camp, sponsored by the union SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West (SEIU-UHW), raised just more than $31m. They were outspent nearly 14-fold.

“All lies have a shelf life,” said Suzanne Jimenez, the chief of staff for the SEIU-UHW. “Billionaire-funded propaganda may mislead voters about the consequences of these cuts today, but as hospitals reduce services, emergency rooms close and families lose access to care, the truth will become increasingly difficult to hide.”

The counties that voted to pass Prop 40 are typically more Democratic and where many of the state’s wealthy reside, including Los Angeles, San Francisco and other areas around the Bay Area. The counties that overwhelmingly voted against the measure were mostly red, rural and poor. While many of these counties swung blue in US House races this election, up to 80% of voters there voted no on Prop 40, according to the latest count.

Rob Lalka, a business professor at Tulane University and author of The Venture Alchemists: How Big Tech Turned Profits Into Power, compared the Prop 40 campaign with Uber and Lyft’s ballot measure crusade in 2020, where the companies spent more than $200m to defeat an initiative over labor rights for drivers. The ride-hailing companies used similar tactics, Lalka said, something he describes as “misleading propaganda and paying for endorsements”.

“The money also seemed astonishing at the time: the amount to influence the outcome, over $200m, was a massive sum,” Lalka said. “Money in politics has only increased in California throughout this decade. That’s the context for Prop 40 this election cycle.”

The colossal funding of political campaigns has broken records nationwide this midterm cycle, said Francesco Trebbi, a business and public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He pointed to Elon Musk dumping $446m into House and Senate races across the county, but noted that it was ineffective in places such as Texas: Musk’s mark, James Talarico, won.

“Maybe it was easier to decouple Prop 40 opposition from President Trump’s agenda, so Brin had an easier target to hit,” Trebbi said. Still, he added: “We need a lot more data and statistical evidence in order to conclusively finalize this discussion.”

Exit polls haven’t yet been released for Prop 40, which will give more details on voters’ decisions. In the meantime, the SEIU-UHW’s Jimenez said that despite the loss, the union and its allies are not going to give up on the long game: “If Sacramento fails to protect patients and deliver a real solution that makes billionaires pay their fair share, healthcare workers will pursue every available avenue, up to and including returning to the ballot in 2028 with a billionaire tax.”

Source: The Guardian Business | Published: 2026-11-10 13:19 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: How wildfire litigation became big business in America
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting with concrete detail and useful vocabulary

On a November morning in 2018, the foothills of the Sierra Nevada were primed to burn. Northern California had received little rainfall, and the grasses and shrubs above the town of Paradise were bone dry. Humidity levels were dangerously low as winds up to 40 miles per hour gusted downslope toward the 26,000-person community.

When a live wire broke free from a 99-year-old transmission tower owned by Pacific Gas and Electric Co., Paradise stood little chance.

The arcing wire ignited the brush below to start the Camp Fire, which claimed the lives of 85 people and destroyed more than 18,000 structures in a matter of hours, charring whole neighborhoods to displace tens of thousands of people. It was the deadliest wildfire in California’s history.

But another metric would later come to define the fire that destroyed Paradise.

Thousands of victims sued PG&E. The utility eventually agreed to settle their claims for $13.5 billion in compensation for the Camp Fire, as well as other blazes ignited by its equipment in Northern California in 2017 and 2018. It was one of the largest civil settlements for an environmental disaster in U.S. history, driving the company to bankruptcy and demonstrating that utilities could be held liable for huge sums when faulty equipment ignites conflagrations.

The settlement sparked a wave of lawsuits against utilities implicated in wildfire ignitions across the country. Today, wildfire litigation is a multibillion-dollar business in the U.S., with more than $18 billion awarded or agreed to in civil settlements for victims in California, Hawaiʻi, Colorado and Oregon since 2017. Utility companies PG&E, PacifiCorp, Xcel Energy and Southern California Edison have so far borne the brunt of such claims.

Litigation focuses on ignitions

This year is shaping up to be among the worst on record for U.S. wildfires. Following a mild winter in which precipitation often fell as rain, mountain ranges including the Rockies and California’s Sierra Nevada were left with one of the lightest snowpacks in recent history. As of October, more than 9 million acres have burned in wildfires across the U.S. — about 1.5 times the average in the past decade for the year to date, according to the National Interagency Fire Center.

Lawsuits have followed in lockstep. Already, some Colorado residents have sued San Isabel Electric Association, a not-for-profit rural electric cooperative, for allegedly sparking the Aspen Acres Fire, which ranks as the seventh-largest wildfire in state history and destroyed more than 320 homes. An investigation into the fire by state officials found that an aspen tree had fallen onto energized powerlines, starting the blaze.

As the wildfire crisis confronting America accelerates and intensifies, some question whether a litigious approach to address mounting losses is sustainable — or just — in a world reshaped by climate change. Especially so because the actual number of wildfire ignitions hasn’t changed much over the decades.

“California hasn’t seen a big increase in the number of fires,” said Chris Field, a climate scientist at Stanford University. “What’s really changed is the probability that a little fire grows into a gigantic, devastating one.”

As the planet has warmed, landscapes have grown more flammable. At the same time, millions of houses have been built in wildfire-prone areas, risking greater property losses.

Yet utility lawsuits have emerged as a seemingly state-sanctioned climate resilience strategy to help homeowners deal with losses as the insurance industry backs out of areas with high fire danger. With such an approach, if your house burns down in a wildfire, you had better hope a large utility with deep pockets was responsible for the ignition, rather than lightning or a private individual.

“The people in the Palisades Fire, they’re just out of luck,” said Richard Bridgford, a California trial attorney who has represented close to 12,000 wildfire victims in cases against utilities in California and Hawaiʻi.

Authorities arrested a 29-year-old former Uber driver in connection with that blaze, one of the two large fires that tore through Los Angeles County in January 2025, causing tens of billions of dollars in damage. (A federal judge declared a mistrial of the alleged arsonist in June, with jurors deadlocked 10-2 in favor of his acquittal in the criminal case.) With no legally definitive source of ignition, thousands of victims are now suing the city of Los Angeles, the L.A. Department of Water and Power and the state of California for $10 billion for alleged contributions to the fire’s damage, including gross negligence in failing to fully extinguish hot spots from a previous fire and failing to provide sufficient water to fight the blaze.

Left to market forces alone, wildfire litigation shows little sign of slowing down. But the U.S. appears to be heading toward a reckoning over ever-rising payouts, as policymakers grapple with whether — and how much — the power sector should be made to bear the costs of a warming world.

America’s reliance on wildfire litigation has sent shockwaves through the country’s social and economic systems, raising electricity rates, contributing to power shutoffs and draining public funds when governments are found liable. And it is jeopardizing interventions, such as prescribed burns, that can meaningfully reduce the destructive potential of wildfires.

But even beyond such consequences lies a more foundational question of justice. Climate scientists and legal analysts have challenged the idea of singular liability versus collective responsibility: Is it appropriate, or fair, to hold one person or entity responsible for a massive wildfire enabled by the burning of fossil fuels alongside decades of federal fire suppression and development policies?…

Source: Grist | Published: 2026-11-22 14:00 UTC | Difficulty: 62/100

item.title: The Defenders of Mexico’s Scorpion Reef
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engaging narrative with direct-action campaign context

ABOARD THE MV SHARKWATER—At 5 a.m. on a Sunday in September, crew members aboard the MV Sharkwater, a ship operated by the Sea Shepherd Conservation Society, readied a small inflatable motorboat tied alongside the larger vessel for a pre-dawn mission.

The night before, the crew received a report about an illegal sport fishing boat anchored just off Isla Desterrada, a sandy islet inside the Alacranes Reef National Park, a federally protected area located about 70 miles off the northern coast of the Yucatán peninsula. At more than 1,300 square miles, the park includes the largest coral reef in the Gulf of Mexico.

Images captured by a drone pilot for Sea Shepherd, an international marine conservation nonprofit, showed seven men from the boat setting up camp on the island. The crew was eager to confront them before they headed out to sea.

“We want to catch them before they leave to go fishing,” said David Hance, Sea Shepherd’s director of operations, slipping on his lifejacket as he prepared to step onto the smaller vessel rocking in the dark early-morning swells. They would need to move fast, though, he said.

Since the 1970s, Sea Shepherd has dispatched crews around the world to investigate, document and disrupt activities that jeopardize marine life. They run direct-action campaigns to stop industrial krill fishing in Antarctica, mass dolphin hunts in the Faroe Islands and poaching in the Upper Gulf of California.

Combating illegal fishing inside Alacranes Reef National Park—commonly referred to as Scorpion Reef—is one of the organization’s newest initiatives aimed at helping Mexico safeguard some of its most prized marine protected areas where fishing and other potentially harmful activities are banned or highly regulated to safeguard important ecosystems like coral reefs.

Globally, coral reefs provide vital habitat for at least 25 percent of all marine life, including at least 4,000 types of fish. But climate change is jeopardizing their future. Rising ocean temperatures and frequent marine heat waves are driving 96 percent of the world’s shallow reefs towards collapse.

To conserve coral reefs and boost their resilience, many scientists say it is vital to include them in marine protected areas where local pressures like overfishing, illegal fishing and pollution are alleviated.

Coral reefs need abundant fish populations to thrive. Herbivorous species like parrotfish feed on algae that can take over a reef, especially when corals are stressed by heat, disease and other disturbances. Predators like grouper and snapper also help keep smaller fish populations in check, maintaining a healthy, balanced ecosystem.

“Effectively managed marine protected areas are one of the strongest tools we have in protecting coral reefs and protecting the biodiversity that they host,” said Mishal Gudka, a coral reef scientist from Kenya who recently spearheaded a global assessment of shallow coral ecosystems for the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

But turning that promise into reality requires more than drawing boundaries on a map. These areas need people to actively defend them.

Flying Drones

The day before Hance set out on the early morning mission to Isla Desterrada, the 141-foot Sharkwater, a former Japanese fishing vessel, had anchored off Isla Perez, the only island inside the park that has a lighthouse and a small Mexican Navy outpost.

Another smaller live-aboard vessel owned by Sea Shepherd called the MV Roger Payne hung closer to Isla Desterrada, which in English means “Exiled Island.”

Every few hours the two crews surveyed much of the area with drones. From this viewpoint, they could not only spot other vessels, but also identify their names, registration numbers and how many people they had on board. This information is then cross-referenced with a daily list the National Commission of Natural Protected Areas keeps of vessels they’ve authorized to be in the park. If they’re not on the list, the crew goes to inspect them. And the fishers spotted on Isla Desterrada were not on the list.

From the drone photos, the crew could see several men making a campfire on the beach. Others rested on inflatable sleeping mats or chairs wedged into the sand where sea turtles are known to nest nearby. Hance and the rest of the crew decided the best plan of action would be to surprise the fishers the next morning.

30×30

In 2022, Mexico joined nearly 200 countries in adopting the Kunming-Montreal Biodiversity Framework, a landmark United Nations agreement aimed at halting and reversing the widespread biodiversity loss driven by climate change, pollution and other human activities that alter natural ecosystems.

As part of this agreement, participating countries have committed to conserving 30 percent of Earth’s terrestrial, inland waters and coastal and marine areas by 2030. Since then, Mexico has made significant progress towards achieving that goal, often referred to as 30×30. Around 25 percent of the country’s marine areas are legally protected or conserved—at least in theory.

At least a quarter of ocean areas designated for marine protection around the world lack adequate funding, surveillance and enforcement, clear rules or regulations. As a result, many become what scientists refer to as “paper parks”—areas that are legally recognized on paper, but don’t have the proper safeguards in place to achieve their conservation goals.

For many years, Scorpion Reef had come close to being one of them, said Tomás Camarena, director of the Alacranes Reef National Park and two other marine protected areas managed by Mexico’s National Commission of Natural Protected Areas.…

Source: Inside Climate News | Published: 2026-11-22 10:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: ‘No time for a culture war’: Victoria’s electricity supply is at risk. Can it avoid power shortages and bill shocks?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Local issue with potential for complexity, but lacks broader context

Victoria’s electricity supply will be at risk when a major power plant shuts in 2028 and neither major party is offering a plan at this month’s state election to deal with it, experts have warned.

All parties concede the giant Yallourn coal plant, which has operated in the Latrobe Valley since the 1970s and supplies a fifth of Victoria’s energy, is at the end of its functional life and will shut in less than two years. Analysts say the parties vying to run the state are failing to properly explain how they will fill the power shortfall the closure will create.

The challenge facing Victoria is exacerbated by the growth in energy demand from datacentres and the electrification of buildings, homes and vehicles. Experts are most critical of the Coalition, under Liberal leader Jess Wilson, which is favoured to win the election. It says it would stop work on new transmission lines – the high-voltage power lines needed to connect new wind and solar farms and allow Victoria to import power from neighbouring states.

Tim Baxter, of consultancy Naru Research, says there is no “time for a culture war on energy in Victoria” because poor choices now would be “devastating” for the state’s economy and create bill shocks for households and businesses.

He says cheap gas helped build Victoria’s past prosperity, but it is quickly running out with offshore gas supply from Bass Strait in steep decline. And there is no evidence the state has meaningful gas resources elsewhere to replace it. This has contributed to a 62% increase in gas prices in five years, he says, while electricity bills have risen by 18%.

Given Victorians rely more on gas than other states, Baxter says it underlines the need for households to move away from gas and increasingly run on renewable energy. “Every windfarm, solar farm and battery that comes online before 2028 reduces how much expensive gas Victoria has to burn when Yallourn goes. That makes speeding up the build-out the single best way to protect households from higher bills,” he says.

What are Labor and the Coalition promising?

Victoria’s wholesale electricity prices are the lowest on the east coast, but households still rely heavily on expensive gas. Regardless of who wins, energy bills are likely to increase, according to a government briefing reported in the Herald Sun.

The Coalition says it would scrap VNI West, a transmission line linking Victoria to New South Wales, and pause work on the Western Renewables Link, between Melbourne and the state’s west. Instead, it would undertake a “short, sharp and independent” review of the state’s transmission plan, which would consider alternatives, such as solar power on commercial and industrial rooftops.

It has also pledged to “throw open the doors to gas exploration”, reverse Labor’s policy of making new homes all-electric, and tender for new firming capacity with an Energy Security Requirement modelled on schemes in NSW and South Australia. There is no plan to change the state’s emission reduction targets – cutting greenhouse gas emissions by 75%–80% below 2005 levels by 2035 and reaching net zero emissions by 2045 – but it has not said how it would achieve them.

Labor says it would continue to expand the power grid, shift homes from gas to electricity for heating and cooking and continue to support the development of offshore windfarms. But the Carroll government is also reviewing the Western Renewables Link. It recently cancelled a renewable energy zone, approved two gas developments (although one has since entered administration), and announced $7.5m to kickstart a “renewable gas industry”.

‘Time to put our foot on the accelerator’

Nexa Advisory chief executive Stephanie Bashir says new transmission is crucial for developing renewable energy and allowing power to be imported across state lines at times of high demand, such as during heatwaves. “This is not the time to be cancelling any of the projects in the pipeline,” she says. “This is the time where we put our foot on the accelerator and go hard.”

Environment Victoria’s chief executive, Jono La Nauze, says the Coalition’s plan – including a proposal to reinstate a policy introduced by the previous Baillieu-Napthine Coalition government preventing wind turbines being built within 2km of dwellings – is “the greatest swindle ever attempted on Victorian voters”.

“The Coalition are promising to stop all the things that are necessary to replace our coal and gas generation. They’ve got some quick slogans for how they’re going to instead rely on gas, with absolutely no substance,” he says.

But analysts say Labor is also not building energy infrastructure fast enough.

Oliver Nunn, managing director of the consultancy Endgame Analytics, says the lack of an adequate plan to stave off an energy shortfall means that “whoever wins [the election], we lose”.

“You can see demand for electricity pulling up rapidly in Victoria, 5% year-on-year growth,” Nunn says. “Coal’s going out, and we just do not have, at this point, a really viable plan.”

In its 12 years in government, Labor has overseen a surge in Victoria’s share of renewable energy from 10% to 44% and the closure of the large Hazelwood coal-fired power station. The number of windfarms has grown from 14 to 44 and large-scale solar farms from two to 57. Labor also ended the state’s moratorium on conventional gas exploration in 2021.

But the state’s auditor general says both VNI West and the Western Renewables Link are behind schedule, and not likely to be completed until after Yallourn’s scheduled closure.

Recent attempts to fast-track the process by legislating for compulsory land acquisition before environmental approvals have been unpopular in regional communities, but Labor says the changes were needed to reduce delays and improve certainty for landowners. Controversially, Labor also passed laws to allow VicGrid and its contractors access to private land without a landholder’s consent, as a last resort to facilitate works.…

item.title: The best thing I ever ate? Lunch on the strait of Hormuz
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: rich in cultural context and personal narrative, with a focus on regional cuisine

When most people think of the strait of Hormuz, the warm, tropical waterway connecting the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, incredible food isn’t usually the first thing that comes to mind. But it should be, and I would know – it’s where I had one of my most memorable meals.

I was visiting Iran, traversing thousands of miles across the country with a local female photographer, mapping out regional specialities for my cookbook The Saffron Tales. Over the course of several months, we cooked and ate in people’s home kitchens, meeting a cross-section of society, from farmers and pharmacists to yoga teachers and restaurant owners, who all shared their favourite foods with us in places as diverse as the snowy mountains outside Tabriz, the rice paddies of the Caspian Sea, and the historic cities of Isfahan and Shiraz.

My mother is from Iran and it was here that I spent my formative early years, before my family settled in the north of England. I’ve travelled back and forth from the country all my life, mostly spending time in the Gilan province, in the rural north of the country. My grandparents were small-scale farmers, so I came to know the local produce intimately; from the abundance of fresh herbs and greens that are chopped, sliced and simmered into stews, to the fragrant long-grain rice that is so artfully adorned with butter and saffron, and rose and cardamom-infused desserts that are washed down with black tea drunk out of tulip-shaped glasses. When I cooked Iranian food at home in the UK, it always leant into this familiar flavour palette, which also involved a full embrace of the sour ingredients so beloved in Persian cuisine, such as pomegranate molasses, dried limes, verjuice and Seville oranges. Visiting the south of Iran changed all of that.

I arrived in Bandar Abbas, a small port city overlooking the strait of Hormuz, in February, when the weather was a cool and balmy (by their standards) 25C. Because of the different waves of migration to the region, brought about by its importance as a strategic port over hundreds of years, I knew the food was different from the rest of Iran: a thrilling blend of Persian, Arabic and Indian flavours, with seafood taking centre stage and fiery spices filling the air of the local markets. For centuries, Bandar (as it’s known to locals) was an important staging post on the maritime spice route from India to Europe. Traders, mercantile companies and empires sought to control the port and its lucrative trade in spices and, more recently, its oil reserves. Chillies, fresh coriander and tamarind form the holy trinity of Bandari cooking, used alongside ginger, cumin and curry powder to add heat and intensity to dishes. Tropical fruits, such as mangoes, pineapples and guavas, are picked green and used to make Indian-style pickles, and fresh fish from the warm waters of the Persian Gulf are poached in stews, grilled as kebabs, or fermented and dried before being ground into powders and pastes.

Wandering around its bustling streets, every corner of the city featured a new discovery. There was balaloot, a cardamom- and saffron-drenched buttery noodle dish, which I ate for breakfast, topped with a fried egg; sambusa, small triangles of deep-fried pastry stuffed with a spicy potato, green chilli and tamarind filling; wafer-thin crepes spread with suragh, a local condiment made with sardines that had been fermented with the local red soil, salt and Seville oranges under the hot sun.

But the best part of my trip was the visit to the home of Goli Heydari, a school teacher, and Ahmad Ravani, a musician, who hosted me for lunch, which in Iranian culture is the main meal of the day (followed, frequently, by a little siesta). As I entered Goli’s home, slipping my sandals off at the door, I was immediately struck by the earthy and pungent scent of fenugreek. Goli noticed me inhaling. “I’m making ghalieh mahi,” she told me, which is a local fish and herb stew. Did I want to come and see? She didn’t have to ask twice.

Goli pulled me into the kitchen to stir the stew simmering on the stove, twisting the lid off a jar of tamarind, which she generously spooned in. She handed me a spoon and, as I lifted the emerald green sauce to my mouth, it was hit by the fiery and bright taste of fresh coriander and green chilli. I watched her gently transfer fillets of firm white fish into the pot before turning her attention to the other dish she was making: fishcakes. I joined her, rolling flaked fish, mashed potato, coriander and yet more chillies into little patties with my hands.

While the fishcakes were frying, we made a salad: a classic Middle Eastern chopped combo of juicy tomatoes, crisp cucumber and sweet white onion, dressed simply with lemon, olive oil and salt. Once the food was ready, we gathered around the sofreh, an ornately patterned cotton tablecloth placed on the floor, around which Iranians traditionally eat. There were only four of us but, in typical Iranian fashion, Goli had cooked for eight. The idea of any guest being hungry, or there not being enough food, is one of the most unspeakable propositions for an Iranian host. As well as the stew, fishcakes and salad, there was steamed rice, toasted flatbread, a platter of herbs, creamy thick natural yoghurt, and small bowls of crunchy aubergine and chilli pickles. We passed bowls and spoons around as we filled our plates to the brim.…

Source: The Guardian Food | Published: 2026-11-22 11:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Cassette, London WC2: ‘One of the greatest dishes I’ve eaten all year’ – restaurant review | Grace Dent on restaurants
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: high-quality restaurant review with detailed descriptions and culinary exploration

I booked my lunch table at Cassette, a new French restaurant in Covent Garden, central London, while watching a viral video of a blasé Parisian couple, mid-riot, sipping wine and smoking Gauloises near the Arc de Triomphe. The Brits keep opening Parisian-style restaurants as a quiet admission that these people are really bloody cool, and this new one from Mark Gurney and Matt Bushnell, the pair behind Peckham’s Levan (also very cool, incidentally), serves the likes of a coq au vin jaune pie with a chicken leg saluting from its crust, and panisse with chopped mussels and green tomato. There’s also pork chop with sauce Talleyrand, Maldon oysters with beurre blanc, and a cocktail called Jet Fuel that combines Get 27, the green mint liqueur that gives every Parisian a starry-eyed memory of their parents’ dinner parties, with calvados and coffee liqueur.

Cassette is a discombobulating brew of the seemingly casual with the actually deadly bloody serious. Yes, dress up fancy, if you wish, but you can also slide in here in jeans and knitwear for a casual midweek vol-au-vent. No one will judge you. Service will at first come at you brasserie-style – casual, no stress – but can very quickly turn nerdy, obsessive and wallowing in ingredients, provenance and technique. If you want to geek out over bleu d’Auvergne or the consistency of the mascarpone cream, the staff will indulge you. The wine list starts at a kindly £29 a bottle, but soon climbs up into nosebleed territory via grower champagnes from the likes of Jérôme Prévost, a 2014 Jura savagnin, a detour to the volcanic Italian island of Pantelleria and a £350 Valentini trebbiano. In other words, Cassette is a clandestine foodie paradise.

The loos are nightclubby, tiled and, frankly, a bit down at heel, and the decor is pretty functional, clean and tidy, but the trump card right now is chef Essa Fakhry. In kitchen terms, Fakhry is Dublin-reared, having run the stoves at 777, a riotous contemporary Mexican and tequila joint, before going on to open Note in 2021, a wine bar that soon turned up on every “go there bloody quick” list and then slid into the Michelin Guide. After that, he put in an appearance at Planque, everyone’s favourite wine fiend’s paradise in Haggerston, east London. Now he is here in Covent Garden, lavishing all of that pedigree on quiche, creme brulee and a Saint-Marcellin cheese course – yes, indeed, the food of 1970s hostess trolleys. I’ll say this quietly, to avoid a rumpus and so that you can book yourself a table quickly: I think he’s one of the best chefs in London right now.

We popped in for just a few plates and ended up ordering much of the menu out of sheer curiosity. First, raw beef croustade with comté – tiny buttons of tartare in a micro case, if you will – with a creamy cheese sauce. Infinitely inhalable.

Then endive, which I can’t normally bear because it’s usually served hard, knobbly and bitter, and dressed in something that accentuates its aggressiveness. But here, the leaves are light and slickly dressed in bleu d’Auvergne, and scented with walnut and a top note of featherlight celery. Roast cauliflower and comté quiche may sound like a very 1970s after-school teatime, your granny standing over you with a wooden spoon, and definitely the sort of thing you’d rather go to bed empty-stomached than face actually eating. Well, please ignore that notion. This nutty delight is one of the greatest dishes I’ve eaten all year.

The maitake mushroom vol-au-vent is equally decadent: a puff pastry case stuffed with an improbable quantity of armagnac-boozy mushrooms and perched on top of a delightfully traditional sauce Parisienne. There is grilled cabbage smothered in a potent smoked eel vinaigrette, a pile of veal with anchovy and radicchio, and an exemplary duck à l’orange on meltingly sweet carrots topped with a pile of hazelnuts.

Our puddings are a classic red wine-poached pear with pleasingly tart mascarpone whipped to a fabulous consistency, and a mousse au chocolat with a slick of olive oil and a definite scatter of salt across it. With all this, martinis served in small or large measures, and calvados instead of gin and tonic.

Cassette is open seven days a week for lunch and dinner, Mondays included, which is the industry’s day off, so it will most probably turn into a hospitality industry hangout. Get there quickly, then, before Fakhry stops doing this.

- Cassette 42 Maiden Lane, London WC2, 020-3006 1600. Open all week, lunch noon-2.30pm, dinner 5.30-9.30pm (Sun 8pm). From about £65 a head à la carte; set lunch/pre-theatre menu, £27 for two courses, £31 for three; all plus drinks and service

item.title: How to make nasi goreng – recipe | Felicity Cloake's Masterclass
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: detailed recipe with clear instructions and cultural background, suitable for learning

Unless you’ve had the admirable foresight to prepare the spice paste in advance, thus turning this into just a quick assembly job, nasi goreng is not a fried rice that you whip up in five minutes from last night’s leftovers. Neither, however, is it particularly complex, and the richly savoury, shallot-sweet base gives it a depth of flavour that more than justifies the modest investment of time.

Prep 25 min

Chill 2 hr+

Cook 5 min

Serves 2

200g jasmine rice, or other long-grain rice, or 525g cooked and cooled rice

2 tbsp neutral oil

1 garlic clove, peeled and finely chopped

2 eggs, beaten (optional)

2 tbsp kecap manis (see step 5)

1 tbsp light soy sauce

4 spring onions, trimmed and chopped on the diagonal

1 bird’s eye chilli, sliced, to serve

For the paste

50g Asian red shallots (about 4)

1 garlic clove

1 red bird’s eye chilli

, or similar

1 tbsp neutral oil

2 tsp terasi (Indonesian shrimp paste; see step 4)

Optional toppings

Crispy shallots (bought or homemade)

Fried eggs

Sliced cucumber or tomatoes

Lightly blanched vegetables

Cooked meat or seafood or cubed tofu or tempeh

Salted peanuts, roughly chopped

1 Cook the rice

Should you happen to have cooked and cooled long-grain rice ready to use, start at step 3; the amount suggested above is fairly elastic, and the recipe easily scaled up or divided. If you’re cooking rice (preferably jasmine, but any long-grain variety will do) specially, put it in a pan with 400ml boiling water, then bring to a simmer, stirring once.

2 Cool the rice

Cover the pan tightly and turn the heat right down. Cook for 15 minutes, then take off the heat and place on a damp tea towel or cloth for five minutes. Fluff the rice with a fork, then spread it on a baking tray and put in the fridge to cool and dry out, ideally overnight, or for up to two hours in the freezer.

3 Start the paste

If you can’t find small, fiery Asian shallots, use 75g of the larger round ones instead, to compensate for their milder flavour. Peel and roughly chop the shallots and garlic. Trim the chilli (remove and discard the pith and seeds if you’re nervous of heat, or use a milder variety instead), then roughly chop and put in a mortar or mini chopper.

4 Finish the paste

Add the oil and terasi (Malaysian belacan, Thai kapi or Vietnamese mắm tôm make good substitutes for this Indonesian fermented shrimp paste); if you can’t find any of them, use a teaspoon and a half of fish sauce and two anchovy fillets (or two teaspoons of red miso mixed with a teaspoon of crumbled dried seaweed). Pound or whizz until smooth.

5 A note on the kecap manis

Kecap manis is a thick, sweet soy sauce that’s easily found in specialist Asian food shops and online. To make your own, put four tablespoons of light soy sauce in a small pan with the same amount of soft brown sugar, simmer until reduced to a slightly syrupy consistency, then leave to cool and use in the recipe below (note: this will make more than you need).

6 … and on the toppings

Prepare the toppings according to taste; nasi goreng exists in countless permutations across Indonesia and Malaysia, so it’s a great home for leftovers and various odds and ends from the vegetable drawer. Like many fried dishes, this one comes together fast, so have everything ready and within easy reach of the hob before you even think about starting the cooking.

7 Start the stir-fry

Put the oil in a wok on a high heat, then fry the chopped garlic until just lightly golden. Pour in the eggs, if using, leave to cook until half set, then break up. Carry on scrambling until the eggs are just beginning to brown, then stir in the spice paste and cook for another minute or so.

8 Add the rice

Once the shallots in the paste have lost their raw smell, sprinkle in the rice by hand, breaking up any clumps as you go, then stir-fry, tossing vigorously, until it’s thoroughly heated through. Stir in the kecap manis, soy sauce and chopped spring onion, ensuring the grains are brown and evenly coated with sauce.

9 Finishing touches

Fry, stirring, for another minute or so, until the rice is just beginning to caramelise and crisp, then taste and season as necessary with more kecap manis and chilli. Divide between plates and top with the sliced chilli and crispy shallots, if using, plus your chosen accompaniments. Serve immediately.

Source: The Guardian Food | Published: 2026-11-22 13:00 UTC | Difficulty: 65/100

item.title: Carolina Herrera’s Wes Gordon and Oribe’s Daniel Kaner on Collecting as a Personal Passion and a Creative Practice
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: high-quality reporting, personal insights, and integration of art into professional life

Wes Gordon, global creative director of Carolina Herrera, and Daniel Kaner, a cofounder of the hair care brand Oribe, stopped by the PMC Studio in Midtown Manhattan to chat with WWD editor in chief Jenny B. Fine about how they effortlessly integrate art into their personal and professional lives. The conversation took place during the inaugural Art Week NYC, a citywide festival of arts programming hosted by ARTnews, Art in America, and Artforum.

Despite being from different generations, Kaner and Gordon have a lot in common. They are both from Minnesota, both now live near each other in Connecticut, and both are deeply enmeshed in the art world.

Gordon spoke about his experience with art almost reverentially, referring to art as his “safe space” as a child and the happiest 45 minutes of his school day. He went on to study art at Central St. Martins in London and eventually launched his own line in New York. Lena Dunham wore one of his designs to her first Met Gala in 2012, and it was through Dunham that Gordon met her mother, photographer Laurie Simmons. He and Simmons traded clothing for art, which is how Gordon ended up with the first real piece of art in his collection: a photo from Simmons’s “Love Doll” series, a piece he says he will have forever.

At Carolina Herrera, Gordon has continued to champion women artists and feminine creative energy; the brand’s fall 2026 ready to wear collection featured many artists as models, among them Amy Sherald, Ming Smith, Eliza Douglas, and Anh Duong, and the 2027 resort collection was an homage to Georgia O’Keeffe’s color palette and personal style.

Kaner is so committed to creating a “beautiful, interesting world” that the sign on his office door says “art project,” not “Oribe.” To hear him talk about art, it’s clear he thinks of himself as an artist as much as, if not more than, a businessperson.

Watch the full conversation in the video above and hear which artworks Gordon and Kaner would most like to wake up and look at. (Hint: neither could choose just one.)

item.title: Rethinking Data Visualisation: A UX Approach To Dashboards That Actually Drives Decisions
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: highly relevant to design and UX, clear and well-structured

Rethinking Data Visualisation: A UX Approach To Dashboards That Actually Drives Decisions

In organisations today, data has never been more available. Dashboards and performance decks exist for almost every function — sales, product, marketing, operations — and the tools to build them have never been more accessible. And yet, in weekly standups and quarterly reviews, the same thing happens constantly: someone shares the numbers, the room nods, and the meeting ends without a decision or clear direction.

When that happens, the data usually takes the blame. The numbers weren’t granular enough, the dataset wasn’t complete, we need more information before we can act. But the data is almost never the problem. The reality is that nobody designed it to deliver insights. The chart was built from what was available, not from the question that needed answering. The audience was assumed rather than understood, and what should actually change as a result of seeing this data — that question — was never asked at all.

Data visualisation and UX are solving the same underlying problem: both are trying to move the right information to the right person in a way that changes something. The vocabulary is different, but the underlying challenge is identical, and the moment you start treating them as complementary disciplines is the moment dashboards stop being a passive collection of charts and start doing something functional.

For designers who work with data, analysts who present to non-technical audiences, and marketers who need their numbers to do more than sit in a slide, this read is for you.

The Chart Was Never The Whole Story

In 1973, the statistician Francis Anscombe (PDF) published a paper that made a quiet but clarifying point. He constructed four datasets that are statistically identical: same mean, same variance, same correlation coefficient, and same regression line. Run the numbers on any of them, and they are identical. Plot them, and they could not be more different.

Anscombe’s lesson to statisticians was about diagnosis: visualisation reveals the operational truth that raw numbers conceal.

But visualisation isn’t just diagnostic; it is also communicative. The form you choose is where understanding either emerges or gets lost in the noise. Does your audience walk away with numbers, or with a story they’ll quote and talk about?

One of the most striking examples is Visual Capitalist’s History of Pandemics. Instead of burying the reader in a massive data table of casualty counts, it maps the death toll of major historical pandemics using a proportional bubble layout on a single timeline.

Before your brain reads a single number, your visual system grasps the sheer scale of the Black Death relative to everything else on the page. The right visualisation does not just plot the data but makes the story impossible to miss.

Edward Tufte codified a foundational principle for the craft with his data-ink ratio: every mark on a chart should serve the data, not decorate it. It remains a widely used framework in data visualisation, anchored in the assumption that clarity and visual hygiene are the goal.

For a chart in isolation, that holds. But a chart is never read in isolation: it’s read by a person, in a specific context, under specific pressure. Strip a chart down to its cleanest form, and you might be removing the exact layer of context a decision-maker needs. Simplicity isn’t the goal in itself; appropriate complexity is.

Data is a message, and the right amount of signal depends entirely on who’s receiving it.

“

Which leads to the core principle of data UX: roughly 80% of the work that determines whether a dashboard succeeds happens before you ever draw a chart.

That dependency is the thread the rest of this piece pulls on.

The 80% That Happens Before The Chart

The high-leverage 80% almost never happens on screen. It happens upstream: before a tool is opened, before a dataset is pulled, before a single design choice is made. It comes down to three questions, and once they become habitual, they change what you notice, what you ask, and what you push back on at the outset of every project.

- Context: What are we trying to show with this data?

This is where you define what the visualisations actually need to serve before you touch any raw data. Writing down the precise operational questions, specifically enough to determine what gets pulled and what gets filtered, is what produces a dashboard that helps with decision-making.

- Audience: Who is this for, and how do they think?

This is the empathy step. Knowing who’s in the room, what they’re accountable for, and how they engage with data determines how much complexity the visualisation can carry, and how it should be presented.

- Insight: What should change once this data lands?

A decision, a new direction, a shift in understanding. If the intended strategic outcome isn’t clear during the design phase, it will remain invisible once the dashboard goes live.

Context: What Are We Trying To Show With This Data?

Most data-heavy projects start backward: teams pull whatever metrics their internal analytics tools already track and build visualisations around them, while the question the data was supposed to answer either gets assumed or never gets asked. This happens simply because we anchor on the data in front of us as the boundary of what’s possible.

Defining a goal first sounds obvious, but in practice, it rarely happens with the necessary clarity. “Show me how the product is performing” is not a goal; “Identify which features drive retention among users who signed up in Q1” is, as it includes three things the first doesn’t: a metric, a population, and an implied action. That specificity is what converts an open-ended exploration into a constrained, answerable design problem. Which one you start from determines everything that follows: what you include, what comparisons matter, and what you leave out entirely.…

item.title: New EU Guidelines For AI Labelling
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: important topic, clear reporting, useful for understanding AI labelling

New EU Guidelines For AI Labelling

There’s been a lot of confusion and panic this week about “huge fines”, “drastic measures” and “sweeping new AI rules” in the EU. In reality, it’s a lot more narrow — and a lot more sensible. And mostly it’s about making AI more obvious when it actually needs to be obvious — especially for AI-generated content.

Starting from Aug 2, 2026, AI labelling is a legal requirement for any company that serves EU citizens. And similar to European Accessibility Act, it’s not limited to EU companies. It affects any company worldwide with EU operations as long as their AI output is used by people in the EU. Let’s see what exactly it means for us.

What Actually Needs Labelling

The goal of AI labelling is to help everyone exposed to AI content to recognize, in a clear and distinguishable way, that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated.

According to Article 50(4) of the AI Act, AI labelling applies to:

- Deepfakes. Any image, audio, or video that resembles a real person, object, place, or event and would falsely appear authentic or truthful. Content that is not deceptively realistic generally doesn’t apply.

- Chatbots and AI agents. Users must be informed if they’re not talking to a human.

- Fully AI-written text. Specifically on matters of public interest, where there has been no human review or editorial work.

- Emotion recognition and biometric categorization tools.

Both providers (who build or supply the AI system) and deployers (who use it) carry legal obligations. Similar to GDPR and EAA, a company doesn’t escape Article 50 just because it licensed an external AI tool from a third party.

However, it doesn’t mean that all AI-generated content must be explicitly labelled.

Not All AI-Generated Content Must Be Labelled

Beyond the use cases above, pretty much everything else — the vast majority of AI-assisted work — simply isn’t covered by new transparency rules. Most notably, the disclosure obligation does not apply where the AI-generated text has been reviewed and edited by a human, with a named person or entity taking editorial responsibility for it.

Some confusion circles around what exactly “public interest” means, where it starts and where it ends. On its own, it refers to health, safety, environment, economy, finances, politics, science, or culture. If AI-generated product claims touch upon them, the disclosure rule applies.

Some law firms recommend labelling realistic AI-generated illustrations or photos as a precaution for advertising, marketing and other commercial content. AI-generated product illustrations, photos, or posters do need a disclosure, as long as they resemble a real person, place, object, or event.

The Fine Line Between “Edited” And “AI-Generated”

But at which point does edited AI content stop being AI content? When a form is pre-filled with AI, but then a user edits it, is it still AI? EU Commission’s guidance is a little fuzzy. Small assistive edits — spellcheck, grammar, formatting, cropping, colour correction, and AI-generated translation — don’t count as AI generation.

AI-generated summaries, composite imagery, substantive rewrites, or adding and removing elements from a photo are considered AI generation. In practice, fine-tuning a sentence a person wrote is fine, but generating the sentence on its own requires a disclosure.

“A human skimmed it before publishing” doesn’t qualify as editorial review. The Commission is explicit that it needs to be substantive, with a named person responsible for the editorial control.

In other words, the fine line lies between intentional manual intervention and automated generation. The latter always has to be disclosed (exception: closed B2B environments).

AI Sparkles Probably Not Enough

As part of the Code of Practice, the European Commission has published an EU AI icon set. It’s a specific “AI” mark (similar to the AI label in Carbon Design System) — not the generic ✨ sparkle that many products use to signal AI. The signal must be “clear and distinguishable”.

The sparkle might be too ambiguous to signal AI clearly. Mostly because it’s often used to mean “AI-powered feature”, rather than “this specific content was generated by AI”. That’s the kind of signal EU guidelines are trying to rule out.

The Commission is explicit: using an icon “does not establish legal compliance by itself.” A barely visible icon, a note buried in the footer, or a label that flashes for a second are all not compliant.

The icon should be clearly visible, with a plain language label and accessible to assistive technologies. A safe bet is to pair any icon with plain text (“AI-generated”) — and it needs to persist when being reshared or downloaded.

In fact, the EU Commission also published Code of Practice on marking and labelling of AI content.

It Isn’t Just EU

It might feel like a yet another regulation coming from the EU, but in reality there are plenty of other similar regulations that emerged recently worldwide:

- China has mandatory AI labelling since 1 September 2025. With visible tags and watermarked metadata.

- California has SB 942, as amended by AB 853, which became mandatory on the exact same day as the EU rules (2 August 2026), deliberately timed to align.

- South Korea has the AI Basic Act that took effect on 22 January 2026, widely cited as the first comprehensive national-level AI law to mandate deepfake labels. Fines are modest by EU standards (roughly $20K per violation), with a one-year grace period before enforcement bites.

- India has an IT Rules amendment, in force since 20 February 2026. Platforms must label “synthetically generated information”, and takedown timing for most harmful deepfakes was cut to 3 hours.

All of these are signs of upcoming AI regulation that looks more like a pattern, rather than a coincidence. So if you’re shipping anything AI this year, it’s probably a good idea to have a conversation about what exactly is going to be AI-labelled, and what not.

Wrapping Up…

Source: Smashing Magazine | Published: 2026-08-13 10:00 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

Original link: https://smashingmagazine.com/2026/08/eu-guidelines-ai-labelling/

item.title: Why Your Website Should Never Stop Changing
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: interesting perspective on website evolution, well-written

Why Your Website Should Never Stop Changing

It runs over your real code, lets your team edit anything visually, and puts agents to work on content, accessibility, and the maintenance you never get to. Incubated at Strapi. Thank you!

Every website is at its best the day it ships. The final branch merges, the site goes live exactly as designed, and it is briefly perfect. It will never be this good again.

Not because anything breaks. The site keeps working. But the market moves, the messaging shifts, a competitor launches something, and the careful thing you built slowly stops matching the company it represents. A year later, it is a period piece. Not broken, just behind. Every team knows this decay, and almost everyone treats it as a law of nature.

It doesn’t have to be that way. A website could keep improving after launch instead of drifting away from its best day, quietly optimizing itself while the team that built it works on something else.

Picture it working: while you sleep, an agent catches that last week’s design-system change never propagated to the pricing page, and fixes it. Another finds a set of images shipped uncompressed in a rushed release and optimizes them. A third flags an accessibility regression a new component introduced, and either fixes it or leaves it for you to check. You wake up to a site that is measurably better than the one you left, and a short list of the few decisions the agents wanted your eyes on. That is the version worth wanting.

And the moment you take that promise seriously, you run into a problem that has nothing to do with the technology:

Almost nobody actually wants a website that changes entirely on its own.

Why “Just Make It Autonomous” Is The Wrong Goal

The obvious move, once you have capable agents, is to hand them the whole site. Let them write, edit, optimize, and publish, and get out of the way. It sounds like the natural endpoint, and it is the first thing most people picture when they hear “autonomous website.”

It is also the thing almost nobody wants once it is real in front of them.

We learned this the way you learn most things worth knowing: by building the opposite first. Building Fimo, an autonomous website platform, we set out to make websites fully autonomous, assumed that was the goal, and then watched what people actually did with it. What they did was hesitate. Not because they distrusted the agents, but because a website has no single owner. Different parts belong to different people, and each one wants a different amount of autonomy. So the question was never whether to trust the agents. It was where to draw the line, and for whom.

Once you ask it that way, the work splits cleanly into three kinds.

Most Of It Is A No-brainer

Start with the largest pile, because it is bigger than people expect. Most of what keeps a website healthy is rule-bound, repetitive, and completely joyless. Keeping accessibility compliant as pages change. Propagating a design-system update once a token moves. Catching a broken meta tag, an unoptimized image, a link that rotted when a URL changed three sprints ago.

None of this is where anyone’s talent lives. Nobody was hired because of their gift for spotting a missing alt attribute. This is the work you are actively relieved to hand off, and it is the work agents are best at, because it is defined by rules rather than taste. An agent that quietly keeps this layer correct across a whole site, unattended, is not a threat to anyone’s job. It is the tedious eighty percent finally taken care of.

Naming how much of the maintenance load actually lives in this pile is what makes the whole idea of an autonomous site feel less like a leap. You are not handing over judgment. You are handing over chores.

Some Of It You’d Never Hand Over

At the other end sits the work you would not delegate at any price. It is a small pile, but it is the reason you exist.

An agent can check a new page against every rule you have given it. It can confirm the contrast passes, the heading order is right, the tokens are correct, the copy matches the style guide. What it cannot do is decide what the page should feel like, or whether the thing you are shipping is, in the taste sense, good. That judgment is exactly what you were hired for, and no amount of capability moves it off your desk.

This is the part people reach for first when they resist autonomy, and they are right to protect it. The mistake is thinking the whole site is made of this kind of work. Almost none of it is. But that small part matters more than all the rest, which is why automating everything feels so wrong.

And A Lot Of It Depends On Who You Are

Between the chores and the untouchable sits the part no product can settle for you, because the line runs through different places for different people.

Take one real change: making dark mode the default theme when someone lands on the site. An agent can do it in seconds. The question is who gets to decide it should happen at all. For the designer who owns the site’s identity, the default theme is not a setting; it is a statement about how the brand wants to be seen first, and they want that call. For the developer shipping the change, it is a one-line default with a clear rationale, the kind of thing they would happily let an agent apply and move on. Same change, same site, and the two of them draw the line in opposite places.

Notice what is happening there. It isn’t that one of them is cautious and the other reckless. It is that the same task carries different amounts of judgment for each of them. For one person it is a decision; for the other it is a chore. There is no default a product could ship that would be right for both, because “right” is a function of where your value sits, not of the task itself.…

Source: Smashing Magazine | Published: 2026-08-25 08:00 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

Original link: https://smashingmagazine.com/2026/08/why-website-should-never-stop-changing/

item.title: Timing Charts: A Blueprint For SMIL Animations
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: technical but accessible, useful for understanding SMIL animations

Timing Charts: A Blueprint For SMIL Animations

<img> tags and can fully animate everything in an SVG without JavaScript.

We know that everything on the web is a box by default, but you’ll find many animated <div>s pretending to be circles. But if you’ve ever met a real <circle>, you’ll know that they’ve got a lot more going for them. Dressed in SVG, they fit into a wider range of crowds than a humble <div> wearing HTML/CSS can. <img> has a strict no .html policy.

The <img> tag is not as static as its name suggests. Any embedded JavaScript unfortunately won’t run if you load an SVG file with an <img> tag, but CSS animations work perfectly fine. Many of the SVG attributes do have CSS property counterparts, and the geometry properties have been supported across the major browsers since 2024. Some attributes that you might want to animate, like viewBox, don’t have equivalents yet.

Besides JavaScript and CSS, there’s another way to animate SVGs: Synchronized Multimedia Integration Language (SMIL). Despite its quirks, it’s still worth learning. Like CSS animations, SMIL animations also work in <img> tags and can fully animate everything in an SVG, without JavaScript.

If you’ve never heard of SMIL or need a refresher, check out Andy Clarke’s well-named article. Then we’ll look at a way to plan an animation and make SMIL markup more manageable.

The Break Up

SMIL has a problem: it gets bloated quickly. Unlike CSS and JavaScript, where you can list multiple properties in each keyframe and easily reuse animations, each SMIL tag can only target one element and only one property of that element at a time. A property can be animated through a list of values. But it is still one tag, one element, one property. The shortest way you can write a color and opacity change that will run is the following:

<animate

attributeName="fill"

to="someOtherColor"

dur="someDuration"

/>

<animate

attributeName="opacity"

to="someOtherValue"

dur="someDuration"

/>

That’s not bad, but consider that it needs to be repeated for every element included in the animation. A SMIL animation can quickly get longer than its CSS equivalent.

To make things easier when starting a new animation, let’s plan all of the elements and properties we want to animate, and create a list of descriptive IDs for each tag.

Charting Animation Time And Space

I like to plan my animations using what’s called a timing chart. A timing chart is effectively a line segment; some choose horizontal lines, others prefer vertical, which is a great analogy for animation as a whole because line segments can run parallel, overlap, and follow each other with or without a gap. Just like animations.

For now, we’re only interested in when animations start and stop. When drawing our charts, we’ll forget about the in-between lines and instead draw a line for each component animation, marking the beginning and end. I like to annotate timing with a circle and a bar. You can draw your chart using whatever, and it doesn’t have to be exactly to scale, as long as the relative timing between all the little animations that make up the whole is clear. Besides, adding labels for the durations is an easy cheat to get around drawing to scale.

Here is a demo of how I typically set up a timing chart with more than one animation:

The important thing to note is that the timing chart lines are arranged according to how the animations are arranged in time. One piece of the animation follows the next piece, which is followed by a subsequent piece, and so forth. It visualizes how the animation’s parts run together and cascade over time.

S(yncbase)MIL

A big part of SMIL is synchronization. It’s even in the name, after all. And there are multiple ways to specify when an animation should start (here’s a test case to check what your browser supports). One of the most useful ways is with a syncbase value, which is a SMIL tag’s ID followed by either .begin or .end, with an optional positive or negative offset.

Let’s piggyback off the previous animation example that includes changes in color and opacity. If we want the opacity animation to start 300 milliseconds before the color animation finishes, we could do arithmetic. Alternatively, the second animation can use the syncbase value colorChange.end - 300ms. This way, the relative timing between the two animations becomes explicit.

<!-- Starts at an absolute time -->

<animate

id="colorChange"

begin="1s"

...

/>

<!-- Starts relative to when #first ends -->

<animate

id="opacityChange"

begin="colorChange.end - 300ms"

...

/>

Using syncbase values, the beginning of an animation is positioned in time relative to the .begin or .end of some other animation. A positive offset moves the start to the right (forwards in time), and a negative offset to the left (backwards in time).

Something with negative offsets is that they can specify a time before the document has loaded or when a click happens. Computers can’t predict the future (at least not yet). The best they can do is jump the animation to where it would have been had the computer peeked into the future to preemptively start the animation. The second animation only runs from start to finish if there is enough room, so to speak.

Syncbase values don’t only allow you to connect animations from .end to .begin. Elect a primary animation; the animation that first comes to mind is usually the best representation of the group. All secondary animations can be set with begin="primary.begin". I’ve only used the ID #primary for emphasis. That way, all the other animations begin relative to that starting point. Stacking animations like this reduces maintenance if, say, we later want the whole group to start at a different time.

Let’s put the idea to work and build a loading indicator (or spinner). Then we’re going to explore how changing the relative timing between the parts changes the effect of the whole animation:

Step 1: Choose An Image Approach…

item.title: Domes depict constellations of missiles in the night sky at Sharjah Architecture Triennial
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: unique design concept, well-explained

Domes depict constellations of missiles in the night sky at Sharjah Architecture Triennial

Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee have created three domed structures that reimagine constellations by mapping military objects in the night sky, which were displayed at this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial.

Titled After Night There is Nothing, the trio of installations aim to bring attention to how communities are responding to drones, satellites, rockets and missiles changing the sky above them.

Covered in thatch, the three curved wood-and-steel structures are segments of a giant globe.

Vinyl lines the inner curves, where Nahleh and Saloojee designed creature-like constellations based on man-made military objects in the sky.

The trio of installations were displayed at three venues at the Sharjah Architecture Triennial – the Al Qasimiyah School, a former slaughterhouse, and in the sandy Al Madam town.

“This is ‘night sky optimism’ – optimism through catastrophe,” Nahleh told Dezeen. “The night sky we are talking about in this project is not the sky of beautiful stars and constellations, but the contemporary sky filled with drones, satellites, rockets and missiles that are changing the way we understand the sky above us.”

“The drones, missiles, rockets and satellites eclipse some of the constellations, and sometimes fuse with them,” he continued.

“That fusion is at the heart of this project – how do these technologies, through cultural practices on the ground, begin to morph into new creatures and new constellations that people try to make sense of to interpret the violence of this military technology that is taking place.”

Nahleh and Saloojee aimed to combine the reality of modern war with mythical storytelling, drawing upon their research into communities exposed to military attacks.

“We have noticed in our research that, especially in geographies witnessing prolonged violence, these objects are producing new mythical creatures – creatures that fuse together technological advancement with epistemic practices and myth-making practices that happen from the ground,” said Nahleh.

“Most of these creatures, these modern constellations as we’re calling them, are populating the night sky in our drawing alongside pathways of flights of drones, satellites and other things that manifest across the night sky we’ve inherited, rather than the one we lost,” he continued.

“We think of these creatures as ones that attempt to tame the military brightness that is populating the sky around us, be it in the shape of missiles, phosphorus, or flares.”

As well as depicting creature-like constellations in their inner curves, the structures themselves were designed as creatures – the nocturnal Solifugi spider known to run out the sun and into shade.

“The project is dedicated to the Solifugi, which is a spider that by nature runs away from the sun, the sun of imperial savagery,” said Nahleh. “It has a very thick skin to protect it from this brightness, and in its belly is a map of the contemporary sky.”

Three openings puncture the shell in each of the installations. In the desert site at Al Madam, a vertical cut-out frames a view of the minaret of a distant mosque, and at the slaughterhouse site, a long opening was set at the height of a cow.

Traditional Hakawati storytellers will narrate stories at the installations as part of the triennial, which runs until April.

“The story is difficult, but it’s about finding optimism,” said Nahleh. “People are carving their own histories on the weapons that are here to annihilate them.”

“There’s a paradox here that we have to confront,” he continued. “When libraries are being erased, and people have no more books to publish or things to write on, they’re writing on the weapons that are sent to devour them.”

“Kids now are finding ways again to dream by placing their wishes upon the shooting stars, which are usually missiles and rockets. It’s a sad and complicated story, but we can no longer escape it by wishing for a sky we no longer have.”

We rounded up eight highlights from this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which includes a draping shelter that pays homage to the improvised learning spaces created by Virginia’s Black community, and a circular canopy with cut-outs that plot 41 medieval Arabic poetic names for the sun.

Sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026 takes place from 14 November 2026 to 14 April 2027 at various locations across Sharjah, UAE. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.
