item.title: Eight furniture designs informed by life in New York City
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: interesting designs, clear descriptions

Eight furniture designs informed by life in New York City

Furniture designers contend with their personal experiences living in New York City through the objects in our most recent roundup.

New York, New York has inspired filmmakers, writers and artists to make work since the city’s inception, and for designers, it’s no different.

The furniture and objects below explore aspects of moving to or living in New York City, whether it’s the difficulty of maintaining a career and community, the dissonance of missing home, the architecture, or dead, smooshed rats on the daily commute.

In many cases, the collections reflect on the designer’s own identities and heritages.

These include pieces by Kim Mupungilaï, Rafael Prieto and studio Tian & Teague, all of whom have lived or passed through New York during their practice.

Read on below to see how the metropolis has shaped their work.

What Still Holds, by Bechara Maalouf

Bechara Maalouf created a series of lamps made out of wooden beams from Lower East Side buildings and intricate screens informed by the window guards at his family home in Lebanon.

The series, first displayed during NYC design week 2026 in May, merged Maalouf’s two homes as the designer grappled with the impacts of Israel’s ground invasion of Lebanon from afar.

Find out more about What Still Holds ›

Designer Massimiliano Malagò created an acrylic chair, covered in his own writings, that explores the challenges of maintaining a life in New York City.

“For me, this was making an object that is incredibly luxurious, incredibly grand, but it’s actually talking about something quite common and sometimes quite sad, because the hardships that people go through to stay in the city are just difficult,” he told Dezeen.

Los Angeles and Lisbon studio Tian & Teague created the NYC Series based on their own time living in New York and some of the jarring aspects residents become accustomed to.

The collection, which includes a flattened-rat rug, came about from things seen on the studio founders’ daily commute.

White Picket Chair, by Han Seungmin

New York-based designer Han Seungmin created this chair using modular components from the metallic fences found throughout Brooklyn.

Find out more about White Picket Chair ›

HUE/AM/I-HUE/I/AM, by Kim Mupungilaï

“I just started thinking about my own cultural landscape and background and upbringing and wanted to dig deeper,” Mupungilaï told Dezeen.

Find out more about HUE/AM/I-HUE/I/AM ›

Metalworker and designer Micah Rosenblatt looked to New York City’s historic architecture for his The City Block collection, which features thin, contemporary lines and geometric elements.

“[The expressions] are based on the cityscape and my relationship to it,” Rosenblatt told Dezeen.

Find out more about The City Block ›

All Other Passports, by Julio Torres and Sabai

The collection is influenced by literal and figurative aspects of Torres’ move to New York City from El Salvador, such as a curtain motif pulled from JFK‘s international Terminal 4.

Find out more about All Other Passports ›

Designer Rafael Prieto integrated building fragments into several furniture pieces for an exhibition at Emma Scully Gallery earlier this year.

Prieto sourced the cast-offs, including pieces of a cornice, from a facade being demolished across the street from his Tribeca studio, which he had become “deeply interested” in.

Find out more about For The Future of the Past ›

item.title: Jony Ive and Margaret Calvert create posters to celebrate decade of Design Museum in Kensington
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: celebration of design museum, informative

Ten leading designers have unveiled posters that celebrate 10 years of London’s Design Museum in Kensington, which was completed by OMA, Allies and Morrison and John Pawson in 2016.

Originally located in an old 1940s banana warehouse on the south bank of the River Thames, the Design Museum opened at its current site in Kensington, west London, on 24 November 2016.

To mark this 10-year anniversary, the museum asked 10 international designers to create posters for the occasion.

The lineup includes British graphic designer Margaret Calvert, who is known for creating the seminal 1960s Motorway and Transport typefaces with fellow British designer Jock Kinneir.

The hugely popular typefaces were invented to clarify the UK’s road signs and are still used today.

Calvert designed a subtle road sign-style poster for the Design Museum’s anniversary, depicting a fork in the road between Kensington and Shad Thames, where the original museum stood between 1989 and 2016.

Former Apple designer Jony Ive also designed a poster in collaboration with his studio LoveFrom, which he founded with Australian practitioner Marc Newson in 2019 after his departure from the technology brand.

Ive and LoveFrom‘s poster features a minimalist grey and white design composed of two understated shapes that resemble the number 10.

American filmmaker Tim Burton is also among the lineup and applied his trademark playful drawings to a poster illustrated with two characters sitting atop the number 10.

Burton’s extensive portfolio was on display at the Design Museum in 2024, charting 50 years of his cinematic career.

Dutch industrial designer Hella Jongerius, meanwhile, created a poster depicting a colourful woven tapestry in a nod to her work, which typically blends contemporary technology with traditional crafts.

The other six designers who make up the lineup are London studio A Practice for Everyday Life, Brazilian graphic designer Marina Willer, British fashion designer Paul Smith and British designers Sebastian Conran, Simone Brewster and Tom Dixon.

The Kensington Design Museum is located within the former Commonwealth Institute building.

Dutch architecture practice OMA worked alongside London office Allies and Morrison to restore the shell of the Grade II*-listed building, while British designer Pawson conceived the museum’s interiors.

Images courtesy of Design Museum

item.title: Evan Edward designs "seductive" Miami Beach pied-à-terre
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: unique design project, detailed description

Evan Edward designs “seductive” Miami Beach pied-à-terre

Miami‘s nightlife scene in the 1990s informed the saturated colours and metallic accents used by local studio Evan Edward inside this apartment in the oceanside city, illustrating what the studio calls its “high-impact minimalism” approach.

Designed for an international family with “personal ties to the city’s storied nightlife era”, the Miami Beach pied-à-terre reflects the hedonistic era that left a distinct stylistic impression.

“Aesthetically, there was a rawness to the excess and glamour,” Evan Edward co-principal Josh Evan Goldfarb told Dezeen. It was a particularly exciting time for colour and design in general in the city.

“The city was in its early stages of redevelopment – the original art deco glamour and run-down beach patina were a sublime tropical combination.”

He and co-principal Michael Edward Moirano set about creating interiors that blend contemporary and vintage furniture and decor to reflect “a more seductive side of Miami”.

In place of a typical South Florida palette of white, beige and turquoise, spaces feature hues of terracotta, burnt orange, burgundy and ochre. These prevalent tones are complemented by flashes of chartreuse, mustard yellow and metallic finishes.

To create a more welcoming space for entertaining, the designers opened the kitchen to the living and dining spaces with the angular island as a central gathering point.

They also connected the foyer to an adjoining unit behind a series of oversized pivot doors.

“The updated floor plan completely changed the experience for the clients,” Moirano told Dezeen. “The triangular island is the hub of the space, serving the kitchen and dining banquette area, while also exposing the living area featuring a dramatic view of Biscayne Bay and the Miami skyline.”

A butter yellow kitchen was paired with richly veined stone countertops that complement the polished-pebble flooring.

The generous island was illuminated by a 1960s five-pendant light feature above, and accompanied by mustard yellow Calligaris bar stools for casual dining and gathering.

Goldfarb was forthcoming about references to personal experiences and spaces.

“One of the references for the kitchen was an artist studio that I visited when growing up in Coconut Grove – the memory is ingrained in my mind’s eye,” said Goldfarb. “It was just so airy – up in the trees, open windows, patina on all surfaces and artwork and materials strewn about.”

“The sense of colour and mashup of materials – stone, tile, painted – it’s hard to forget,” he added.

Nestled into a corner, a banquette with olive-toned Rubelli velvet upholstery wraps a circular stainless steel table, while a pair of 1970s folding chromed-steel and leather chairs provide additional seating.

An adjustable lamp by Tito Agnoli for Oluce with a custom shade extends from the wall to hang over the table.

The mellow tones of the kitchen were contrasted by the fiery orange-red of the pivoting foyer doors – a hue that reappears in a bold artwork above the bed in the otherwise neutral-toned primary bedroom.

Metallic accents are dialled up in the powder room where a silver metal mosaic clads the walls and metallic zellige tiles cover the floor.

Moirano described it as a “very sexy disco-inspired discovery off the foyer”.

“The result is a small but impactful space that captures the project’s more theatrical influences through materiality rather than overt decoration,” the studio said.

The team describes the project as an example of its “high-impact minimalism, in which architectural restraint provides a framework for distinctive materials, collectible furnishings, and unexpected moments of visual interest.”

Located on a barrier island along South Florida’s Atlantic Coast, Miami Beach is renowned for its 1920s art deco architecture and more recent influx of luxury hotels.

Another apartment, on the city’s famous Ocean Drive, was renovated by MW Works to include tropical hardwood and sand-coloured plaster.

Photography by Ori Harpaz

item.title: How can we explain psychosomatic illnesses?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

When Diego started seeing bright flashing lights in his field of vision and felt his legs go weak, he thought he knew immediately what was happening. His mother had a stroke in her 60s, and although Diego was active and (unlike his mother) didn’t smoke, he had always expected that the same would happen to him. So it was a huge relief to be told – after seeing a stroke specialist and having a brain scan – that he had not had a stroke at all. Unfortunately the relief was short-lived. The visual disturbances and the weakness were real and debilitating. If this wasn’t a stroke, what was it?

Some illnesses aren’t caused by disease or damage, but arise when the coordinated functioning of the body goes awry. In a percentage of these cases a person’s psychological health is an important element in their symptoms. Intuitively this seems mysterious. We are accustomed to thinking about physical symptoms as being caused by physical events; viruses, inflammation, bleeding. How can something as intangible as a thought have any impact on something as physical as a leg? How can the mind make us ill?

The work of Freud still dominates the public and medical imagination here, even though there are important ways in which he was wrong. Freud proposed that quite dramatic physical symptoms can arise as a result of repression, where the memory of an upsetting experience is pushed into the unconscious, leaving a sort of free-floating emotional energy. He saw the mind as being like a pneumatic device: emotions represented energy and that energy had to go somewhere, often leading to the development of a physical symptom.

These days, psychologists are more sceptical about this, but the influence of Freudian psychology lives on in the way we talk about psychosomatic illness – a condition where there’s no damage or disease, but clear impairment nonetheless. The terms “conversion” and “somatisation” are derived directly from Freud and still pop up frequently in the literature.

Their use is a stark reminder of the fact that, when it comes to explanations, our language can lead us astray. Importantly, the words conversion and somatisation strongly imply an active, even deliberate, process; that the patient with a psychosomatic illness is doing something that brings their symptoms about. They are converting their distress into paralysis, or somatising their sadness into pain. Is that how things really are?

There is still much to be explained about how, in the absence of damage or disease, a body can produce a symptom as dramatic as paralysis or a seizure-like episode. But we are beginning to understand what seems to be important in getting these experiences going.

First, remember that our bodies often respond to acute distress in dramatic ways. Strong emotion can entail so called tonic immobility, in which motor areas in the brain are inhibited, and voluntary movement prevented. More familiarly, it can induce trembling, speechlessness and confusion, all of which resemble neurological symptoms. Our perception of these experiences is important. Recognising strong emotion for what it is makes it more manageable. If I tremble while understanding that I am afraid, I might give myself time for the fear to pass and my nervous system to settle down.

But when these feelings are taken as a potential sign of disease, we tend to become anxious, with consequences for how we experience and attend to our bodies. Fear increases pain, so any feeling that there is bodily damage (a frightening idea) can be enough to turn up the perceptual volume on physical discomfort or unusual sensations. Paying attention to and trying to control a shaking limb will tend to increase the trembling; attending to a difficulty with movement is likely to increase how severe we think the problem is. What might have started small becomes amplified.

People vary in terms of how easy they find it to identify emotions. The term “alexithymia” (translatable as something like “no words for emotions”) refers to a difficulty with labelling and distinguishing feelings. It can range from a near full-on emotion “blindness” to a coarser grain of emotional experience, with distinctions only between, say, feeling “good” and feeling “bad”. It is not uncommon for people with psychosomatic illnesses to report that they struggle to identify emotional states.

What this could point to is that psychosomatic illnesses arise not because of what a patient is doing with their emotions, but because of what they have not been able to do with them. When we label our emotions, when we allow them to find their expression, we are allowing ourselves to know more fully what we are feeling and what we need. In a clear departure from the Freud-inspired model, it’s not that patients with these problems are “converting” their emotions into something else. It’s that they aren’t always registering them as emotions in the first place. Instead, they’re interpreted as something having gone wrong with the body, beginning a vicious cycle of anxious attention.

This is still an uncertain area of clinical practice. Emotion is not the whole picture, but it is important for understanding why some people find themselves with otherwise unexplained symptoms. For example, one way of thinking about non-epileptic seizures (a deeply distressing and disabling experience with all the hallmarks of a seizure, but without any of the expected electrical anomalies in the brain) is that they might start off with physiological elements of a panic attack – the muscular tension and the involuntary movement – but without the accompanying subjective feeling of dread; “panic without panic”.…

Source: The Guardian Books | Published: 2026-11-22 12:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: The Highway
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear, well-structured English worth reading as a model of good prose

SHIFT 1

Ivy’s new uniform itched. The cherry red polo tee stretched across her breasts and cut beneath each arm, as if made for a man. The belt that cinched her stiff khaki pants was in an unflattering mahogany. Close-toed shoes squeaked against fresh tile. Her hair was slicked back into a ponytail, her nose ring flipped up into her nostrils. A tattoo of a squashed moth half-hidden by her shirt sleeve. She crossed two fingers behind her back, praying they wouldn’t enforce the corporate-required visor.

Ivy knew it was lame to feel excited about a menial job, but she couldn’t help it. Just last night, she’d overheard her own mother call her “loser-adjacent” through her bedroom door, still stickered and collaged from her teenage years. This would be a fresh start. A way out. Ivy mentally rattled off the list of staff perks, touching each finger as if they added up to something. 30-minute lunch break. 15-minute smoke break. Forty percent off any meals ordered during her shift. Maybe free refills.

There was a subtle scratching in the back of her throat—the beginning of a cold, thirst, or first-day jitters. The air reeked of trapped air, distant grease, and Slushies as she hovered inside the door, surveying the Berry Bright Market Store, one of twenty-seven constructed along the New York State Highway in the past year. The newness was blinding, the space acidic and bleached. Each location contained a Chicken Place, a Burger Place, and a Coffee Place. A trash can fashioned to look like a frog. You deposited garbage into its mouth. Ivy kind of loved him. Pigments popped—a stark parallel from the grayness outside. Ivy had been hired at the Chicken Place. She dug a fingernail into her belt. It made a half-moon indentation that didn’t go away.

“Guess we didn’t scare you away, huh? You’re back!” A man appeared and paused, tilting his head and grinning. “Darren! From the interview. Floor Manager.”

Darren’s forehead shone like an ice rink, a dyed-blonde shock of hair poking from his visor. His teeth were perfect doors. Despite knowing it was hardly a career, she felt kind of excited. She rubbed at a strange bruise in the crook of her elbow. An imperfection, like her, she hoped would improve with time. This job was a start, a change, something to make anyone in her life proud of her. Like the highway that loomed beneath its overcast sky outside, being here was transitory. A place on your way to another place. Ivy affixed a sincere smile to her face, pulling the sleeve over the top of her tattoo. Her throat still tickled, but barely. She eyed the slick counters, the bustling groups of travelers, and the distant soda station. Newness, she thought. Exactly what she needed.

“So ready to get started,” she stated. Each word a bubble.

SHIFT 8

It was about a week in when Ivy noticed Darren’s extra finger. He knew how to hide it as he clasped his hips, posture soldier-perfect, the eleventh slab, tucked into the folds of his polo or enveloped just inside the mouth of his pocket. A flesh stump, projecting off his pinky, the nail weak and translucent like an unborn fetus. Finally, something interesting, Ivy thought.

Ivy stood at the entrance to Berry Bright again, a gentle doting sun warming the crispness of the outdoor autumn air. Darren greeted her as she traipsed to her work station—bagging. Her partner Naomi was already there, a gum-snapping girl with above-ground pool eyes who always seemed to hand her the wrong items. Fries instead of tater tots. Coke rather than Sprite. One time, the girl handed her an empty bag. A bag with nothing in it. But Ivy felt settled—that feeling you get when you get the hang of a pretty simple job.

There was already a line of people. Men in suits staring at their watches. Families in different states of chaos, kids hanging on the ropes and dropping their sippy cups. A girl in a workout set scrolling her phone. Where were they going? She liked to wonder. She stared out into the vestibule of the rest stop. She rubbed at the bruise that was now almost gone. The restaurants were shaped in a perfect triangle, each with their own little world. Besides the Chicken Place People, there were Burger Place People and Coffee Place People. She hadn’t spoken to any of the workers apart from Naomi—everyone seemed to stay in their own Place.

Ivy’s hand went to her pocket, where a cell phone would be, to snap a pic of the sunrise. Damn. It was in the car. She’d always been so bad at keeping her phone on her.

Distant music played from the kitchen area, pop music Ivy couldn’t quite place. If she listened carefully, the voices were gibberish. Like when she forwent college, choosing to stay home and play The Sims instead. Boys love that weird EDM shit, she thought. And the cooks fit the mold, with their neck tattoos and gold teeth, jeering and slapping meat on buns. One of them winked at her, rolling up his sleeve to show off his peach pit-shaped bicep. Ivy cheerily rolled her eyes and clocked in, helping herself to a bottle of water and downing it, hoping to quell the itch that remained present. Dry air, she figured. Eager heat, pumping through the vents.

Naomi popped another wad of Bubble Yum into her glossed mouth and flipped open a bag, plopping a cradle of waffle fries inside.

“Nice tat. Musta hurt.” One of the line cooks, cologned and smarmy, leaned over the counter, jabbing a finger at Ivy’s arm. It wasn’t nice, and it hadn’t hurt. At least not compared to the reason why she got it.

“Thannnnks.” Ivy cleared her throat and pulled a ticket. “Worst idea ever. It’s a matching one.” She shrugged. “Toxic ex.”

The cook winked. “Looking for another one?”

Ivy snorted. “Maybe if you stop playing that raver music.”…

Source: The Rumpus | Published: 2026-11-22 14:11 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Alysa Liu Feels It All
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: explains an idea or a development clearly, with useful vocabulary and context

There’s no wrong way into LIFE Magazine‘s first proper new issue in almost 20 years, a relaunch powered by more than 100 contributors and lively with photo-forward features. There are moving interviews with Paralympic powerlifter Garrison Redd and Chris Bledsoe, a North Carolina man who communes with mysterious apparitions, each richly complemented by portraits (by Melchizedek Gayle and Walker Bankson, respectively). There’s the great Stacey Kranitz, snapping away alongside Mesha Maren in a dispatch from West Virginia coal country. Whatever your path, stick the landing with Bonnie Tsui’s profile of Alysa Liu, the Olympic figure skating gold medalist who, at 21, has shaped her own dynamic with her chosen sport by walking away when she must and returning when she wishes. (Nice photos, too, by some guy named Spike Jonze.)

Women’s figure skating is the marquee event of every Winter Olympics. In the world of elite competitive sports, it isn’t alone in having a history of prioritizing winning over well-being, but it has a special reputation for cruelty. As with gymnastics, the physics of ice skating favors youth and a high strength-to-weight ratio; girls are especially vulnerable to body-shaming and social pressures. Eating disorders are a known problem. The tendency toward perfectionism and emotional stoicism — and toward keeping injuries hidden — is long-established.

In this quietly conformist culture, the fact that someone would abandon a meteoric rise sent a shock wave through the sport. But to Liu, that was exactly the point. She was 16, and she had come to hate skating.

The idea of a hotly anticipated video game isn’t new, but the runup to Grand Theft Auto VI certainly seems unprecedented. It’s been 13 years since the last title in the massive open-world franchise, and the cultural appetite is undeniable. The game’s “extended reveal” crashed Netflix’s servers in August. Other video games’ sales are suffering because of it. NBA fans joke that this week will feature lethargic games and questionable injury reports—all because athletes will have stayed up all night playing GTA VI. For The Guardian, Christian Donlan talks to developers, fans, and critics to get a handle on what exactly makes the Rockstar Games series such a juggernaut.

In the run up to its release, it is easy to focus on the game’s lavish variety, but to say that you can simply do a lot of things in GTA these days – sky-diving, off-road racing, manning your own taxi cab, annoying alligators – is increasingly missing the point. The point instead lies with the density of every frame: the fuzzy edges of exposed drywall in an apartment that has been hastily refitted as a drug den, the brisk splatter of blood that appears on paintwork when someone’s face collides with it. And it goes beyond these vivid details into the realms of things you may only vaguely be aware of. Fly over the mountains in GTA V and the game delivers turbulence in little bursts of haptic feedback through the controller. You may not even notice it, but afterwards you might notice its absence in other games. They don’t pull you into their worlds as convincingly.

item.title: Embrace Your Obsessions: Susan Orlean on the Antidote to the Meaninglessness of Life
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: explains an idea or a development clearly, with useful vocabulary and context

Embrace Your Obsessions: Susan Orlean on the Antidote to the Meaninglessness of Life

Every great book, whatever its subject or genre or style, is about one thing only: the eternal question of what gives meaning to our tiny, transient lives. And every answer given, however faintly whispered, points to one thing only: the quality of attention we pay to those lives.

If attention is the lever of love, the particular — the sacred specificity of something small and singular, something easy to overlook — is its fulcrum. “Love quells fear,” Octavia Butler wrote in contemplating creativity, “and a sweet and powerful positive obsession blunts pain, diverts rage, and engages each of us in the greatest, the most intense of our chosen struggles.” Our highly clinical culture, with its tendency to pathologize the tendrils of personality that make us who we are, regards obsession as unambiguously negative — something that kidnaps us from the actuality of life. And yet all the creative energy that has given us our greatest works of art and most revolutionary breakthroughs in science has sprung from such a “powerful positive obsession.”

Susan Orlean takes up this question in her 1994 classic The Orchid Thief: A True Story of Beauty and Obsession (public library). One answer to what we long for in our existential longing, she posits, may be “to know what it feels like to care about something passionately” — to have an obsession, something very particular to which you pay rigorous and rapturous attention.

When she asks her protagonist what it is about orchids he finds so irresistible, how it is they are the animating passion of his life, he shrugs:

Oh, mystery, beauty, unknowability, I suppose… I think the real reason is that life has no meaning. I mean, no obvious meaning. You wake up, you go to work, you do stuff. I think everybody’s always looking for something a little unusual that can preoccupy them and help pass the time.

Often, it is not we who find that unusual something but it that finds us, jolts us awake from the stupor of near-living. Considering her own obsession with telling the story of the orchid thief, which had begun with a random article she read in a newspaper on a random day and ended up consuming years of her life, she observes how these obsessions take hold of us:

[It begins with] some glimpse of life that expands like those Japanese paper balls you drop in water and then after a moment they bloom into flowers, and the flower is so marvelous that you can’t believe there was a time when all you saw in front of you was a paper ball and a glass of water.

As Susan finds herself traveling through the vastness of Florida in the footsteps of the orchid thief, she comes to see these obsessions as our most powerful antidote to the hollow feeling of meaninglessness that visits upon every life — against the overwhelming bigness of life, we have the saving grace of smallness:

The land was marble-smooth and it rolled without a pucker to the horizon. My eyes grazed across the green band of ground and the blue bowl of sky and then lingered on a dead tire, a bird in flight, an old fence, a rusted barrel. Hardly any cars came toward me, and I saw no one in the rearview mirror the entire time. I passed so many vacant acres and looked past them to so many more vacant acres and looked ahead and behind at the empty road and up at the empty sky; the sheer bigness of the world made me feel lonely to the bone. The world is so huge that people are always getting lost in it. There are too many ideas and things and people, too many directions to go. I was starting to believe that the reason it matters to care passionately about something is that it whittles the world down to a more manageable size. It makes the world seem not huge and empty but full of possibility.

Nothing counterbalances our helpless givens and shapes our lives more powerfully than our relationship to possibility. To be overwhelmed is to be paralyzed by possibility. To be obsessed it to be catalyzed by it. Whatever the obsession is one of collecting or creating, whatever form it takes — orchids or oboe, birds or baking, writing or trapeze — it is a way of centering into our only task here: to fill our allotted days with maximum aliveness.

—

—

Source: The Marginalian | Published: 2026-11-14 14:31 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: How to Hear the Song of Life
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: explains an idea or a development clearly, with useful vocabulary and context

How to Hear the Song of Life

“When we have learned how to listen to trees,” Hermann Hesse wrote in one of his least known, most beautiful essays, “then the brevity and the quickness and the childlike hastiness of our thoughts achieve an incomparable joy. Whoever has learned how to listen to trees no longer wants to be a tree. He wants to be nothing except what he is. That is home. That is happiness.”

To be ourselves is rooted in the recognition that, rather than a tree, a self is a forest; to be at home in the world is rooted in the recognition that a forest is a self. While indigenous cultures have known this since the dawn of knowledge, we are only just beginning to unlearn everything we have been taught by the erasure of our creaturely belonging that we call civilization in order to remember what we were born knowing: Life and its rights are not something we can claim for ourselves unless we accord them to everything else that exists, bound to us by the mesh of mutuality that makes this drifting rock a living world.

In 2021, Ecuador led the way in this great unlearning by granting the Los Cedros Cloud Forest legal rights of personhood: the right to exist and flourish in the future.

Five years later, four pioneers of the rippling rights-of-nature movement have joined forces with the forest itself to celebrate the landmark decision, as Copernican in the history of our civilization as the Cambridge Declaration of Consciousness: Robert Macfarlane (who has asked the urgent, self-answering question “Is a river alive?” and who remains the closest thing to a Rachel Carson of our time), Giuliana Furci (who has changed not only how we think about nature with her Fungi Foundation work but the very container of our thoughts, language, coining the word funga, now inducted into the Cambridge Dictionary, to stand alongside flora and fauna in our classification of the living world), César Rodríguez-Garavito (whose legal scholarship and activism have anchored the rights-of-nature movement), and Cosmo Sheldrake (who has devoted his life to turning the soundscapes of the living world into music). That they have named the Los Cedros Cloud Forest itself as co-author is both a radical gesture — a first in the history of literature — and a kind of homecoming to an elemental reality our sciences are only just beginning to confirm: that we think not with the brain but with the world, that place and personhood are indelibly entwined, that life is a song singing us back to ourselves so that when we die we may be sung across the threshold into the rhizomatic everythingness of everything.

Illustrated by Ecuadorian artist Paula Terán Ospina, Song of the Cedars is a painted serenade to what the cloud forest can teach us about the song of life: about the time of stones, about the wisdom of rivers, about the creative tenacity of fungi.

It is a project breathtakingly beautiful in spirit and in matter, the song sung along the river that carries the ecosystem and unfolds like a paper harmonica to carry the words that break the civilizational spell of indifference with enchantment.

Trees speak in your leaves please

And streams tell me your dreams

Birds sing me your rhymes please

And stones teach me your times

Earth cover my limbs now

And mold thrive on my skin

Clouds deepen my sight please

And storms lend me your light

The back matter, following five short essays by the different contributors, is a painted encounter with the cloud forest’s wonderland of flora, fauna, and funga — 81 creatures each identified by their common and Linnaean names, occupying every niche and scale of existence, from the fierce ocelot (Leopardus pardalis) to the tender rosy flannel moth (Trosia neigropunetigera), from the air plant hovering ethereal midway between the canopy and the ground to the lichen clinging to the rocks more tenaciously than gravity itself — a vibrant reminder that, as Giuliana writes in her essay, “wherever we look, life is there.”

Beholding this loving song of life, I am struck by what a rare achievement it is in this culture to teach without preaching, to protest not with militancy but with tenacious tenderness, to remember that care is a stronger and longer lever of change than complaint, that how we show up for the summons of conscience, as individuals and as a civilization, is the deepest measure of who and what we are.

—

Published November 12, 2026

—

https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/11/12/song-of-the-cedars/

—

item.title: What Makes You Yourself: Posidonia Australis, Pando, and the Paradox of Personhood
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: explains an idea or a development clearly, with useful vocabulary and context

What Makes You Yourself: Posidonia Australis, Pando, and the Paradox of Personhood

An organism is a mortal unit of matter distinct from other organisms by its genome — the possibilities encoded in its particular genetic makeup — and its phenotype — the set of traits expressed, the actualities summoned by adaptation and chance from its possibilities. Human beings are organisms encased in the hardest yet most vulnerable exoskeleton in nature: a self. A self includes but surpasses the organism to encompass its environment and its social context, the psychological terrain of memory and desire, the fingerprints left on it by the touch of other selves. An organism ends at the physical boundary of its body, but a self does not — we spend our lives negotiating where we end and the world begins.

Humans are the only animals, save perhaps the bowerbird, who can alter their phenotype by means of their own making — grow, cut, and dye their hair, tattoo and tan their skin, increase and decrease the size of various body parts with scalpel and silicone. We are also the only animal who can radically alter both its environment and its social context, building elaborate homes on faraway landmasses, reconstituting our families and friend groups, changing the labors by which we put food on our table. Our selves are not like our cells, replacing themselves with clones in the course of living, but like Russian nesting dolls, each prior self outgrown but contained by the next. (“We are well advised to keep on nodding terms with the people we used to be, whether we find them attractive company or not,” Joan Didion wrote.) Our lives a relay race, running from the selves we have outgrown or wish to outgrow towards the selves we try to become to or are unconsciously becoming, the baton of personhood passed from one to the next along the arrow of time, the track of our mortality.

This puts us in a peculiar predicament: Each human lifetime is lived by a single organism that contains a multitude of selves, genetically continuous and psychologically discontinuous, making it impossible to define where and what the person is. What, then, makes you yourself across all those replaced cells and reconfigured selves?

Organisms like Posidonia australis, which both conceal and reveal the nature of the self, may give us the best hint at an answer — one which evolutionary biologist Rowan Hooper articulates beautifully in his book Togetherness: Symbiosis and the Hidden Story of Life’s Greatest Collaborations (public library). Considering Earth’s largest living tree, he writes:

The Pando aspen grove in Utah comprises 47,000 trees, all genetically identical, connected by a vast root system. Language immediately becomes limiting when trying to describe Pando. Do we call the forest an organism? An entity? It has been estimated to weigh nearly 6 million kilograms, or 6,000 tonnes. If it helps, that’s about thirty-five blue whales or 1,000 elephants. It is one of the oldest organisms on Earth. Its cells are living and dying over time, but the DNA remains pretty much unchanged. That is, the entity lives on, even as its parts die.

With an eye to the Ship of Theseus — Plutarch’s timeless thought experiment about the nature of the self — he reflects:

Pando is biology’s Ship of Theseus — is it the same tree as when it first sprouted? I think not. It’s more like a continuation of the idea of Pando… The 47,000 stems of Pando start off genetically the same, but grow phenotypically different; a forest, but also a mass of individuals.

“The word for world is forest,” Ursula K. Le Guin wrote in her subtle insistence that symbiosis — the ultimate unselfing of the organism — is what made this rocky planet a living world. Rustling through the canopy of the Pando is the whisper of an answer to the unnerving question of what makes a body a person: You are not your roots, not the stem of your circumstance, not your branching choices. You are the idea of you, the forest of your selves in constant conviviality with other selves, called again and again to unself into who you really are.

—

—

Source: The Marginalian | Published: 2026-11-10 01:10 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: The best recent science fiction, fantasy and horror – review roundup
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: explains an idea or a development clearly, with useful vocabulary and context

Alfa by Lilja Sigurծardóttir, translated by Larissa Kyzer (Orenda, £10.99)

The first speculative fiction by the Icelandic crime writer is set 26 years from now, with European countries united under the benevolent “omniocratic” rule of the titular artificial intelligence in Reykjavik. Universal basic income, autonomous vehicles and constant surveillance steering citizens towards their best lives are welcomed by most Icelanders, where only a few dissidents insist on living off-grid. When one of them is found murdered in a way that should have been impossible, questions are raised about the supposedly perfect system, creating fractures in the victim’s family – one of whom helped to establish the ruling AI, and still works closely with it. A fascinating, thoughtful, suspenseful tale grounded in believable characters, this could hardly be more timely.

The Lost Spectacular by Zoé Duhaime (Solaris, £18.99)

At the core of this debut is a Danish folk tale about Lukǿje, a Sandman-like character who knows more stories than anyone in the world. Set in a “City Not-Unlike-Montréal” and another that could almost be New York, it follows the careers of two former best friends, now enemies. Munro envies Noon’s magical ability to jump into different places and times through books or pictures, and has never forgiven her for inheriting the bookshop he thought should have been his. In his role as a museum curator, Munro has developed a stalkerish method by which he tracks down and eliminates every access Noon could have into the worlds of her favourite stories. A fantastical literary battle unfolds. Whimsical with a dark edge, this bookish fantasy could develop a cult following.

Look What the Cat Dragged In by Jason Rekulak with illustrations by Doogie Horner and Will Staehle (Sphere, £22)

The second illustrated horror novel from the author of Hidden Pictures features Penny, creator of a popular series of comic books inspired by life with her cat, Popcorn. After Popcorn goes missing during a blizzard, Penny is grief-stricken and spirals into depression. When she’s convinced to foster another cat, Godfrey, she is comforted enough to make progress on her new book. But strange and unpleasant things are happening around her, and the panels she compulsively works on don’t look like her usual work – they frighten her. Echoes of Rosemary’s Baby hint at the danger threatening Penny. The illustrations are equally well done, adding another dimension to this very enjoyable spooky chiller.

China +100: Stories from a Century after the Outbreak edited by Xueting C Ni, various Chinese authors and translators (Comma, £11.99)

Eleven Chinese writers imagine a version of their country 100 years after the first outbreak of Covid-19. While the threat of another novel virus features in a few stories, most concentrate on how new inventions and discoveries, along with climate change, could alter the way people live. I Want a Different World by Zhou Dedong, one of China’s most famous horror writers, brings the China of 2019 into direct contact with 2119 as researchers in the future use a new invention capable of capturing data from traces of body heat left in the past. They are attempting to solve the mystery of how a man named Xu Zhi managed to disappear from his Shanghai apartment in the early days of lockdown, never to be seen again. A compelling tale with unexpected twists, it packs a strong emotional punch as we learn of Xu Zhi’s desperate attempts to reach his wife, confined in hospital. Many things will undoubtedly change in 100 years, but some, like the anguish of being separated from loved ones, won’t. A fine batch of diverse stories, and an opportunity to read SF from a Chinese perspective.

Everything Happens So Much by Andrew H Murray (Orion, £18.99)

In a world very like our own, the existence of alternate universes has been monetised with the invention of a drug that allows the consumer to observe an alternate existence from behind the eyes of an alternate self – usually a happier, richer, more successful one. Esme Good, stuck in a boring job, has become addicted to these second-hand experiences, until one day everything changes. Suddenly Esme has become the most important person in her universe, and unless she finds a way to get her boring old life back, it could mean the end of her world. A confusing, fitfully amusing, snarky comic fantasy with touches of surrealism (there’s a talking leg), somewhat in the vein of Douglas Adams.

item.title: The cost-of-living crisis was harming Claudia’s mental wellbeing. Together we worked out strategies to help her cope | Bianca Denny
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: clear, well-structured English with original reporting

“It all feels so hard. It’s impossible to get ahead. It’s not even two steps forward and one step back, now it’s one step forward and two steps back.”

Like many people, Claudia* was feeling the impact of the cost-of-living crisis. Despite professional qualifications and full-time employment, she felt increasing financial insecurity and a lack of confidence about future opportunities. Claudia lamented her chance of fulfilling her long-held dream of buying a home. Meanwhile, her peers who had already entered the property market were feeling the pinch due to work insecurity, interest rate hikes and falling property prices.

Financial stress was damaging Claudia’s psychological wellbeing. Her complaints of poor sleep, flat mood and irritability seemed a consequence of her worries about money. Constant checking of her bank balance and finance-related news exacerbated rather than quelled her fears, yet she found it difficult to curb this compulsion.

It was little wonder Claudia was feeling flat and demoralised. She had sacrificed many of the things that brought her joy and fulfilment – gym membership, concerts, an occasional brunch or dinner with friends – to meet the goal of saving for a house deposit. With this aim seemingly out of reach, she understood the perspective of some of her peers, whose sense of financial doom informed their decision to spend in the present rather than save for the future.

Financial stress is both a cause and consequence of mental ill health. People experiencing financial strain – particularly single parents, renters and those who are unemployed – are at increased risk of poor psychological wellbeing (including depression and anxiety), due to the loss of daily structure, social isolation and restriction of leisure activities that bring physical and psychological stimulation and satisfaction. Individuals who experience mental illness (particularly severe or unremitting conditions, such as schizophrenia) are especially vulnerable to financial strain and associated stressors, including co-morbid physical illness, unemployment and insecurity surrounding food and housing.

Financial stress also affects the capacity to seek treatment for mental health conditions. The availability of services is heavily shaped by socioeconomic status and geographic location. The needs of the “missing middle” of the population (those experiencing mild to moderate psychological distress) are often unmet as they are typically ineligible for public services but find private treatment costs prohibitive. Existing private therapy clients experiencing new financial hardship may space out or terminate sessions, harming treatment efficacy.

Initial work with Claudia focused on defining her financial concerns. Recognising the limits of a therapy setting to problem-solve around this, a referral to a financial counsellor was made to provide her with help on financial literacy, budgeting and assessing eligibility for financial aid.

Our therapeutic work together focused on the impact of financial strain on Claudia’s psychological wellbeing. Reducing checking her bank balance had a positive impact on rumination and irritability, with a recognition that small account fluctuations were unlikely to be meaningful. Claudia also made efforts to cap her consumption of finance-related news, limiting media intake to one trusted news source and resisting speculative online commentary.

Like many of her peers, she felt anger at the generational disadvantage that she believed to be a key contributing factor to her predicament. She had fulfilled obligations of study and employment but external and societal factors meant she could no longer expect to receive the rewards of home ownership or financial freedom enjoyed by previous generations. Acceptance of the changed social and economic landscape went some way to helping her reduce feelings of disappointment and personal responsibility.

Social comparisons were a clear trigger of distress for Claudia. To this end, she tried to stay out of conversations about money. She was envious of others’ financial positions and, understandably, found it difficult to sympathise with friends complaining of the costs of home ownership or the changing conditions of owning assets such as investment properties.

Increasing Claudia’s participation in leisure and social activities was an important strategy to lift her mood and improve wellbeing. Here, we resisted all-or-nothing thinking that previously led her to cancel all events. Instead, we recognised the value of free or low-cost events – time in nature, making use of her local library, meetup groups with like-minded people, and attending exercise classes at training institutes and community centres.

Last, despite the doom and gloom perpetuated by the media and social commentary, we made a concerted effort to remain curious and hopeful about the future. We recognised that financial circumstances change over time. It was important to keep perspective and seek good news where possible.

Therapy was not a panacea for Claudia’s financial concerns. Like many people, she continued to experience cost-of-living stress and held valid worries about home ownership and generational inequity. But making changes to some of her thinking and actions about money remedied some of her money-related psychological distress.

*All clients are fictional amalgams

item.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting and clear analysis

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of sexism. But one of the tragedies of Labour’s 18 long years of exile from power and the climactic defeat of organised labour in the miners’ strike was the fact that they opened the way for the wholesale reinvention of work and watershed developments that we seem to be only just waking up to.

The Welsh writer Richard King’s oral history of his home country, Brittle With Relics, contains a fascinating quotation from Nicky Wire of those sons of the South Wales coalfield the Manic Street Preachers. Wire’s father was a miner before he joined the army and then came home to work as a carpenter and builder in a local economy that was thriving. Back then, to be working class did not axiomatically mean you were short of money; workers’ collective clout, moreover, delivered exactly what the 21st-century labour market so lacks.

“The pay levels in the 60s and the 70s were brilliant for working-class people,” says Wire. “Everyone in our valley was wearing suits and going to Tunisia on package holidays … My dad just worked his bollocks off; he was one of the great workers. When he passed away, we had ‘Father, son, brother, worker’ on his memorial stone, because that’s what he did.”

Far too many lives, in wildly diverse parts of the economy, are now a long way from that kind of everyday pride and contentment, something proved by no end of research. Only a few weeks ago, for instance, the Resolution Foundation published analysis of new information from the British Social Attitudes survey. The headline findings were that job satisfaction in the UK has dropped to the lowest level ever recorded and that “the proportion [of workers] willing to work harder than required to help their employer succeed has fallen to its lowest ever level over the past decade” (it stands at a pretty miserable 55%). The proportion saying they had an interesting job fell from 74% to 63%. The share reporting opportunities for advancement went from 35% to 26%.

In its soul Labour still thinks its basic mission is to right such wrongs. But from the Tony Blair years onwards, the party’s thinking has also been regularly warped by inclinations that it ought to find objectionable: to shove people into work irrespective of what that entails, and to emphasise the need to redesign human beings to somehow fit with the mercurial, often cruel ways of modern capitalism rather than making perfectly justified demands for the latter to change.

Which brings us to the report about young people and employment – and more specifically Neets, or those not in education, employment or training – put together by the former New Labour high-up Alan Milburn and published this week. On a long train journey I read all 1,005 of its numbered paragraphs and was struck by a few things: the thoroughness of its research and the urgency of its tone – but one glaring absence: of any meaningful examination of what might be shorthanded as “bad work” despite its centrality to just about everything Milburn has worked on.

Milburn partly blames the current crisis on how the state delivers benefits, education and health. (There is a whole other piece that could be written about how a proposed £3.6bn of cuts to so-called “welfare” risk so impoverishing vulnerable young people that they will be pushed even further away from the labour market.) He rightly points out a “long-term decline in entry-level employment, youth apprenticeships and employer investment in training”. But though he also rather grandly proposes “a new bargain between government and employers to create and sustain more opportunities for young people”, you soon realise what he means – as evidenced by whispers currently circulating about the abandonment of some of Angela Rayner’s new programme of improved workers’ rights, Milburn gets close to proposing not to expect more from employers but less.

“Employers have faced higher costs, a maze of schemes, fragmented support and growing uncertainty about the rules of the game,” he says, and have been “treated as if they were the problem rather than a central part of the solution”. He has picked up concerns about Rayner’s workplace changes, he adds, centred on “the impact the new legislation may have on youth hiring, especially in hospitality and retail”. But that kind of talk risks defending the indefensible: a recent report from the TUC not only highlighted the low pay and job insecurity seemingly endemic to those sectors of the economy but also pointed out how they contribute to “economic inactivity generally and specifically the rise in mental distress and economic inactivity among young people”. Letting them off the hook, in other words, may not ease the Neets crisis but worsen it.…

Source: The Guardian Opinion | Published: 2026-11-22 10:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: There’s probably a cult hiding in plain sight on your high street. At last, Britain is confronting the problem | Rachael Reign
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting and clear analysis

Britain is confronting its cult problem. Better late than never.

They don’t advertise themselves as cults. They don’t register as cults. And they certainly don’t have the word above the door. But make no mistake: cults operate in communities across Britain. Chances are, there’s one on your local high street.

Today, I support survivors through Surviving Universal UK, the country’s only Black-led specialist organisation dedicated to spiritual and cultic abuse. After years of campaigning, 2026 is shaping up to be a historic year for survivors in Britain. The silence is finally beginning to break.

On Monday, MPs debated support for people leaving what are officially called “high-control religious groups”. Led by Labour MP Sam Carling, the debate brought a neglected issue into mainstream British politics. Carling explicitly described the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (UCKG) as a cult. Other groups were also named in the debate. MPs raised concerns about constituents harmed by high-control groups and inadequate protections.

For survivors watching, the significance was immense. Many had waited years for this moment of public acknowledgment and political attention. The UCKG is no obscure underground movement. It is a registered charity with branches across Britain, investigated by the BBC’s Panorama and by national newspapers.

But what made the debate even more significant was the discussion of change. MPs pressed for stronger protections and a serious examination of whether existing legislation is fit for purpose. The government was urged to act. Survivors were finally being heard openly in parliament itself.

I welcome that political attention. I also know that recognition alone cannot protect anyone.

There have been other encouraging developments. In February, the Crown Prosecution Service included spiritual abuse in its updated guidance on honour-based abuse, including harmful practices associated with supposed demonic possession. Plans for an all-party parliamentary group examining spiritual, ritual and cultic abuse are taking shape. Meanwhile, Surviving Universal UK has demanded a national call for evidence.

Britain has hardly been short of warnings. From the Jesus Army to SPAC Nation, alleged and documented cases of abuse involving high-control groups have made headlines for years. Yet each scandal is treated as isolated.

Such abuse is not exclusively religious. High-control groups can emerge in political movements, therapeutic settings or around charismatic individuals. What matters is not what members believe, but how power is exercised over them. We already recognise coercive control within domestic abuse. We understand how manipulation erodes independence. Yet when similar behaviour occurs within a group, our legal and safeguarding responses become far less assured.

I know how frightening that control can be. When questioning authority supposedly endangers your relationships or salvation, leaving is rarely as simple as walking through a door. In February, the Home Office said it did not intend to extend the coercive control offence under the Serious Crime Act 2015 beyond personally connected relationships. Asked specifically about cults, extremist groups and gangs, it argued that expansion could create uncertainty for police and prosecutors.

That response troubled me deeply. Since when did the complexity of protecting survivors become a justification for leaving them without adequate safety? Existing laws can address rape, assault and fraud. But sustained psychological coercion does not always fit neatly into those offences. Survivors should not have to wait for another crime to occur before the harm they are experiencing is recognised.

Elsewhere, governments are beginning to approach this differently. France has a dedicated public body, Miviludes, monitoring harmful sectarian practices. In July, a parliamentary inquiry in Victoria, Australia, made 39 recommendations concerning cults and organised fringe groups, including consideration of legislation addressing group-based coercion.

The inquiry focused on harmful conduct, not legitimate belief. That distinction matters. Religious freedom is fundamental, but it cannot mean freedom from scrutiny when abuse is alleged. Accountability is not persecution. Britain should be capable of upholding both principles.

The consequences extend beyond courtrooms. Someone leaving an abusive relationship can, at least in principle, access established safeguarding procedures and specialist services. A person escaping a cult may discover that the professional responsible for helping them has little understanding of what they have endured.

For Black and global-majority survivors, those barriers can be compounded by racism, religious stigma and a shortage of culturally competent support. I have spent years advocating for people whose experiences are too often misunderstood by the very institutions to which they turn for help.

And we must challenge the idea that people join cults because they lack intelligence. People seek belonging. They want answers, reassurance and somewhere to feel valued. Exploitative groups can manipulate those entirely human needs until the community that once offered comfort becomes almost impossible to leave.

Britain needs a national call for evidence, specialist training for frontline professionals and serious consideration of legal protections against group-based coercion. Survivors must be central to shaping that response. Survivors still struggle to have their experiences recognised as abuse.…

Source: The Guardian Opinion | Published: 2026-11-22 07:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/22/britain-cult-problem-survivors-abuse-high-street-politics

item.title: Why ‘patient influencers’ should come with a health warning
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting and clear analysis

Emily Miller was a 20-year-old university student in the UK when, shortly after a COVID-19 infection, she started having sensations that mirrored a heart attack. Other bewildering symptoms followed – dizziness, fainting, and uncontrollable muscle spasms. ‘By the time my classes ended I felt drunk, disoriented and my ears would ring,’ Miller wrote in a pinned post on her Instagram page, @thatgirlwithlongcovid_. ‘I couldn’t remember getting home from class.’

Miller is a ‘patient influencer’ – one of a growing number of people who share vivid accounts of their health experiences on social media. She first started posting about life with long COVID because her experience was incredibly isolating while her peers were still partying and going to classes like normal, and she hoped posting online would connect her with other young people in the same situation. Today, she has a small but engaged community of about 4,000 followers on Instagram and 3,000 on TikTok. Miller shares intimate details of life with long COVID, such as photo timelines outlining the onset of her symptoms and videos discussing everyday difficulties.

Patient influencers like Miller often build deeply personal bonds with their followers, many of whom live with the same condition. On a recent pair of Miller’s posts featuring the medical interventions that did and didn’t help her, followers have posted long comments detailing their own treatment experiences and thanking her for her advice.

As valuable as chronic illness content is for spreading awareness and building communities around stigmatised illnesses – maybe you too have found a sense of support and camaraderie from individuals whose experiences you identify with – there are also concerning aspects to this new trend. At the heart of it is the way social media serves up a distorted version of reality, drawing on selected content from patient influencers in ways that often don’t reflect the full range of chronic illness experiences people have in real life.

Patient influencers are often well meaning but can find themselves forced to choose between leaning into these narratives and losing engagement. ‘You’re not [posting] for followers or to get as many views as you possibly can,’ says Miller, ‘but you do want [your content] to be reaching the right people.’

Like Miller, Kaysie was in college when she first developed symptoms she couldn’t make sense of. Along with dizziness and sleepiness, Kaysie started falling down frequently. ‘It was super unclear exactly what the problem was,’ she says.

Hoping to alleviate her uncertainty, Kaysie turned to Reddit – another online environment where patient influencers share their stories and advice – where she saw her symptoms reflected in people’s posts about postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), an autonomic nervous system disorder that causes dizziness and fainting. Reading other people’s stories was comforting, giving Kaysie a framework to make sense of what was happening.

Diagnosis of a chronic illness can take years, particularly for conditions like POTS that aren’t well-understood, so it’s understandable why patients like Kaysie may be drawn to social media’s focus on diagnostic labels (a 2025 study led by the paediatrician Lindsey Daon analysed hundreds of chronic illness posts on Instagram and found that 87 per cent mentioned a specific diagnostic label). Yet this desire for the certainty of a diagnosis can lead to problems. Patient influencers with their own specific diagnosis often list the early signs of their illness that they originally overlooked – such as constant exhaustion, joint pain and dizziness. But symptoms like these can be associated with many different conditions, and followers who latch onto an influencer’s diagnosis often do so prematurely.

People become vigilant to body sensations that match their expectations, and filter out sensations that don’t

This is exactly what happened to Kaysie. Two years after being convinced by patient influencers that she had POTS, she was diagnosed by medical professionals with a different condition – narcolepsy. She learned that she was actually falling down because narcolepsy can cause cataplexy, a sudden, temporary loss of muscle control. ‘I definitely ended up on a weird path that wasn’t quite accurate,’ she says.

A related concern is that patient influencers can teach their followers to centre their own identities around a diagnostic label. ‘I’ve seen people that have ultimately felt a lot of grief because they really feel that they don’t have much left, other than their illness,’ says Sara Davin, a pain psychologist at the Cleveland Clinic.

Patient influencers could also be affecting their followers’ symptoms through a process called social transmission. Health researchers believe this phenomenon occurs because, when people develop expectations about what they should experience, they become vigilant to body sensations that match these expectations, and filter out sensations that don’t.

A 2023 study makes this process vivid. Participants observed someone else undergoing a virtual reality (VR) experience before undergoing it themselves. What participants didn’t know was that some of the people they observed were actors, who modelled the symptoms of cybersickness, a feeling of nausea and discomfort sometimes caused by VR.

Participants were told that the study was about online learning in VR, assessed through a series of memory-based questions, but the researchers’ real aim was to measure participants’ cybersickness. They found that those who viewed an apparently sick actor subsequently reported feeling more cybersickness symptoms themselves, compared with other participants who saw someone use the VR without getting sick. The study serves as a proof of concept confirming that seeing other people’s health experiences can shape our own.…

Source: Psyche | Published: 2026-11-11 11:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://psyche.co/ideas/why-patient-influencers-should-come-with-a-health-warning

item.title: How to help someone whose thinking seems delusional
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting and clear analysis

A ‘delusion’ might sound like a belief that is obviously unreal. But if someone in your life is experiencing one, it will certainly feel real to them. In some cases, it might even seem plausible to you at first – especially when it draws on real experiences or common fears.

A delusion could look like:

- a friend or partner feeling convinced that they’ve been sabotaged by their co-workers, and hyperfocusing on past conversations and emails;

- a university student believing that social media posts and songs contain messages intended specifically for them, making it harder to focus on anything else; or

- a family member saying they have been chosen for a special mission – that they are the only person who can expose a vast network of corruption.

If you have a loved one who has a concerning belief and who you think might show signs of delusional thinking, it’s normal to feel frightened for them, overwhelmed and unsure how to respond. You might wonder whether it’s best to question the belief, to just ignore it or to encourage the person to get help. Many people find themselves caught between two fears: the fear of saying too much and making things worse, and the fear of saying too little and overlooking a serious problem.

This Guide is for people in your situation. As a clinical psychologist, I’ve spent much of my career working with people who are experiencing delusions and other symptoms of psychosis, as well as with the loved ones who support them. My approach is informed by a framework called cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis (CBTp), which emphasises curiosity, collaboration and reducing distress. I’ll draw on these experiences throughout this Guide. After saying a bit more about what delusions are, I’ll describe how to consider whether someone in your life is truly experiencing one – and if so, what you can do to help.

What mental health experts mean by ‘delusions’

In everyday language, people use the word ‘delusion’ loosely, but clinically it refers to a belief that remains fixed despite clear evidence to the contrary, and one that is not widely shared within a person’s cultural or social context. What matters is not just the content of the belief, but how a person experiences it.

Often, it’s not one unusual statement that alerts loved ones, but the growing certainty a person feels and the increasing distress and disruption to daily life. I’ve seen versions of this pattern many times. For example, parents might initially hear their university-age child say that a group of students in the library seemed to be watching them, or that cars of the same make or colour kept appearing around campus. The comments may sound a little odd, but still plausible enough that the parents brush them off. Over time, the student may become increasingly certain that the other students, the cars and other seemingly unrelated events are all connected and are evidence that someone is monitoring them. The parents might eventually find out that the young person has lost weight and has been avoiding the dining hall and other places because they no longer feel safe there.

Some people have a single delusional belief, while others have several, often with related themes. They may occur on their own, or alongside other symptoms of psychosis – such as hearing or perceiving things that other people don’t, or disorganised speech or behaviour. Delusions can also coincide with mood disorders, substance use or periods of extreme stress or sleep disruption. (They are also seen in medical conditions such as dementia and Parkinson’s disease, and can appear at any stage of life, but this Guide focuses primarily on adults and adolescents who have delusions in the context of mental health conditions.) For loved ones, it is usually less important to determine the exact cause than to notice that something has changed and that it’s affecting the person’s wellbeing.

You do not need to diagnose someone, nor convince them that their belief is wrong, in order to help. In fact, approaching them with curiosity and compassion, and focusing on staying connected, can help preserve the trust between you and make it easier for them to accept support.

Source: Psyche | Published: 2026-11-10 11:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://psyche.co/guides/how-to-help-someone-whose-thinking-seems-delusional

item.title: “It’s either this or death”: Canada renews the Local Journalism Initiative and extends journalism tax credit
item.description:

Why it is here: original reporting and clear analysis

Canada’s proposed federal budget includes some good news for local journalism. The federal government is extending its journalism tax credit by $501 million, expanding eligibility to audio and audiovisual news organizations, and renewing the Local Journalism Initiative, which supports journalism in underserved communities.

Sarah wrote about the Local Journalism Initiative in its early days. A study earlier this year found that reporters paid with LJI funding believed they maintained their roles as watchdogs and wrote balanced stories, though two-thirds of interviewees were concerned about the perception of a conflict of interest. A growing number of journalists say the benefits of government subsidies for journalism outweigh the drawbacks.

A recent report in The Tyee suggests government support is essential to the survival of local media in Canada. (The Tyee has received support from the Local Journalism Initiative.)

“It’s either this or death, frankly,” LJI program director and Canadian Association of Journalists president Brent Jolly told The Tyee. “It’s not about local news editors getting their marching orders from the Prime Minister’s Office like some conspiracy theorists want you to think. It’s about infrastructure.”

Lisa Sygutek, publisher of the Crowsnest Pass Herald in Alberta, credited the LJI with growing the publication from “a 16-page paper to a 24-page paper.”

Read more in The Tyee’s look at Canadian local news here.
