item.title: Student journalists are reporting more local news for real audiences. Their professors are exhausted.
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting and clear analysis

If there’s one big takeaway from the past two decades of local news struggle — the often perilous, occasionally brilliant transition from dominant newspapers to online media — perhaps it’s this: Passion alone isn’t enough.

A newspaper newsroom filled with committed editors and brilliant reporters still stares into the same headwinds as its more middling peers. The devotion of those leading a nonprofit outlet can mean little if revenue can’t keep the doors open. And even when the money is less important — when journalism is somewhat protected from the demands of the market — passion is still a finite resource, and it’s not always renewable.

That truism came to mind when I was reading a recent article by Sima Bhowmik of the University of Vermont and Andrea Lorenz of Kent State. It looks at one specific corner of the contemporary news ecosystem: journalism schools that use their students to fill voids in local coverage.

J-schools, after all, have faculties full of experience and students who need it. A few decades ago, an early-career journalist might have spent a few years covering city council meetings and school board budgets before moving up the chain to a bigger outlet. That path barely exists these days, and journalism programs know their students need the chance to do real work. What if these reporters-in-training could handle some of the local stories that the city’s daily no longer can?

If you happen to live near a college with a journalism program, you’ve probably seen this idea — often called the “teaching hospital” model — in action. Here in the Boston suburbs, many of the stories I read about my town are written by Boston University students. According to UVM’s Center for Community News, where Bhowmik is an assistant research professor, there were 282 such efforts as of 2025, producing local news inside 205 colleges and universities. Those numbers were up from 227 programs in 172 colleges the year before — a boom fueled by a surge in philanthropic funding for these partnerships.

Bhowmik and Lorentz’s paper — published in Journalism & Mass Communication Educator — is the result of interviews with 118 faculty and staff at 101 of those colleges, and their major takeaway is one that will be familiar to many in local news: They’re exhausted.

Participants repeatedly used phrases such as “at capacity,” “don’t have the bandwidth,” “not enough hours of the day,” and “it’s just a lot” to describe the workload. Several described long workdays and exhaustion, with one participant saying the amount of editing “just about kills me every semester.” At many institutions, faculty workload was intensified by staffing shortages, retirements, hiring freezes, and budget cuts. This left faculty with little time to provide the one-on-one coaching necessary to elevate student stories to publishable quality…

“What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me. “But the extra work they’re putting it isn’t always getting acknowledged within the system. A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how important the work is.”

(See above: Passion alone isn’t enough.)

Here’s how one faculty member described their situation:

Think about it: Like, how many reporters does the average assigning editor at a mid-sized newspaper supervise? Half a dozen? So try, like, 20 of them, and each of them is writing for a different outlet maybe, which has its own set of deadlines and editor. And they’re all at varying skill levels, and broadly, they’re all pretty new. Their copy requires a lot of work, their reporting often requires a lot of handholding.

Another talked about the responsibility of getting student work up to the level a news outlet expects. You can’t just give a meh student story a C- and be done with it if a local editor is expecting publishable copy.

It takes a lot of work to get student work up to the quality of professionally published work. And a lot of students start out with really good ideas, do some good reporting by the time they’re done in the semester, it needs work, and that tends to fall on the faculty person. And that’s a lot of work outside of uncompensated work…But bridging that gap between what a student produces at the end of a semester and what can actually be published is still a big gap that needs to be addressed.

And aside from the editing work, faculty described the administrative burden of being the connective tissue joining two distinct worlds. Negotiating pitches, coordinating deadlines, dealing with revisions, shepherding copy flows — all of it with students who are juggling other courses, work-study jobs, and the life of college student — can be “difficult to sustain without administrative support, dedicated staff, or funding for editors,” they write.

Just to save a few dozen proud Mizzou alums from emailing me: Yes, the “teaching hospital” model is not a new idea. The idea of giving journalism students real-world experience in public-facing outlets has been central to the Missouri Method for more than a century, and other major journalism schools have long done versions of this work. But Bhowmik notes that many of these new efforts are in smaller colleges with smaller journalism programs — places without the in-house infrastructure of a Columbia Missourian or KOMU, where media partnerships involve more ongoing negotiation. That can leave more of the pressure of sustainability on one or two overworked faculty members. As Bhowmik and Lorenz put it:

…faculty labor is not incidental to the model;…

Source: Nieman Lab | Published: 2026-11-09 18:52 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

For the series Once Upon an Artwork, children are paired with paintings from the collection of the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York City. They’re given free rein to bring their own storytelling and interpretations to the work, and the results are given lively professional animations. In this instalment, two young friends named Dili and Amalia explore I and the Village (1911), a colourful, Cubist-inspired work by the Russian and French Jewish artist Marc Chagall, which draws on his early years in the Hasidic community of Vitebsk, in today’s Belarus. Through the eyes of Dili and Amalia, however, the scene becomes a world where it’s day and night at the same time, memories become visible, everything is upside down and, as such, handstands become a cinch. The resulting short is immersive and playful, serving as a warm reminder of how art inevitably awakens the storyteller inside each of us, no matter our age.

item.title: ‘A hundred literate children’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: one short sentence

Q: In a NY Times obituary, a historian refers to Ayatollah Ali Khamenei as “arrogant, literate, obdurate, revengeful,” etc. Is it not odd to describe an Islamic scholar as “literate,” i.e., merely able to read and write?

A: The word “literate” meant educated or learned when it first appeared in English in the 14th century. Although the primary meaning now is able to read or write, you can still find the original sense in standard dictionaries.

Merriam-Webster includes “educated,” “cultured,” “literary”; American Heritage, “familiar with literature,” “literary”; Cambridge, “having a good education or showing it in your writing”; Collins, “intelligent and well-educated”; Webster’s New World, “well-educated,” “showing extensive knowledge, learning, or culture.”

So one could defend the use of “literate” by Abbas Milani, director of Iranian studies at Stanford University, in the Feb. 28, 2026, Times obituary. But we would have used “learned” or a similar word to avoid confusion with today’s general meaning of the adjective.

As for its etymology, “literate” originally meant “acquainted with letters or literature; erudite, learned, lettered,” according to the Oxford English Dictionary.

The OED’s earliest citation refers to “a c. childer litterate” (“a hundred literate children”). From Polychronicon, John Trevisa’s translation, sometime before 1387, of an earlier 14th-century work by Ranulf Higden.

In the early 17th century, Oxford says, “literate” took on its “weakened” use—“able to read and write”—which is “now the usual sense.”

The dictionary’s first citation, which we’ve expanded, is from The Description of Penbrokshire, by George Owen of Henllys, Lord of Kemes (composed in 1602-1603 and first published in 1892):

“to indorse the wittnesses names on the backe of the deede, and this to be done by the wittnesses themselves, if they were literate; otherwise by some clerke or other for them.”

The OED describes this sense of “literate” as “opposed to illiterate,” which had appeared a half-century earlier. The two terms are derived from the Latin litteratus (lettered, learned) and illiteratus (unlettered, unlearned).

Here’s the dictionary’s earliest “illiterate” citation: “No more can Iudgis, Illitturate Discus ane mater” (“No more can illiterate judges discuss [adjudicate] any matter”). From Ane Compendious and Breue Tractate (1556), a tract by the Church of Scotland minister William Lauder on the duty of kings, pastors, and judges.

Getting back to “literate,” the adjective took on a new sense in the 20th century: “competent or knowledgeable in a particular area,” such as as “politically literate,” “culturally literate,” or “computer literate.”

The first example in the OED for this sense is from a US newspaper: “The American people were busy becoming ‘politically literate’; that is, learning how to run their political system” (Boston Daily Globe, March 23, 1919).

The dictionary’s earliest citation for “computer literate” is from a 1961 lecture by the British novelist and chemist C. P. Snow about the danger of relying on computers and computer adepts to make decisions:

“It is going to take a major effort to make all scientific administrators computer-literate. It is going to be quite impossible within foreseeable time to make nonscientific administrators computer-literate.” From a report in Technology Review (July 1961) on “Men and Machines,” a conference at MIT.

Help support the Grammarphobia Blog with your donation. And check out our books about the English language and more.

Source: Grammarphobia | Published: 2026-03-23 12:10 UTC | Difficulty: 62/100

item.title: tips, dumps, fly-tipping, fly-posting, post no bills
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: useful vocabulary and context

On my way home from work, I pass the windowless side of an end-of-terrace house, on which this sign is posted:

Such signs are a common sight in England, and not immediately transparent to AmE speakers, who are more accustomed to 'No dumping' signs:

(There's more we could say about these signs, but we haven't got space for that right now. For more on NO TRESPASSING, see this old post on AmE POSTED signs.)

The Brighton sign is an official local-government sign, while anyone can buy those US examples. The equivalent anyone-can-buy it signs in the UK might have both the terms tipping and dumping:

Tipping (first cited UK early 1800s), like dumping, relates to tipping, and thereby releasing, the contents of a truck or cart into an area for waste, hence BrE tip for what AmE would call dump: a (probably official) place where the waste from a particular area can be left (for processing, piling up, burial, etc.). The verb dump ('to fall with sudden force') goes back to Middle English, but it's only in the late 1700s, in the US, that it starts to be used transitively to refer particularly to getting rid of waste. (See this old post for more on AmE dumpster. See the comments of this old post for discussion of dump truck.)

Tipping or dumping could be legal, but fly-tipping is specifically 'illegal dumping'. Why fly? It's not to do with the insects that inevitably follow illegal dumping. It's the fly in the expression on the fly: that is, in motion or 'on the wing'. Dumping/tipping that is "on the fly" is without prior arrangement and probably surreptitious. You're taking a load of waste away from where it's not needed, and you just leave it someplace that is conveniently unobserved. The term fly-tipping is first noted by the Oxford English Dictionary in the 1960s, and the back-formed verb fly-tip only comes up in the 1980s.

On the fly developed different uses in BrE and AmE in the mid-1800s. In BrE it could be a slang term for begging (or committing crimes) while moving about/around town. (See Green's Dictionary of Slang.) With that extension, fly-tipping makes some sense as a term for an illegal activity. In AmE, on the fly became a description of a baseball that's been hit, but has not yet touched the ground—so you want to catch the other team's ball on the fly. (The term fly ball comes some decades later, as a result.)

fly-posting

If you know that fly-tipping is illegally dumping waste "on the fly", then it's easier to see what BrE fly-posting means: putting up posters on the move—all over town. (Often, but not necessarily, illegally.) If you don't make the on the fly connection, you might think it's about posting (orig. AmE) flyers (late 1800s). But since flyer also comes from that same 'quickly, while moving' sense of fly, you're not far off.

An earlier term for this is bill-sticking (late 1700s, esp. in 1800s), which one occasionally still sees in the UK, especially the agentive noun bill-sticker. We rarely call flyers or posters bills or handbills these days, but that's what they were from the late 1700s and into the 20th century.

While it's possible to find uses of fly-posting in the US, it's a much rarer term there. Instead of signs saying No Flyposting you might see a stencil(l)ed Post No Bills.

item.title: hadn't have VERBed
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting and learning value

A great thing about being Facebook friends with linguists is that I get to benefit from their daily observations of English. Here's a recent observation from John Wells:

Something I've just heard on the telly about someone who nearly drowned: "If the fisherman hadn't've spotted him, he might not have survived."I keep hearing this grammatical construction in BrE, with extra "have" ('ve) as compared with the standard "...hadn't spotted...".But I have never come across any comment on, or discussion of, this usage.

In the comments, some people claim it's much used in the US, but it soon becomes clear that there's some confusion with a different construction than Wells was talking about. So, let's look at it.

I'm using the News on the Web corpus (because my usual go-to GloWbE corpus isn't co(-)operating in giving me the contractions). There I searched for "had n't have VERB" and got it with a range of verbs:

So, it's looking pretty British, but in Caroline McAfee's 'Characteristics of non-standard grammar in Scotland', she says "as in American English". (Bold = my emphasis, so it's clear which [more BrE] bits of the example we're talking about.)

In Scottish speech, as in American English, there is a sequence had – (ENCLITIC NEGATIVE PARTICLE) – have PAST PARTICIPLE. The identity of the second have, which appears as a weak or enclitic form, is problematic (as witness the writers who spell it of):

‘Ah wouldnae of came if Ah had of knew,’ he insisted (Helen W. Pryde, the First Book of the McFlannels, 1947: 24)

Adams (1948) suggested that it was a survival of English dialectal y- before past participles, reinterpreted as have via the latter’s weak form a. The occurrence of the form in Scotland and the USA is compatible with diffusion from Ulster. Fodor and Smith (1978) offer a purely synchronic analysis, seeing the first have as a modal and the second as the auxiliary of the perfect.

The British usage may have started in Scotland and now is more widespread. But what about that "as in American English"? Well, the historical picture in Google Ngrams gives us a different story from the contemporary NOW corpus. Here it is with had and been as the last verb in the search term:

item.title: nostalgia for present-day British English
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: learning value and freshness

I get various Google Alerts for things related to my interests, and today I got one for a story in The Sun and the Daily Express about the '20 English words the public wants to revive'.

But I've got enough of a gist from the Google Alert (orig. AmE) blurb:

The "research", it seems, has been done in the hallowed halls of the Tesco Mobile marketing department, with the celebrity endorsement of Tom Daley and Gyles Brandreth. (There is a video on the various tabloid websites, again, if you want to allow them to put the devil's cookies in your computer.)

But it's enough to read that little blurb: flabbergasted, chuffed, and gobsmacked. The "British public" (Tesco Mobile customers?)  wants to "revive" these "classic" words. You know, those moribund words that... wait a minute...

All three of these words seem to be in (BrE) rude health. Have a look at their use in British books. More and more in the 21st century:

Calling something that didn't exist before 1980 a "classic" that needs to be "revived" when in reality, it's just reaching its prime is blatant ageism, I say. Gobsmacked, I feel your pain.

But maybe books are weird. Maybe "real" people don't use these words. Maybe not, but the tabloid newspapers have certainly been reviving them for the past 30 years. Here's what you see if you search for these words in the archives of The Sun (courtesy of Nexis):

Are we the British public really missing these "classic" Britishisms? Or are we just missing feeling good about ourselves?

item.title: Hull City v Brighton: Premier League – live
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

24 mins: Slater hooked it into the box, with Mendy heading well wide. That’s Hull’s first chance of any kind and it did not worry Bart Verbruggen.

- Premier League updates from the 2pm GMT kick-off

- Live scores | Table | Follow on TikTok | And mail Dom

Sun 22 Nov 2026 09.25 EST

First published on Sun 22 Nov 2026 08.00 EST

Sun 22 Nov 2026 09.25 EST

First published on Sun 22 Nov 2026 08.00 EST

23 mins: Some really strong and determined play from Iroegbunam earns his team a free-kick. The referee tried to play an advantage for Hull before bringing the play back.

Is this worth a shot? Slater and Belloumi stand over it.

21 mins: Another chance for Brighton, this time Ayari picking up the headed knockdown from Rutter and scuffing his effort, which means it’s an easy save for Tzolakis.

I’ve got a horrible record of live-blogging nil-nils, by the way. Just saying …

20 mins: Brighton are starting to tick here. Their short passing, their movement, their invention … it’s all superb to watch. A fluid move ends with Costinha having a shot, but he guides it wide. That was another big chance.

18 mins: A deflection runs kindly for Gomez down the right and then Rutter gets it wrong in taking the return away from his teammate. Brighton keep the pressure on, before Costinha’s cross is held by Tzolakis.

17 mins: Ironic cheers from the home fans as their team get a free-kick. Slater bundled over. Brighton have been fairly spiky in their tackling so far, and perhaps the Hull fans felt that free-kick was overdue.

A huge save from Tzolakis! That looked goal bound. It was De Cuyper whose low cross from the left was brilliantly precise, and Gomez should probably have finished it off. The Hull keeper made himself big to deny the Paraguayan at close range.

14 mins: Both keepers have had crosses to catch and errant through-balls to collect, but we haven’t really had a shot in anger yet. Gomez drills in a powerful cross low from the right but nobody in a Brighton shirt is anywhere near it.

13 mins: Brighton are actually playing more on the counterattack at the moment, which isn’t quite what I envisaged for this match, against the low-blockers of Hull City.

Boscagli’s speculative cross does not find Rutter.

11 mins: Dunk has to be alert to snuff out a Hull chance, as the home side get themselves a long throw opportunity on the left.

9 mins: I’ve said this before but ‘duh, duh, duh, football in a library’ is one of the worst chants in our great game.

8 mins: Brighton are finally getting into it, pushing Hull back with a prolonged period of possession. The black and amber shirts are shuttling back and forth to keep the visitors chanceless, at the moment. Good disciplined defence.

6 mins: Hull’s shape does resemble more of a 4-3-3, or 4-5-1, with Cho and Belloumi being asked to get forward into wide positions and support McBurnie. The home team have started confidently.

4 mins: Rutter and Gomez link up nicely down Brighton’s inside-right channel but Tzolakis is there to catch the former’s cutback. Nice pacy start to the game, this.

3 mins: Boscagli asks for an early corner but the referee isn’t having it.

Hull then hump it long from the resulting goal-kick, with McBurnie battering his way through bodies and feeding Cho, whose shot is wild.

2 mins: Brighton’s press baiting play deep in possession might not be so successful against a Hull team who are happy to sit in a low block, even at home. But the home side have come out quite aggressively, with Regan Slater barging into Diego Gomez to concede a free-kick.

KICK OFF

A bleat of Peter Bankes’s whistle gets us off and running in Humberside.

Teams are out. Let’s do this thing.

Some important pre-match news for me personally … my significant other has brought a tube of sour cream and onion Pringles into my home office. Huge. Absolutely elite live blogging snack. Less than 10 minutes until KO now.

Fabian Hürzeler sounded a little way of Hull in his pre-match press conference, citing the Tigers’ narrow 1-0 defeat to table-topping (and possible title rivals) Arsenal as a template for how today’s game might go.

“I think they do an impressive job,” Hürzeler said. “They had a brilliant start in the Premier League. They are very structured. Against Arsenal, I think Arsenal suffered. They [Arsenal] didn’t create a lot of big chances, and therefore we need to be patient because we also know that Hull are really good in transition.

“They also have individual quality in their team. Very well structured, very well organised, good in transition, good in set pieces, and I think it’s not an easy place to go to.”

Hull obviously beat Manchester United 2-0 in their opening home game and have drawn four successive matches at the MKM Stadium since, so that proves Hürzeler’s point somewhat.

Well, maybe only City will lose this afternoon, Elisabeth Terland scored for United as I was typing.

Women’s Super League: Both Manchester clubs are in serious danger of suffering shock defeats in the early WSL games this afternoon. The two matches are approaching their denouement, so catch the latest with Emillia Hawkins on our clockwatch blog.

My personal two-pennies-worth is that Brighton will probably fall away from the title race at some stage after Christmas. Their fixture list in the short term is fairly inviting, so I see their lofty position being sustained for a little while.

But realistically, a top five finish and Champions League qualification should be their primary objective. That’s really not impossible when you consider the struggles of Manchester United and Chelsea, and the possible fate of Manchester City if and when a verdict/punishment arrives re their 115s charges.

The fact Fabian Hürzeler could achieve that just after his 34th birthday would be an astonishing feat in itself.

A reminder you can follow The Guardian’s live Premier League Golden Boot tracker here:…

Brand beaten by Casasola for second day in a row in X20 Beringen thriller

24 hours after her first win of the season at HG Cross Lokeren, at which Lucinda Brand succumbed to Sara Casasola's superior form, the Italian national champion triumphed again on hilly Beringen course, round 3 of the X2O Badkamers Trofee.

In Beringen, Casasola picked up where she left off on Saturday, leaving Brand and everyone else behind in the opening laps. This time, though, the world champion stayed within 10 seconds of the Italian and after a flying fourth lap (of six), Brand had joined the front of the race. However, Casasola stayed glued to her rival's wheel until late in the fifth and penultimate lap when Brand went flying over her handlebars on the descent, reportedly injuring a rib in the fall. The Italian then almost doubled her advantage in the final lap to take another terrific victory and prove her stellar form just a week out from the start of the UCI World Cup.

The battle for third was the closest of the race, with Aniek van Alphen ultimately beating Fem van Empel to the final step of the podium.

item.title: Frick delivers on 'heavy metal football' promise
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Frick delivers on 'heavy metal football' promise

If "heavy metal football" is what Aberdeen did, indeed, serve up at Kilmarnock on Saturday, Dons supporters will be eager to see more of this type of concert.

New head coach Mario Frick used the phrase in the build-up to his first game in charge and his team did not disappoint.

The 4-2 Rugby Park victory was bombastic, chaotic and end-to-end - just one of six goal-laden Scottish Premiership games on Saturday.

The four Aberdeen strikes - two from Kevin Nisbet and one each from Brad Lyons and Findlay Marshall - showed Aberdeen's attackers at their best with fine finishing.

In the work in progress column, though, is defending, with the visitors lapsing badly for Killie goals scored by Greg Kiltie and Tyreece John-Jules.

All in all, it was an ideal start for former Luzern boss Frick.

'Just the beginning', says new head coach

Frick was not a complete unknown to Scottish football when he was appointed during the international break - but the reference point was somewhat obscure.

Playing for Liechtenstein at Hampden in 2010, Frick gave the visitors a shock second-half lead.

The end of that game was reminiscent of the kind of heavy metal the head coach was talking about pre-match as Stephen McManus headed Scotland's winner after Kenny Miller's leveller.

Speaking after his Premiership bow, the former Luzern boss described himself as "very happy, very proud" of his new team.

"With only three training session, you can see so many attacking patterns in that first half, which was amazing," he told BBC Scotland.

"We struggled the first few minutes with some players that hadn't played in a long long time and the 1-0 lead helped. First half was very good, the second half, complicated, because Kilmarnock played very well. We were very lucky, but at the end, I think it is a deserved victory and we are very happy."

When asked if he was happy with the players trying to show his style, Frick replied: "Yes, for sure, after two training sessions, I saw a lot of it in the first half.

"It is a good start for us, but it is just the beginning."

Former Scotland midfielder Derek Ferguson took in the match at Rugby Park and was impressed with the visitors.

"As an attacking force, I thought they were good to watch," the former Rangers player said.

"They've got a big game on Tuesday night, against Rangers, so Rangers will need to be at their best, on their toes if they're going to get a result.

"It was the perfect result, obviously, for the manager coming in.

"There was more energy, more legs, more running power. They were winning a lot of the duels.

"It's something to build on, but they've got to work on that defence. They've got to be more solid if they're going to go forward."

Next up Ibrox and a season's third meeting with Rangers.

The two previous encounters, in the Premiership and League Cup semi-final, finished 1-0 to the Ibrox side, with the winning goal coming in the second half both times.

Meetings of Aberdeen and Rangers are typically just as fraught as the Rugby Park game on Saturday.

So, more heavy metal? It probably won't be smooth jazz.

'Recovery evident' - Aberdeen fan views

We asked for your views following Aberdeen's 4-2 win over Kilmarnock.

Allan: One simple question. Why was [Ante] Palaversa nowhere to be seen under Stephen Robinson? I think the fans are due an explanation as to why both he and [Nicky] Devlin fell so far down the pecking order.

Brian: Much, much better is probably an understatement. Great entertainment and a big threat going forward and,as long as we score one more (at least) than the opposition then I will be happy. It is very noticeable that Jack Milne is much more steady when Nicky Devlin is playing. I am looking forward to the rest of this campaign.

Mike: Green shoots of recovery evident. Working as a unit from back to front has been a rarity at Aberdeen. If this is only after three training sessions, I am drooling at the mouth for what's to come. Stiff test on Tuesday, but the confidence must be there so nothing to fear.

Fred: Very positive start under the new manager. Good to see some direct attacking play but still a problem defending. An acid test coming against Rangers.

Get in touch

Send us your views on Aberdeen

item.title: England will not get carried away by beating All Blacks
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

England will not get carried away by beating All Blacks

In his latest BBC Sport column, England World Cup winner Matt Dawson reflects on Steve Borthwick's side's record win over New Zealand and previews the final round of Nations Championship fixtures.

If England had produced that performance two years ago against New Zealand, there would have been a lap of honour and wild celebrations.

Saturday felt like business. Job done, move on. And that is how it should be.

It was a record victory for a northern hemisphere side against the All Blacks, yet at full-time you would hardly have known it.

Even the post-match messaging from their leaders - Maro Itoje, Ellis Genge and Steve Borthwick - was that this performance had always been in them and that nobody was surprised.

However, they will want to back it up.

A tired but hurting New Zealand side will arrive at Allianz Stadium next Saturday looking for revenge.

England beat the All Blacks in back-to-back Tests in 2002 and 2003. Matching that achievement on Saturday was a significant statement.

Three consecutive wins over New Zealand, followed by a third-place finish, would leave England in a strong position heading into 2027, when the Rugby World Cup takes place in Australia.

Lose, though, and it will be a waste of some great momentum.

We have had many a false dawn with Borthwick's England, but something feels different this time.

For me, that comes down to the players taking responsibility.

Many of us ex-pros called for it during the Six Nations, and finally we are seeing the players take the lead on the style of rugby they want to play.

It is an exciting, free-flowing brand of attacking rugby that mirrors what they are used to playing in the Prem.

England's backs can compete with the very best and they tore through New Zealand on multiple occasions.

Credit also has to go to Borthwick for allowing the players to take control. That, in itself, shows how he is learning and evolving as a head coach.

Once players start getting 40, 50, 60 or 70 caps, they know more about certain aspects of the game than the coach because they are the ones out there experiencing it.

If the environment does not allow players to turn around and say 'this isn't going to work', then it is never going to work.

The reports before the Australia game suggested honest conversations took place, with the players wanting a greater say in how the team operates.

The Six Nations was probably a big turning point. The change in mood and the feel-good factor are clear in the way England are carrying themselves.

They now feel in control and, crucially, have a genuine sense of ownership in shaping the team and how it plays.

'An enormous statement about English rugby'

Lewis Moody, a former team-mate of mine, joining the team to face the New Zealand haka was an enormous statement about English rugby.

Whether you are playing in 2026 or 1926, this is England rugby. We are together.

It was a united and extraordinary moment, one that will stay with me until the day I die. There was a clear bond as Lewis embraced every England player before leaving the pitch.

That was a huge driver for England. They were able to show their emotional vulnerability before quickly switching into game mode.

A record victory over New Zealand was so fitting for the occasion, but I am not getting overly carried away by the big scoreline.

The southern hemisphere teams are coming towards the end of a brutally long season. They have done a lot of travelling and played considerably more international rugby.

New Zealand and South Africa, in particular, had the added emotion of four summer Tests against each other in the 'Rugby's Greatest Rivalry' series.

The Springboks also looked tired and strangely out of sorts in their defeat by Ireland.

At the beginning of the tournament, we were probably looking at it thinking it was a shame that the two top teams in the world were going to be on the same side of the draw.

Now, they have both lost back-to-back games, with injuries also playing a part.

England should not get carried away, by any stretch. It will be incredibly difficult for New Zealand to pick themselves up after that defeat.

The flight is waiting to take them home, they need some rest and will want to start thinking about next year's World Cup.

England, by contrast, will be chomping at the bit. They have momentum, and everybody is itching to get the white shirt on and run out at Allianz Stadium.

Saturday will provide another really good test of how England deal with being favourites. I expect changes to be made, but I still expect England to win.

After some difficult moments during this World Cup cycle, we are now seeing proper depth start to come through.

I can name at least two quality options in every position.

Fresher France my favourites

France will probably go into the final as favourites against South Africa.

Closing out back-to-back Six Nations titles and last week's victory over the world champions has given them the confidence to believe they can secure further silverware.

The Nations Championship has been a big success in replicating tournament rugby and, crucially, teaching teams how to win tight games.

Never write off the Springboks, but France are flying high after their performances against Argentina and South Africa.

Rassie Erasmus' side have lost back-to-back games, ending any perceived sense of invincibility. However, they only needed a point to reach the final and got that in Dublin.

Now it is winner takes all, and the world champions - with back-to-back Rugby World Cups and Rugby Championships behind them - should be in their element.

Fabien Galthie has rotated his squad tremendously well, and France will have more energy heading into next Sunday's final.

Those two points gained away to New Zealand with a second-string team in July ultimately proved decisive in the final standings.…

Source: BBC Sport | Published: 2026-11-22 12:45 UTC

item.title: Watford seek sixth manager in 18 months after sacking Dionisi
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Watford sack boss Dionisi after 18 games

Watford are looking for their sixth manager in 18 months after they sacked head coach Alessio Dionisi following 18 games in charge.

The 46-year-old Italian was appointed in June after the departure of Ed Still, who himself lasted only three months at Vicarage Road.

Still, Javi Gracia and Paulo Pezzolano were all also given full-time contracts after Tom Cleverley left in May 2025.

Dionisi was Watford's 12th head coach, not including interim bosses, since the end of the 2020-21 season, and leaves the Hornets searching for a 25th since the Pozzo family took over the club in 2012.

The club have had 57 permanent managers in their 145-year history.

The decision to replace him comes after Saturday's crushing 4-0 defeat by Sheffield United at Bramall Lane.

Dionisi's dismissal caps an underwhelming start to the season, with the Hornets having won just four league games to leave them 21st in the table.

"We thank Alessio and his staff for his professionalism and their efforts," sporting director Luke Dowling told the club website., external

"As I'm sure the supporters have seen, Alessio is a really good guy and we wish him the best for the future.

"The process has started for a replacement and we hope to be in a position to announce that shortly."

Dionisi was sacked by Serie B club Empoli in March after only five months in charge following a run of five wins in 22 matches.

His spell in charge of the Hornets was his first outside his homeland and started promisingly when his youthful side beat Southampton in their opening league game.

But they won only two of their next 12 in all competitions, and despite deservedly beating Charlton on 17 October, reverses at Wolves and Norwich followed, before four points from Dionisi's final three games in charge of the Hertfordshire side and his dismissal means further upheaval for the Hornets.

Since sacking Cleverley at the end of the 2024-25 campaign, the club has now been through four permanent head coaches, as well as interim boss Charlie Daniels' two-game spell in charge.

Of those four, only Gracia, in his second spell at Vicarage Road, took charge of more than 20 games.

On the morning of their final-day drubbing by Coventry last season, chief executive Scott Duxbury wrote a statement on the club website saying Watford had made mistakes, labelling their end to the campaign "unacceptable" and "truly disappointing in the extreme".

Source: BBC Sport | Published: 2026-11-22 12:00 UTC

item.title: Why I love Madrid in winter: ‘Locals get into the spirit by doing their shopping in novelty hats’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: engaging narrative, cultural insight, and vivid description

Live in Madrid long enough and you hear the same weather-related proverbs again and again. One old saying goes that the seasons in the Spanish capital break down to “nine months of winter and three months of hell”. And if the city never quite freezes over in the coldest months – except for the blizzard of the century that came with Storm Filomena in 2021 – it is also said that the subtle, evil wind coming in from the mountains could kill a person without snuffing a candle.

Personally, I prefer it here at this time of year, though if you’re looking to escape the crowds you might be disappointed. Madrid has only got busier in the 11 years I’ve lived here, and Christmas feels more crowded than midsummer on the central streets around Puerta del Sol. All the main public squares get their own giant Christmas trees, while Plaza de España and Plaza Colón install ice rinks too, and a festive market fills the cobbled core of Plaza Mayor with painted wooden huts. Many local people get into the spirit by doing their shopping in novelty hats, and one of my seasonal highlights is spotting couples or whole families engaged in furious arguments while wearing reindeer antlers or giant turkeys on their heads.

It’s nice to see the Christmas lights up close, especially where they’re themed and art-directed by guest designers across the facade of the Four Seasons hotel and the flagship store of Spanish leatherware brand Loewe. But it’s often better to get a little distance, and El Cielo de Montera is my favourite of the city’s competing roof terraces. With the Gran Vía below and the glowing blue art deco clock of the Telefónica building above, winter in Madrid looks a little like 1930s Manhattan from this angle.

Civic life continues outdoors, and there’s great sensory pleasure to dining in the cold air under lap blankets and patio heaters, though I also love the huddled feel of retreating deep inside a vintage tavern. Mulled wine isn’t a big thing in Spain but they do a good one at Vinícola Mentridana, an atmospheric bodega, and if you think of sherry as a winter drink, at the beautifully basic La Venencia it’s the only thing that has been served since 1922. There are five varieties poured straight from the casks.

For something truly warming, cocido madrileño is this region’s signature stew of chickpeas, noodles, cabbage and pork meats, rationed out in three courses, or vuelcos, of such absurd abundance at Malacatín that fourth-generation owner Jose Rodríguez says only three diners have ever completed the full meal in the century-plus his family has run the place.

Most winters, the only snow to be seen is in paintings such as Goya’s La Nevada at the Prado, which is best enjoyed in the relative quiet of lunchtimes during mid-November or mid-January, when the city empties a bit. Some flakes will likely fall across the Sierra de Guadarrama though, where King Felipe II built El Escorial circa 1580. Above that palace and monastery, forest trails lead to mountain lookouts. Seen from there, a distance of about 30 miles (50km), faraway Madrid becomes a winter mirage – sharp and glinting under crystal-blue skies, a futuristic vision seen from a now-remote past.

Where to stay

7 Islas (doubles from €113) in the city centre has light, airy rooms and a designer lobby with an art gallery and craft cocktail bar.

Source: The Guardian Travel | Published: 2026-11-22 07:00 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Opinion: If AI Does the Junior Work, How Will Young People Become Experienced?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: Thought-provoking and well-structured, with a focus on the impact of AI on professional development.

If AI Does the Junior Work, How Will Young People Become Experienced?

Poluhina: Artificial intelligence is replacing the work that beginners do, limiting opportunities for graduates to develop judgment and experience.

Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter

I serve on a local school board and have spent my career in finance and strategy. Those are very different parts of my life, but lately they have led me to the same question: How do people develop judgment and experience if artificial intelligence starts doing more of the work through which beginners used to gain them?

Early in my career, I built financial models, checked numbers and prepared presentations. More experienced colleagues reviewed what I’d done, sometimes sending me back to reconsider an assumption that looked perfectly reasonable on paper. With enough practice and feedback, I learned that a correct calculation can still lead to a poor decision.

That work was producing two things at once: an output and a more experienced person. The company received something useful, and I gradually became capable of handling more complicated problems.

AI may change the economics of that arrangement.

Junior employees contribute useful work while they learn, helping offset the cost of supervising them. If AI can produce an initial analysis more cheaply, a company may decide it no longer needs as many beginners. The savings are immediate, while developing experienced staff takes years. And even after investing in someone, the employer cannot be certain that person will stay.

A company could automate junior assignments now and hire experienced professionals when it needs them. That may be a reasonable decision for one business. But if enough companies make the same choice, where will those experienced workers come from?

There are early signs that entry-level hiring is changing. A 2026 study of U.S. software job postings found an almost 15% decline in junior vacancies relative to senior ones following the public arrival of generative AI in late 2022. A U.S. Census Bureau working paper reported weaker initial employment and earnings among graduates of college majors most exposed to AI. These include such jobs as junior software engineers, financial analysts, graphic designers and marketing associates. Neither study proves that AI caused these changes or measures employers’ investments in training.

AI may also help beginners learn faster, and some companies may find better ways to train people with it. We cannot assume, however, that every employer will continue to find it worthwhile to hire inexperienced workers.

The gap may begin in school

AI is also changing how students complete their work. A polished assignment may tell us little about how much a student understands or could reproduce independently. Teachers already work to assess that understanding. As schools decide how AI belongs in education, preserving opportunities for students to practice and demonstrate what they know independently should remain a priority.

In a 2025 randomized study of university students, those assigned to study with ChatGPT scored 57.5% on a surprise test 45 days later, compared with 68.5% among students studying without AI. The study was small and measured knowledge retention rather than critical thinking. It does not establish what is happening across K–12 classrooms, and AI used differently may improve learning.

Still, I worry about students who become accustomed to relying on AI to complete their assignments and then enter workplaces where the routine tasks that once helped beginners learn have been automated. Employers may expect them to exercise judgment sooner, while offering fewer opportunities to develop it through practice and feedback.

Districts already consult employers about changing skill requirements. Those conversations are valuable, although today’s vacancies and lists of required skills can only tell us so much about the work students will encounter several years from now.

Conversations with people working in education and workforce development have made me more aware of how difficult that planning can be. Labor-market information often lags behind changes in actual jobs, while educational pathways take years to complete.

An occupation may remain in demand even as employers change what they expect from someone applying for the first position.

I would like schools and colleges to look further ahead when reviewing career pathways with employers. Alongside the usual discussion of skills and credentials, we should ask how entry-level work is likely to change and where new employees will gain the experience needed to take on greater responsibility.

There are already internships, apprenticeships and other opportunities to learn through work. Are they giving students meaningful practice and supervision? Will enough opportunities be available as traditional junior roles change? We may also need to reconsider how the costs of developing beginners are shared. Schools on their own cannot replace every disappearing step in a professional career.

I worry especially about young people without professional connections. A student whose family knows people in an industry may find introductions, advice or informal opportunities to learn. Someone without those connections depends much more on accessible programs and employers willing to provide a first chance.

If those opportunities become scarcer, the differences could grow. Students who already face barriers to entering professional careers may find it even harder to gain the experience employers expect.

From my school-board perspective, I would rather see us examine these questions while we still have time to adjust how we prepare students. We may continue to see strong demand for experienced professionals while the opportunities that once helped beginners develop into them become harder to find.…

Source: The 74 | Published: 2026-11-22 11:30 UTC | Difficulty: 62/100

Original link: https://www.the74million.org/article/if-ai-does-the-junior-work-how-will-young-people-become-experienced/

item.title: Moms Feared What the Midterms Would Mean for Their Disabled Daughters. Then Came Some Hope.
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engaging narrative with clear reporting on healthcare policy and its impact on individuals.

Moms Feared What the Midterms Would Mean for Their Disabled Daughters. Then Came Some Hope.

Democrats have pledged to make reversing healthcare cuts a top priority. Caregivers know relief won’t come quickly — or easily.

Yasmina Halim approached this year’s midterms with “a sense of dread.” On election night, the 44-year-old went to bed early after Republicans won the major statewide races in Florida, where she lives with her family. Her 13-year-old daughter, Lily, is dying from a neurodegenerative condition called juvenile Tay-Sachs disease, and Halim works full-time caring for her. That sense of dread stemmed from looming cuts to Medicaid, as well as attacks on the right to inclusion for people with disabilities like her daughter.

But when she woke up on Wednesday morning, things had shifted.

Across the nation, Democrats triumphed at the polls, crucially winning majorities in both chambers of Congress. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a front-runner to become speaker in January, said rolling back major cuts to healthcare social safety net programs would be a top priority. For Halim and many family caregivers and disabled people, these Democratic gains and the promise of a legislative agenda that prioritizes trying to undo these cuts are a source of relief.

President Donald Trump’s signature legislative policy achievement, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, raised the cost of buying health insurance for individuals while instituting nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts that will take full effect in 2027, driving major reductions over the next decade. Medicaid is the primary funder for the home care services that people rely on to receive assistance in dressing, using the bathroom, eating and more. That funding is statutorily optional, which means when state legislatures need to navigate cuts, they’re often the first on the chopping block.

“Until you’re in the thick of it, you really truly don’t realize how much politics is affecting your everyday life,” said Halim, who described the midterm results as giving “us a little hope.”

Halim, who describes herself as “purple,” rather than a dyed-in-the-wool Democrat, said her vote is often determined by policies, and specifically disability policy, which became a necessity after her daughter became ill.

She hopes that a Democratic majority in Congress will successfully push back against the healthcare cuts and changes that have made her life and her daughter’s life more difficult. She also hopes the top-of-the-ticket losses that Republicans sustained in other states will motivate party leaders in Florida to rethink their priorities.

“I hope that the government of Florida realizes just how important it is to protect our special needs children, especially our medically frail and disabled children, and not eliminate our home-based services,” Halim said.

She is nervous about the Medicaid work requirements that will kick in January 1 and apply to parents caring for disabled children over the age of 13. There is an exemption for “medical frailty,” but what, precisely, that means is still up in the air after a federal judge struck down the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ proposed definition.

Halim will need to prove that she is working, although she isn’t sure how the process will function yet in Florida. She works full-time caring for her daughter through a state program that allows family caregivers to take paid caregiving roles that would otherwise go to home health aides and even skilled nurses. The paid hours she does through the program count toward the requirement.

For Halim, the greater administrative requirements will be just one more burden parents of ill and disabled children like her have to face.

“Medically frail and special needs parents are already stressed to the max,” Halim said. “We are between appointments, respiratory therapies, nursing, keeping jobs, keeping roofs over our heads.”

Across the country, Stephanie Walters, 56, feels a similar mix of hope and anxiety about the near future, post-election. She and her daughter, Shelby, 30, live in Meridian, Idaho.

The 19th spoke with them in March about the impact of the proposed dissolution of home care services in their state. Shelby needs significant assistance with her everyday life. The program still exists, but $22 million in cuts did eventually pass.

Walters recently struggled to organize Shelby’s redetermination — that is, the process Medicaid recipients must go through every year to demonstrate that they still have a qualifying disability, whether or not that disability is permanent. Shelby has cerebral palsy and intellectual disability, conditions people are born with, and that remain more or less unchanged over the course of a person’s lifetime. Nonetheless, she and Shelby still need to prove, every year, that Shelby is still disabled.

This year, the redetermination was delayed by a few months due to a series of errors. This means that some of Shelby’s care wasn’t funded for a few months. Walters also had to fight for Shelby to receive services she had been approved for and had received in previous years. She couldn’t go to an extension of her day program she’d attended for years. Walters isn’t sure if it was because of cuts or simply bad luck.

“There’s a lot of a lot of things that aren’t going the way they’re supposed to be going at Idaho Medicaid,” Walters said.

Growing up, Walters’ father was Republican. She voted for Republican candidates for most of her life. But that changed as she got older.

“I think the last Republican I voted for was [John] McCain,” Walters said. Her daughter’s disability was not a major force in her shift. Until recently, she felt that those services vital to her care were protected. Instead, she shifted based on her experience as a nurse and her interest in public health.…

Source: The 74 | Published: 2026-11-22 11:30 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

Original link: https://www.the74million.org/article/moms-feared-what-the-midterms-would-mean-for-their-disabled-daughters-then-came-some-hope/

item.title: Trump’s immigration crackdown drives international students away from US universities
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed and informative, though slightly more technical in nature.

Until 2025, students from Brazil, Nigeria, Thailand, Turkey, Turkmenistan and Zambia eagerly accepted a full scholarship to attend Indiana University in Bloomington, a town in the midwestern United States where fans are passionate about the Hoosiers – the school’s basketball and football teams.

The town also hosts the Little 500, a famous bicycle race that can attract more than 25,000 people. And most importantly for prospective students, the school has well-regarded academic programs.

“There was a general sense that this was the beginning of a great new phase in people’s lives,” said Christoph Irmscher, who for 13 years directed the Wells Scholars Program, which covers the full costs of attendance, including living expenses.

But things changed in January 2025, when Donald Trump started his second term and launched a shocking immigration crackdown.

That year, Irmscher offered the award to a Black man from South Africa and a woman from Central America. Both declined.

“People are cautious now, and it’s more like weighing the benefits versus the disadvantages” and whether to take a risk, said Irmscher, who grew up in Germany and came to the United States in 1993 on a scholarship through the Fulbright Program, a federal initiative.

That hesitation appears to be increasingly common among international students, and the number who enroll at American schools has plummeted in the last two years.

Their absence on campuses takes money away from colleges, causes a brain drain and robs American students of the chance to meet their counterparts from around the world. It also ripples out into the wider economy – especially in the many small college towns dotted across the US.

In fall 2026, there was a 15% decrease in foreign students studying for the first time at a US college or university as compared to last year, according to the Institute of International Education. That follows an 18% dip in fall 2025.

“To think that the system could go on functioning politically, socially, economically without those students is to misunderstand what US higher education has always been, for as long as it’s been the best in the world,” said Veena Dubal, general counsel for the American Association of University Professors.

To study in the United States, a foreign student must get accepted by a college or university and get the federal government to approve a visa, like an F-1 for academic programs or an M-1 for vocational or non-academic programs.

During the 2023 to 2024 school year, more than 1.1 million international students came to the United States, a record high, according to the International Education Institute.

But interest in coming to the United States has waned, college leaders say, since Trump retook office in January 2025 and deployed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents across the country to conduct raids and arrest and deport alleged undocumented immigrants.

Images of masked officers roaming US cities spread across the globe and unsettled people in America and abroad.

Indiana University, Bloomington saw its international student enrollment decrease 15%, from 4,428 in fall 2025 to 3,768 this year, according to university data.

In addition to the federal actions, the Republican-led state also passed legislation this year requiring schools to conduct background checks on students from China, Iran, North Korea and Russia before allowing them to attend. Irmscher, who stepped down from the Wells position last summer, described the requirement as “totally unnecessary” because the federal government already conducts such checks on visa applicants.

“In the culture of social media and TikTok, these clips of ICE agents brutalizing people on the street have an enormous ripple effect,” Irmscher, an English professor, said. “If you look different, if you feel that you are different, I’m sure that is something that affects your decision.”

At Cleveland State University, international enrollment dropped 46%, from 1,542 in fall 2025 to 828 this fall.

That was largely due to potential students having trouble obtaining visas, according to provost Nigamanth Sridhar.

In May 2025, the Trump administration ordered US embassies to stop scheduling visa interviews for foreign students as it prepared to implement social media screening for applicants.

“We have people who want to go to Harvard and other schools; they can’t get in because we have foreign students there,” Trump said at the time.

In January 2026, the state department announced it had revoked 8,000 student visas. In October, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) also proposed a rule that would require schools to pay a $70,000 fee for each international student who participates in a training program that allows students to take jobs related to their major during or after their time in school.

That enrollment drop cost Cleveland State between $2m and $4m, Sridhar estimated. International students typically pay a higher tuition than domestic students.

There are also, of course, less tangible ways foreign students affect US colleges, including in social life.

Sridhar, a former computer science professor who came to the United States from India in 1999 to attend graduate school at Ohio State University, said that international students bring “a diverse group of viewpoints to campus in various kinds of conversations, whether they are in the classroom or outside the classroom”, which creates a “richness and intellectual diversity”.

After a 2025 earthquake in Myanmar killed thousands and left millions needing humanitarian assistance, a student from the country studying at Indiana University organized a fundraiser with Burmese food where she spoke about the country.

“It was not just a culturally enriching event. It was also an exercise in putting yourself into the shoes of somebody else in ways that are normally not accessible to students in landlocked America,” Irmscher said.…

Source: The Guardian Education | Published: 2026-11-22 13:00 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/education/2026/nov/22/trump-immigration-crackdown-international-students

item.title: Revealed: profiles of UK experts on gambling harm being hijacked to push illegal online casinos
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Interesting topic but the article is more about the unethical practices of online casinos rather than education.

Prof Heather Wardle has dedicated 20 years to researching the harm caused by gambling.

“I would never review these things and promote them to people,” she said. “It’s completely out of kilter with the research I’ve conducted across my entire career.”

Wardle is far from alone in being targeted like this, evidence reviewed by the Guardian suggests.

At least six prominent academics appear to have had their identities misappropriated by almost 30 casino websites. Most appear to be “affiliates”, businesses that earn commission by directing online traffic towards gambling firms. Several of the websites promoted unlicensed casinos that are not on GamStop, a UK scheme to help people suffering from problem gambling shut themselves out of betting sites.

Nor is it just academics whose public profile appears to have been misused in this way. Dozens of websites with no previous links to betting appear to have been bought up on the cheap and redesigned, capitalising on their existing search engine recognition.

The result is that people visiting what they think is a site dedicated to politics, tourism or even HIV research, can end up being lured in by offshore casinos.

The findings highlight not just the unscrupulous tactics used by the multibillion-pound illicit market but also the enormous challenge facing the UK authorities.

‘It’s completely egregious’

One site, called 666 Casino, features a photo of a smiling Wardle, described as “the woman behind the reviews”.

“Every trustworthy casino review needs someone who’s actually done the legwork, and that’s precisely the role Heather Wardle has carved out for herself in the UK gambling content space,” it reads.

In a lengthy “biography”, the page claims she began as a casual online gambler but later began analysing and rating the best casinos, including the quality of their bonuses and the speed of cash withdrawals.

“I was saddened but I wasn’t surprised,” said Wardle. “Some quarters of the gambling industry will go far to undermine academics who are doing work in the public interest.”

Wardle is one of at least six prominent academics whose reputations, built on their research into how gambling can exploit and harm people, have been co-opted in this way. All told the Guardian they had not consented and were alarmed by the use of their names and images.

“It’s a deliberate misuse of our profiles to mislead consumers into believing that these products, which are objectively the most harmful, are safe,” said Wardle.

The social scientist has been forced to write to the organisations that help fund her work, many of whom do on strict conditions governing any engagement she might have with the gambling sector, assuring them that her name is being used without consent.

Academics at the universities of Swansea, Loughborough and Bristol have also been targeted. Some of the wording on the sites appeared to have been generated using AI, the academics said.

“It takes years to build up an academic reputation, and only a few lines of this AI slop to damage it,” said Prof Gerda Reith, another victim of identity misuses, who also works at the University of Glasgow.

The aim of hijacking these academics’ profile, it appears, is to convince people to part with their money by clicking on links to casinos.

Of the casinos the Guardian viewed, none had a licence to operate in the UK and appear, therefore, to be doing so illegally.

“It’s completely egregious,” said Wardle.

Hall of mirrors

In practice, a lack of transparency about who owns and operates websites means that tracking down who is behind this phenomenon can be dizzying.

Of 28 websites purloining the names of British academics, including 666 Casino, most appeared to be registered in Ukraine.

A contact page for 666 Casino claims it is owned by a Malta-based business with a licence from the UK Gambling Commission. This appears to be untrue.

The site gives a London address but appears to have no connection to any companies registered there. A link to Google Maps shows an address in Sydney, Australia.

Casino games advertised on the site, such as Wild Lady Cash and Lucky 100 Bells, redirect players to a website called Elite Spin, whose Trustpilot page states that the site is based in Canada. Elsewhere on the internet, casino review pages claim Elite Spin is licensed in Costa Rica.

When the Guardian tried to contact 666 Casino via an email address provided on its website, the email bounced back.

This international hall of mirrors is typical of illicit casino operations, including some previously exposed by the Guardian.

It is not just academic reputations that appear to have been co-opted.

Jonathan Harbourne, the founder of the LGBT History Project, a volunteer-run national heritage archive, became suspicious after one of the community-led archive’s former web addresses was taken over.

He has since identified about 40 websites that appear, like the academics, to have been misused for the benefit of rogue casinos.

They include a hospital trust, an Italian restaurant in Croydon and the home of the Labour party in the now defunct London constituency of Hornsey and Wood Green.

They also include Sigma Research, part of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine dedicated to researching HIV and sexual health.

Harbourne said: “Once an address has belonged to a hospital, a charity or a council, it should not be possible to buy it and fill it with casino adverts aimed at people who have asked to be excluded from gambling.”

Most of the sites were auctioned by a small company called DomainLore, which trades in expired UK domains.…

Source: The Guardian Education | Published: 2026-11-22 08:00 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026/nov/22/profiles-uk-experts-on-gambling-harm-hijacked-to-promote-online-casinos

item.title: Tories would scrap Burnham's deal with EU, deputy leader says
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Clear reporting on a significant political development with concrete details and useful vocabulary.

Tories would scrap Burnham's deal with EU, deputy leader says

Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart has said his party would scrap the deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday, if the Tories win the next general election.

The agreement signed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham covers a youth travel scheme, emissions trading and British food exports.

The government has argued scrapping most checks on British food exports will cut costs for businesses and could bring down prices for shoppers.

Burghart told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme the deal was "a dog's dinner", which would not lead to lower prices in the shops and would mean the UK "gives up our ability to set our own rules".

Under the agreement, the UK will also have to follow some EU regulations.

Burghart acknowledged the deal would reduce some trade "friction" but he said it would put a "massive additional burden on the 90% of farmers that don't do any trade with the EU".

Pressed over whether the Conservatives were committed to scrapping the deal if the party wins the next general election, Burghart said: "I don't think that there will be positive outcomes, and yes, we would scrap it."

He added: "I also don't think it is a good idea for a country like Britain to hand over control of its rules to another power and have no say over how those rules are created right into the future."

Food retailers have welcomed the deal, saying it will cut costs, reduce bureaucracy and remove barriers to trade.

However, they have not committed to cutting prices as a direct result of the changes.

The British Retail Consortium has said it does not expect prices on supermarket shelves to fall in response to the deal.

It has said upward pressures on prices remain and will not be alleviated by the agreement.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband insisted the deal "reduces pressure on trading costs", adding: "They're the things that go into prices."

"It will reduce the costs that the retailers face, all of that Brexit red tape, millions of forms that they were having to fill in, frankly pointlessly, as a result of the bad deal that we had," he told the BBC.

Challenged that the UK was also giving up some powers to set regulations itself, Miliband argued businesses were already "rule takers" from Brussels if they wanted to sell into the European market.

"So they have to abide by the rules of the European Union. But at the same time, because we are not integrated into that market for food and agricultural products, they have to fill in a whole bunch of forms... to confirm that they're observing the right standards, which is frankly crackers," he said.

Under the deal, he said the UK would "be able to shape decisions" for the first time.

Reform UK has also criticised the UK-EU deal.

Deputy leader Richard Tice told Sky News that while "a few exporting food businesses may benefit", companies that do not export to the EU will still have to align with EU rules.

"Divergence is now our strength. We need to be scrapping net zero so we can bring down energy bills, whereas the EU is still ideologically obsessed with it," he said

"The extra burdens of EU regulations that will be forced through dynamic alignment across all UK businesses is way more than that small net benefit."

Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week, with the food exports deal in force from 2028.

Elsewhere in the agreement, a new "youth experience scheme" will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31-year-olds to work, study or travel in the EU for up to three years.

The same number of young people from the EU will also be allowed into the UK.

The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.

A proposal from the bloc to lower the level of university tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed and talks on this aspect will continue. Miliband has said Friday's deal is not dependent on an agreement on tuition fees.

The Conservatives have also criticised the youth experience scheme, saying people from the EU will be competing with young Britons struggling to get jobs.

The Liberal Democrats have welcomed the scheme as "a big step forward" but have said "it's nowhere near enough".

The party has called for the UK to rejoin the EU single market and customs union to help cut the cost of living and grow the economy.

item.title: Closer EU ties will give UK say on Brussels decisions, says Ed Miliband
item.description:

Why it is here: Explains the potential benefits of closer EU ties with clear prose and useful context.

Closer links with the EU will mean the UK having a say on decisions made by Brussels, Ed Miliband has argued as ministers faced pressure to move further after Friday’s landmark deal with the EU.

Emily Thornberry, the Labour MP who chairs the Commons foreign affairs committee, said Burnham should push for membership.

“The problem with being outside the bloc is that we end up in a permanent state of negotiation, because we always have to play catchup, rather than having a seat at the table,” she wrote in an article for the Sunday Mirror. “That’s why I think we should simply be back in the European Union.”

Speaking to BBC One’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg show, Miliband refused to say whether he now supported discussions on potentially rejoining, but said the deal reached at Friday’s summit – on food and drink, emissions trading and a mutual youth mobility scheme – showed the benefits of closer links, including UK input to EU regulations that were being followed anyway.

“At the moment, what the situation is is that we are essentially rule takers,” the foreign secretary said. “Businesses are rule takers if they want to sell into the European market. So they have to abide by the rules of the European Union, but at the same time, because we are not integrated into that market for food and agricultural products, they have to fill in a whole bunch of forms.”

He said this was “the worst of all worlds” and it meant there was a clear case to integrate more closely into EU markets.

Another reason for even closer ties, he said, was the transformed geopolitical order since 2016, including Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the US’s distancing from Europe under Donald Trump.

He said: “I was not in favour of Brexit, as you know, but I accepted the result, and I think it was right to accept the result. [But] I think there’s a key point: the world has changed massively since 2016, and we can’t stand still.

“How can we say: ‘Well, this is all it is, the status quo is fine, even with the summit today. We’re not even going to look at the future of our relationship with the European Union.’ Of course, we’ve got to do that, and we’ve got to lay out the options.”

Speaking for the Conservatives on the Sunday morning broadcast round, Alex Burghart, Kemi Badenoch’s deputy, said Burnham should simply be concentrating on better defence ties with Europe, arguing that the public would not want to return to the EU.

Asked if the Conservatives would undo the deal made at Friday’s summit if they won power, Burghart said they would. He said: “Yes, we would scrap it. I don’t think that there will be good outcomes from it. And I also don’t think it is a good idea for a country like Britain to hand over control of its rules to another power and have no say over how those rules are created right into the future. This is a silly idea.”

Burnham faces some nervousness in his cabinet and the parliamentary Labour party more widely over talk of possibly rejoining, with some MPs wary about the bitter political fight this could set off.

But Thornberry in her article praised Burnham for having “finally ended the conspiracy of silence over Brexit”, saying polls indicated that a majority of the UK public now backed rejoining.
