item.title: Theresa May 'aghast' at Burnham's EU plans and says 'Brexit is done'
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth analysis of the former Prime Minister's perspective on EU plans with clear reporting.

Theresa May 'aghast' at Burnham's EU plans and says 'Brexit is done'

Former Prime Minister Theresa May has warned Andy Burnham he should "move on" from Brexit, telling the BBC she is "aghast" the prime minister could be considering rejoining the EU.

At the Brussels summit this week the PM said he wanted to "brainstorm" options for the future relationship between Britain and the trading bloc.

In an exclusive interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Baroness May, who spent three years negotiating an EU exit deal, said: "Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on."

May claimed Burnham "wants to pat people on the head" by suggesting: "Remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn't you. So have another go and come out with the right answer."

May, who was prime minister between 2016 and 2019 urged Burnham to "just get on with" today's challenges rather than re-opening the conversation around being in the European Union.

Before becoming PM she had campaigned to stay in the EU, but when in No 10 she presided over three years of tortuous negotiations.

The deal she concluded was rejected by MPs. She was forced to quit and was replaced by Boris Johnson in 2019.

Telling Burnham to "move on", she said: "What I saw was that the extent of those negotiations, the hours that have to be put in - it's across the whole of government.

"It's not just prime ministerial time, cabinet ministers' time, officials' time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations. Because you have to negotiate hard in order to make sure that you're getting out what you want.

"And that's one of the reasons why I look slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham is talking about, further negotiations of going into the EU. And also we, as a country, we voted for Brexit.

"When I was prime minister I was very clear, we should deliver on that vote. So I'm afraid my message to him really is, you know, people voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on."

Warning against another vote, May told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "I almost think this is what Andy Burnham is saying to the British people, sort of patting them on the head.

"He wants to pat them on their head and say, you know what, remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn't you? So have another go and come out with the right answer.

"Or what he thinks is the right answer. But as I say, let's just get on with making sure the UK is as strong economically, in security terms, and in terms of opportunities for people as it can be."

Speaking to the BBC back in 2023, she said the UK "would have been better off if MPs had backed her deal to leave the European Union".

Her deal had included the prospect of a vote on holding a second referendum, and a vote on a temporary customs union, as well as promises on workers' rights and environmental protection.

May claimed her plan was thwarted by "hardline" Brexit-supporting MPs and those who wanted to remain in the EU.

- 'Move on!'

On Saturday, Sir Tony Blair - another former prime minister - weighed in on the UK's future relationship with the EU.

Speaking to The Sunday Times, external, Sir Tony has said Britain should only rejoin the EU if it reforms - and allows more innovation on technology.

Sir Tony, a prominent opponent of leaving the EU, told the paper: "I do think Brexit was a real mistake."

But he added the debate was different now than it was in 2016.

Referencing the need for technology innovation, he said Europe could and "probably are" moving in the wrong direction.

It comes after Burnham struck a deal with the EU in Brussels on Friday, covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

The prime minister also said that over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at the options for their long-term relationship.

He has previously suggested potential options for the future could include rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.

However, Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK-EU relationship before the next general election, saying he will stick to Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.

Theresa May has said she feels “aghast” at Andy Burnham’s plan for potentially rejoining the EU, arguing in a rare interview that the prime minister should “accept Brexit and move on”.

Speaking to the BBC after Friday’s UK-EU summit, at which Burnham secured the biggest step towards renewed ties with Brussels since Brexit, May said that a further move towards membership, as talked about by the PM, would dominate the government’s time.

“What I saw was that the extent of those negotiations, the hours that had to be put in,” said May, who took over in No 10 from David Cameron shortly after the 2016 referendum and shaped the basics of the very hard departure deal that Boris Johnson eventually sealed.

“It’s across the whole of government. It’s not just prime ministerial time, [it’s] cabinet ministers’ time, officials’ time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations, because you have to negotiate hard in order to make sure that you’re getting out what you want.

“That’s one of the reasons why I looked slightly aghast at what Andy Burnham was talking about – further negotiations of going into the EU. As a country, we voted for Brexit.

“When I was prime minister, I was very clear: we should deliver on that vote. So I’m afraid my message to him really is: people voted for Brexit. Brexit is done. Just accept Brexit and move on.”

May said it was damaging for governments not to trust the results of referendums: “I almost think this is what Andy Burnham is saying to the British people … He wants to pat them on the head and say: ‘You know what? Remember that vote? Well, you got it wrong, didn’t you? So have another go and come out with the right answer’ – what he thinks is the right answer.”

May’s intervention is an unusual step from the former prime minister, who has typically reserved her public statements since leaving office for areas of cross-party consensus. On taking office, she opted to push for minimal residual ties with the EU as a way to maintain unity in the Conservatives. But she struggled with the Brussels negotiations amid dissent among her MPs, and was ousted in 2019.

Pressed on whether Brexit had been a success, May refused to say, arguing that with global shocks such as Covid and Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine, it was impossible to know.

Asked outright if she believed the UK was in a better or worse state as a result of the decision to leave the EU, she replied: “I don’t think Britain’s state today is about whether or not we left the European Union.”

The summit in Brussels on Friday saw the announcement of three deals, on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme which will allow 100,000 young Britons to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with reciprocal access for Europeans in the UK.

Burnham, who has condemned the May-Johnson departure deal for hampering growth and gumming up trade, has raised the possibility of even closer ties and that the UK could rejoin the EU in the future.

None of this would happen until after another election, with Burnham committed until then to the Brexit “red lines” of Labour’s 2024 manifesto, which rules out being part of the EU’s customs union or single market.

While the changes in the new deal will be presented to parliament as a bill next week, at the summit, Burnham slightly slowed down the pace of any further moves. He said he would “brainstorm” with the EU over future ties, with the timetable talked about in terms of months, while reiterating that he would not get ahead of public opinion.

The Conservatives have been pushing back against the deal made on Friday, briefing newspapers on Sunday that signing up to the emissions trading system would add costs to domestic energy bills because of EU carbon taxes.

Downing Street argues the deal will bring down energy and food costs, with Burnham saying on Friday it could add as much as 0.5% to GDP in the long term.

item.title: The looming UK winter may spawn a double headache for Andy Burnham | Richard Partington
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed look at the economic challenges facing the Prime Minister with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

Andy Burnham faces two, related problems: Britain faces deep regional disparities and it is entering the coldest months of the year with rising inflation.

Since entering Downing Street, raising “growth in every postcode” has been the prime minister’s rallying cry, as he bids to close the gaping chasm in living standards between the richest and poorest areas of the country. But as the war in the Middle East intensifies, the task of spreading prosperity far and wide has only become more difficult.

On Wednesday, the regulator Ofgem is expected to confirm a 26% increase in the energy price cap from January, pushing the annual bill to £2,166 for a typical household.

Rising petrol prices and diesel hitting a record high lifted the UK’s headline inflation rate to 3.6% in October, its highest level in a year. The Bank of England says inflation could hit 5% next year.

It is now half a decade since inflation first went above the 2% target set by the government. Consumer prices have galloped by almost a third over that same time. A return to the target is not expected until 2028 at the earliest.

So far, households have proven surprisingly resilient. Consumer confidence surveys bear this out. Retail sales in October were stronger than expected, even though some of this was driven by a rush to stockpile emergency supplies.

But there is a storm coming. Especially if the El Niño forecast is right and we have a very cold January.

As autumn gives way to winter, low-income households will be hardest hit as the mercury drops. Record numbers of families cannot afford the essentials. The places feeling the pinch most will also be the ones where Burnham has promised to turn things around.

Analysis by the Centre for Cities shows that after the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine, inflation rose most in towns and cities that entered the cost of living crisis in a precarious position. Small towns in the north of England, Midlands and Wales were most exposed. Households in Burnley, Blackburn and Blackpool faced an inflation rate nearly three percentage points higher than those in London, Reading and Cambridge.

Part of this is because the recent inflationary burst has been driven by the price of energy and food, hitting low-income families most because they spend proportionally more on essentials than the wealthiest. And that means some places are harder hit than others because despite the promises of successive governments, Britain’s regional income gaps have barely shifted in three decades.

According to research from the Resolution Foundation, the places that were performing worst in the late 1990s are still at the bottom of the living standards league table a generation later. Disposable incomes in Kensington and Chelsea, at £60,584, remain four-and-a-half times higher than in Leicester, at £13,398.

But in response to the cost of living squeeze, Burnham’s government has, perhaps surprisingly, taken a remarkably blunt approach.

At the autumn budget, the “breathing space” measures announced by John Healey prioritised an across-the-board freeze in fuel duty and £100 energy rebate for every household in council tax bands A to D. The removal of standing charges from gas bills that was also announced will not come into effect until the end of 2027.

The poorest households will benefit from the £150 warm homes discount, on top of a universal VAT cut to electricity bills. But charities warn that overall the government’s limited ambition and relatively poor targeting will fail to meet the moment.

Despite the gloom, there are caveats. After more than three decades of entrenched regional inequality, it would be unreasonable to expect Burnham to turn things around overnight. The legacy of austerity and Britain’s tight fiscal position make his task harder. After years of politicians pursuing a quick fix – often with disastrous consequences – his long-term approach is to be commended.

There are also signs that the outlook could improve. The global oil price has fallen back since the blow to Donald Trump’s authority in the US midterm elections. Brent crude has dropped to about $90 a barrel, down from a peak of close to $120 as recently as the end of October. Growth in Britain’s economy has proven more resilient than feared, helped by the rollout of AI, and unemployment has fallen back in recent months.

Figures show food price inflation was lower than expected in October, at 0.9%, the lowest increase since September 2021. How long this lasts, however, is a moot point, amid expectations of a surge in grocery prices next year linked to higher energy costs and El Niño hitting harvests worldwide.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, suggested last week that the pull back in global energy prices could lead headline inflation to fall short of Threadneedle Street’s forecasts for next year.

However, the longer the Iran war rumbles on, the greater the chance of the Bank raising interest rates to keep inflation in check. Financial markets predict three quarter-point increases next year, adding to the financial squeeze for most households. The first could come as early as next month.

In Britain’s poorest postcodes, a tough winter looms. For Burnham’s No 1 political priority, that is a problem.

Source: The Guardian Politics | Published: 2026-11-22 11:24 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: 'Move on!' Former PMs pile in with advice for Andy Burnham, but will he listen?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Analysis of former Prime Minister's advice with clear reporting and useful vocabulary.

"Move on!" That's Theresa May's frank instruction to Andy Burnham.

She spent years wrangling with the EU to try to forge a decent Brexit deal before being shoved out of her job by her party. Her leadership was broken by Britain's relationship with Brussels. Now she is warning the current resident of No 10 not to risk the same.

In a rare interview, Baroness May - who presided over negotiations with the EU between 2016 and 2019 - told me Burnham ought to respect the public's decision 10 years ago, not "pat them on their head" as if they gave the wrong answer and should have "another go".

And she said she was "aghast" at what he was doing, dangling the possibility of rejoining the EU, warning it would absorb huge amounts of government effort.

"The hours that have to be put in, it's across the whole of government," she said. "It's not just prime ministerial time, [it's] cabinet ministers' time, officials' time, to-ing and fro-ing on those negotiations."

But while some on his own side are very keen to get on with a campaign to rejoin the EU - and the foreign secretary tells me this option is on the table - May is not the only voice urging caution.

Earlier this month David Cameron also said starting a conversation about rejoining would be "long and painful".

And former Prime Minister Sir Tony Blair has told the Sunday Times this weekend that Britain should only rejoin the European Union if it reforms and allows more innovation on technology.

- Theresa May 'aghast' at Burnham's EU plans and says 'Brexit is done'

- Published2 hours ago

Burnham promised a "brainstorm" on stage in Brussels yesterday, so what's his plan?

The prime minister's precise message on Europe is, maybe characteristically, not that precise.

From the by-election platform in the summer where he promised not to reopen old arguments and emphasised he was not proposing the UK considers rejoining, to telling the BBC the country could "go all the way" and go back in, to now the promises of a "national conversation" and "brainstorm" with the EU - his words have varied over time.

No 10 plainly wants to move closer to the EU, even if ministers suggest there really is no end fixed position and so this period of working it out is genuine.

They tell me that, in private, "Andy is pretty clearly where he is publicly - he does think it's a big discussion we have to have as a country, it's a national discussion in the context of the 10 year plan, but also has to involve the Europeans".

In other words, even though he makes no secret that he'd like to be in the EU and wishes we had never left, the prime minister won't conclude whether he'll promise to take the country back in until he has a better idea of what relationship he might get out of the EU - and, perhaps too, how the public responds.

Two quick reminders: Burnham has said it wouldn't happen before another election; and, remember there are elections in Europe too. This whole conversation might be transformed if Marine Le Pen becomes the president of France, or the march of other parties who are suspicious of Brussels continues.

The prime minister's body language in Brussels yesterday, though, and his proclamation that it was a "good day" for Britain, displays happiness in government at what they have achieved so far - closer ties on food exports, energy, and allowing young people to live and work more freely on both sides of the Channel.

Despite a last minute classic spanner in the works with a lack of agreement on tuition fees, the UK side feels positive they didn't back down on that issue yesterday, and the broader deals were concluded anyway.

And despite the protestations from the foreign secretary that the deals will all come into force whatever happens on fees, the government will start the legal processes to turn the agreements into law - although there are still plenty of opportunities for other countries to try and unpick them further down the track.

Of course, politicians' reactions to the deal depend which side they were on in the Brexit debate.

The Lib Dems, SNP, Greens and Plaid Cymru plead the case that it's not far enough. The Conservatives complain it's not fair, for example, that British farmers will have to follow EU rules to make life easier for those who trade with the bloc. Reform scream it's a betrayal of the 2016 vote.

But the feeling in government is the summit was a success and showed the EU will allow the UK to pick and choose where to cooperate, and is willing to listen to what the prime minister wants to do next. It's worth saying just as in any negotiation, the EU might always be up for giving if it receives in return.

Yet as May warns, doing deals with the European Union is simply, a long hard slog.

And one senior Whitehall source cautions the prime minister not to kid himself that an early feel-good factor doesn't mean future haggling would be a doddle: "British prime ministers can be oddly delusional about the EU - they can get seduced by the hope that good relationships with individual leaders will overcome the ideological inertia in Brussels which is overseen by French and German lawyerly high priests and priestesses.

"European leaders might actually be your friends, but they are not the ones in charge of decision-making in Brussels."

And a former negotiator warns that in his "brainstorm," the prime minister might well find the deal he's concluded this week just about rubs up against the limits of what can be done without going for the full-fat option - telling me: "There isn't much more to go with a strategy of incrementally building on the deal before it becomes quite a binary choice."

They add a reality check for any deal-making with the EU: "The EU have a very set way of doing things, that is more about their own unity than about who they are negotiating with."…

item.title: Are you team ‘stuffing’ or ‘dressing’? Why Americans can’t agree on a beloved Thanksgiving side dish
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Thanksgiving is a holiday of strong culinary convictions. Americans argue about whether marshmallows belong on sweet potatoes; whether green bean casserole counts as a vegetable; and, perhaps most insistently, whether that humble side of herbed, cubed bread should be called “stuffing” or “dressing”.

The dish itself is undeniably popular; the 2025 Roots & Recipes report by turkey brand Jennie-O found that 69% of 5,000 surveyed Americans identified it as a favorite side dish. But while some people proudly declare themselves #TeamStuffing or #TeamDressing, the actual distinction between the two is considerably less straightforward.

At first glance, it seems simple enough: if it’s cooked in the bird, it’s stuffing, right? Many members of #TeamDressing will tell you there’s no question for them, saying dressing is just safer (in an informal Facebook poll I conducted regarding people’s preferences, one longtime friend simply responded: “I look at stuffing and say: ‘Not today, food poisoning’”).

The cooking method does matter. “For optimal safety and uniform doneness, cook stuffing separately,” the US Department of Agriculture advises. Stuffing cooked inside the bird can absorb juices containing harmful bacteria, including salmonella. To ensure those bacteria are killed, the agency recommends using a food thermometer to ensure the center of the stuffing reaches at least 165F.

Preparation aside, the lines between camps and terminology are not always clear. Maybe they never have been. Butterball’s Turkey Talk-Line, which has fielded holiday cooking questions since 1981, acknowledges the ambiguity. “And yes, we’ve received countless questions about stuffing/dressing,” said its director, Nicole Johnson. She notes the terms are often used interchangeably, although dressing is more commonly associated with southern casseroles.

I tried to lasso turkey brand Jennie-O into the debate, but a spokesperson politely declined to take sides, explaining the company does not “have an official position on whether consumers should call the dish ‘stuffing’ or ‘dressing’”.

Even classic cookbooks don’t always draw a clear distinction. The 1950 Betty Crocker’s Picture Cook Book offers “stuffing tips” for filling poultry, then advises readers to form the leftover “dressing” into balls to bake individually.

Home cooks and eaters tend to judge on flavor and texture. Ali Whitman, general manager and co-owner of Bev’s Steak in Black Mountain, North Carolina, never cared much for dressing growing up. “I imagined it being some mushy, herby gloop,” she told me.

Not far away, in Blowing Rock, North Carolina, chef Kyle Martin owns Café Violette and Tout Suite Bakery with his wife, Sunshine. He grew up on Stove Top stuffing – a product that promised to remove the bird from the equation altogether when it first appeared in 1972.

Martin bakes his stuffing in a separate pan, finishing it uncovered in a hot oven “to get some textural crunch on the craggy surface”. Some would call it dressing. Martin won’t: “I’ll always call it stuffing, thanks to successful marketing!”

Meanwhile, Sunshine had an “extremely opinionated” grandmother who insisted on stuffing the turkey. Eventually, though, dressing (baked in a separate pan) joined stuffing (cooked inside the bird) at the family table. Both contained finely chopped turkey neck and giblets, and the mixture was never “too soggy”.

My own grandmother also stuffed it in the turkey, but only sometimes. Her recipe for what she called turkey dressing survives in a spiral-bound family cookbook, where a now-vintage droplet stains the line calling for one whole stick of butter. She specified 10 cups of cubed bread, but left it up to readers to intuit how much chicken stock to add.

She was one of those Americans who move between preparation styles with ease. In her neat cursive, she offered two preparation options in the family cookbook: “stuff turkey or bake in 13x9 pan.”

According to my mom, she sometimes took a third approach, forming individual dressing “cakes” that my dad would drown in velvety turkey gravy. Mom wasn’t impressed. “I remember he tried to get me to make them when we first got married,” she texted me recently. “And I said: ‘They’re hockey pucks, not dressing.’” She sent a follow-up buzz: “And it’s funny because I will interchangeably use the words ‘stuffing’ and ‘dressing’ the whole holiday season.”

Keith I had tuna tartare, and a very passable carbonara.

The big beef

Ibbi I’m fairly critical of the amount of integration that we’ve achieved as a country. When my family arrived in 1972, we made the effort and took up the offers that were here, to learn, to improve our English. I’m a firm believer that people get something to get by, but there should be a carrot and a stick. My brother works in a government-funded academy in Manchester mainly for recent refugees, and even though they’ve nothing else to do, they aren’t willing to participate. They drop out, or don’t take it as seriously as they should.

Keith Ibbi is Ugandan Asian, came over as a child and ended up doing quite well in IT, because of the insight and support of a particular teacher in Bolton. His experience was really positive, and he feels the current wave of immigrants are less likely to assimilate. That’s why he believes that immigrants should lose their benefits if they don’t learn English. I think the failure to assimilate is a myth. I trained as a teacher and a lot of my friends are teachers, one in a predominantly Somali school in an area that gets called Londonistan. These kids all speak in east London accents, talk about the same things any kids talk about: who’s going out with who; Love Island. You’ve got European punks with earrings holding hands with girls in hijabs. They’re getting on with their lives; it’s politicians and adults making up these things.

Sharing plate

Ibbi When people talk about wokeism, some of that debate has been created opportunistically, and not even necessarily from within this country. Hostile states will try anything to influence people. Ideas that were previously borderline are now mainstream because they’ve got 1,800 thumbs up on Facebook.

Keith Because I spent a lot of time in Nigeria, I have a lot of friends of colour, and their experience is the same: that race relations were improving in this country until the change of language that came about during Brexit. A lot of immigrants of Ibbi’s generation are fearful because of the more aggressive stance in politics, and I think the response is almost: “Don’t cause a fuss. Don’t allow more boat people in, because you’ll make things worse for people who have settled here.”

For afters

Keith We met in Woking; that’s where the first mosque was built in the UK, and the first Muslim burial ground. Ibbi was very knowledgable about it and regularly attended that mosque.

Ibbi The burial ground, 15 or 20 years ago, was boarded off and looked quite dilapidated. Then the graves were exhumed and the remains removed to the main cemetery, and it was turned into a remembrance garden. It’s a worthy place to visit; I go there often.

Takeaways

Ibbi Obviously, he’s coming from a very leftwing perspective and mine is from the centre – we can’t convince each other. But it’s nice to have that different view. That’s what allows us to get on with each other in this country.

Keith I thought he was a lovely bloke.

Additional reporting: Kitty Drake

Ibbi and Keith ate at Bacaró, Woking, Surrey.

item.title: On a budget? We found 50 gifts under $50 that punch above their weight
item.description:

Why it is here: useful information, clear prose

It’s a classic holiday conundrum. You’ve set aside $50 for a gift but are left wondering: how do I find a quality present within my budget?

To answer this question, we ate a lot of chocolate, tried on many sweaters and asked actual tweens what’s in this year. We ended up with 50 recommendations – including a pretty bamboo box of Japanese skincare, a neck warmer our Alaska-based writer calls her “secret weapon” for the cold and a cushy dog bed that may inspire envy amongst humans.

Kitchen

A Moka pot makes espresso-like, strong coffee at a far lower price. In our global gift guide, the Filter’s Lauren Gould recommended gifting one of the colored Moka pot options for a coffee maker your recipient will want to show off on their stovetop.

This handwash is “made with bread yeast enzymes to neutralize cooking odors and leaves behind sophisticated notes of bergamot and pepper that give off high-end hotel vibes,” writes veteran kitchen writer Emily Farris in our holiday gift guide. Grab this for the amateur chef who cooks with a lot of garlic.

These plastic-free deli containers have a cult following, including Farris, who called them “endlessly versatile, lightweight and durable.”

This quirky candle “can act as anything from a dinner party curio to a kitchen candle that reduces odors,” writes Filter commissioning editor Karen Yuan. Grab this for the person who could use a dash of whimsy this winter.

Home

Diaspora Spice Co’s Sana Javeri Kadri swears by this North Carolina-based ceramics brand. “I have two toddlers, and I’ve had East Fork for about eight years, and I have not had a single break yet,” she told the Filter. “There’s something about the clay compound in East Fork that is hardy to the max.”

Chef and author Mariana Velasquez calls this pot “aA perfect vessel,” for beans, braised short ribs and slow-cooked pork. “But because its shape is so beautiful, I sometimes fill it with flowers – carnations or roses – and it makes a great centerpiece.”

“I covet a good tea towel – though I’m often loath to use them to wipe up messes,” writes Cynthia Greenlee, the Guardian’s deputy editor for special projects. She recommends, among others, the Nasturtium towel for its “Christmas-ey color scheme.”

“I once spotted Kinto’s Sepia Cup and Saucer at a painfully cool cafe in Brooklyn, which was very validating for me, a not particularly cool person who nonetheless appreciates a nice trinket,” writes Yuan. Grab this as an artsy upgrade for a cabinet full of chipped white mugs.

Sleep

After testing a slew of pillows, this pillow was our favorite down-free option, and is especially ideal for bibliophiles. “I think bed readers will enjoy how well the Quince pillow props you up when leaning against your headboard,” writes contributor Jon Chan.

Sleep writer Richard Baguley “continued to sleep better, with fewer interruptions, especially on colder nights,” since adding this weighted blanket into his life.

You don’t need to know what a capybara is to appreciate this adorable creature. You can pop it in your microwave for warmth or your freezer if you struggle with hot flashes or someone in your house refuses to keep the thermostat below 80F.

Baguley adores this satin pillowcase for protecting his skin and hair. The quirky print adds a personal touch for the sleepy Star Wars fans.

Beauty

“When I want to air-dry my hair without dripping water on to my shoulders, I pop on one of these,” says beauty writer Maria Ricapito. These are ideal for the low-maintenance person in your life who can’t be bothered with a blow dryer.

These sheet masks from the popular K-beauty brand Biodance have earned Filter commissioning editor Karen Yuan’s stamp of approval. “Unlike many other masks, you wear this one overnight, when it gradually turns from white to translucent as its collagen and oligo-hyaluronic acid do their work to boost skin elasticity and hydration,” she writes in our guide to the best Korean skincare brands.

“This Japanese skin ritual in a very giftable bamboo box aims to fix dryness and uneven texture,” writes Ricapito in this year’s comprehensive holiday gift guide. The $42 set comes with two serums, a moisturizer and cleansing oil, ideal for skincare fanatics who love testing new products.

Filter contributor Tobey Grumet Segal recommended this multi-tasker makeup product in her guide to the best beauty products for people over 50. “I’ve been known to use it all over my face for a subtle glow, dab it on my cheekbones, use it as a refreshing lip gloss, or even smooth over my eyelids,” she writes. Its many uses make it a safe gift because your recipient can use it as a highlighter, bronzer, blush and more.

Fashion

These were one of my favorite gifts last holiday season. They feel fancier than the oversized T-shirt I’d otherwise wear for bed, and I love the stretchy, soft material.

This artful hair accessory adds a unique touch to your look. It comes in a variety of colors to match your recipient’s style, including a bold cherry red and a marbled pink.

Hear us out: socks aren’t a boring gift. The UK-based brand Rock and Ruby makes cheery knit pairs your recipient can wear with their favorite sneakers or boots.

This past spring we asked stylists about the best wardrobe upgrades. One recommendation from Kelsey Ellstrom, a celebrity stylist who has dressed Zac Efron, Ben Affleck and John Krasinski, was a versatile sweater, also practical for the cold months ahead.

Food

On paper, a tin of fish may not be the obvious gift for the foodie in your life. However, Fishwife’s trendy tuna is amongst our favorite cans after eating our way through over a dozen.

It doesn’t count as a gag gift if it tastes good, right? These little fish look like sardines, but are actually made of milk chocolate.…

item.title: My husband has such bad breath we haven’t kissed in years – but he won’t see a dentist | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: learning value, real-life situation

I’ve got a very upsetting problem in my marriage: my husband has extremely bad breath. We have been together for 20 years and it has always been noticeable, but has got worse in recent years. Recently, he lost a tooth, which he said he knocked out, but I’m pretty certain it fell out due to gum disease.

I have spoken to him about this issue in the past, and even managed to get him to the dentist once, but he became so frightened that he ran out of the surgery. Since then, whenever I mention his breath or the dentist, he becomes very defensive.

I feel embarrassed when he is talking to other people because I know they can smell it too.

We haven’t kissed in years as the thought of kissing makes me feel sick. He often complains that I don’t initiate sex, and asks why I’m not more affectionate towards him. The truth is that his breath puts me off. I don’t want to hurt him by saying this, but it is becoming increasingly difficult for me to feel physically close to him.

I know his fear of the dentist is real. I don’t want to shame him or make him feel unattractive. But I also feel frustrated because I have tried to help him and he simply won’t address it.

How can I talk to him about this?

It’s going to be difficult to talk about this in a way that won’t upset him, but it’s about minimising the impact and, crucially, getting his teeth and gums seen to. I went to two specialists this week, psychotherapist Chris Mills and “gentle” dentist Dr Neera Maini, who works with nervous patients.

Mills was unequivocal: “You are the one person in the world who can and must tell him his breath smells, and it’s also worrying in terms of what it signals about his health. He needs to hear it’s intolerable for you and that for him to dismiss this as irrelevant is wholly unacceptable.” Mills even suggested telling him his breath repels you. I think that’s strong, but as he said, “It leaves no room for doubt.”

“Your husband’s terror is making victims of both of you,” said Mills. “You clearly love him, but do you love yourself enough to no longer let him get away with this?” Mills suggested starting the conversation with something like: “There’s something I need to say to you that I don’t think you’re going to want to hear. It’s important, so please hear me out before you respond. You have bad breath and I need you to see a dentist in order to assess what’s wrong. I know that scares you, and I will support you however I can. Your breath is preventing me from being intimate with you, and that’s a terrible loss. Plus, I’m worried what it might indicate about your health.”

Maini explained: “It takes effort to get a tooth out, so for it to just fall out like that suggests really advanced gum disease.” She also said certain medical conditions and medications can cause a dry mouth and bad breath, but in the first instance “a trip to the dentist is called for”.

To find a gentle dentist near you, do a Google search for “gentle dentists for nervous patients + your area”. Such a practice would make a longer than usual appointment, everything would be done at the patient’s pace and you can sometimes visit the surgery beforehand to get acquainted with the environment if that helps. Then there’s sedation, which isn’t a general anaesthetic, to calm the patient.

I’m afraid there’s no way around this other than you saying something. I wish he hadn’t left it to you to do, but here we are.

Every week, Annalisa Barbieri addresses a personal problem sent in by a reader. If you would like advice from Annalisa, please send your problem to ask.annalisa@theguardian.com. Annalisa regrets she cannot enter into personal correspondence. Submissions are subject to our terms and conditions. The latest series of Annalisa’s podcast is available here.

item.title: This is how we do it: ‘One time my son said: “I heard you having sex. It was disgusting.” That killed the vibe’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: learning value, real-life situation

Anna, 48

I’m a much more active participant sexually now. I used to be more reactive

I’ve learned that sex can get better with age and time. Last year, our children left home to go to university, and that has made a big difference. There were times when the kids were at home and thought they heard Richard and me having sex. I remember my son told us it was a traumatic experience, which made me not want to do it.

I couldn’t be in the moment because I was worried: are the kids going to come home? Will they hear us? Then I felt guilty because we wouldn’t be having as much sex.

I’m a much more active participant sexually now. I used to be more reactive, like it was happening to me, which stemmed from low self-esteem when I was much younger – I wasn’t very sexually experienced and I was very timid. I didn’t initiate sex in our relationship, and that caused tension.

But I’m older now, and I have a little bit more life experience, especially being in a relationship with someone for 23 years. We’ve been to couples’ therapy and have learned how to better manage conflict. In the past, I felt Richard would shut down difficult subjects, which made me feel that I couldn’t ask for things, like support with the kids. I felt that I’d lost a sense of control in the relationship. But we were able to identify the areas where we needed help and built trust. That leads into our sexual relationship.

Now, having time and space in the house where we don’t have to worry is a luxury. It has made sex a lot more fun, as I don’t feel split or divided in my role as a wife and mother. Sex feels a lot more like play. We both enjoy role play and I enjoy Richard taking photographs of me.

Sex with Richard was always positive and pleasurable, but it didn’t feel the same way as it does now. About 90% of the time I was in my conscious brain and overthinking, but now I can much more easily switch into a different space where I’m really not thinking consciously at all. And there’s real pleasure in that escape. On top of the physical pleasure, that in itself is a joy.

Richard, 53

After being intimate with someone for more than two decades, the sexual moments can feel like celebrations

We became empty nesters last year when our kids went to university. Being able to make noise was huge for arousal – we were free of that self-consciousness and fear that the kids would hear us. One time my son told me: “I heard you having sex last night. I thought it was disgusting.” That kind of killed the vibe.

Having the house to ourselves after about 18 years is a lot of fun and I’ve found that I’m very present when we have sex. It is not rushed at all and I want to savour it. It really feels trippy sometimes. That’s partly to do with our kids moving out, but I also think that after being intimate with someone for more than two decades, the sexual moments can feel like celebrations.

But there are also challenges at this new stage in life. I was really marked when our children left. It was the sense of having a role as a parent and then suddenly we’re just left with memories and photos. I felt quite emotional for a few months, and still do at times. In some way that does affect our intimacy because of the sadness of our kids reaching a certain age and our family dynamic changing.

I’ve always been the one to suggest we have sex. Anna and I have a different rhythm, which has sometimes created a wedge between us in terms of sexual intimacy. If she’s ever concerned about something else in life our intimate life hits pause and we won’t be having sex. It’s tough because there’s an estrangement there.

I get afraid when there are these breaks in our intimacy and we start feeling like roommates. It scares Anna, too. What I’ve learned over time is to communicate more so we don’t feel distanced. That loneliness physically hurts. So we make sure to have a moment together, even if it’s not sex. I could go out for a walk by myself, but I want to share it with her.

Names have been changed
